Chapter-by-chapter guide

Designing data-intensive applications

Reliable, scalable aur maintainable systems ke peeche ke bade ideas: data kaise store hota hai, copy hota hai, split hota hai, transactions mein use hota hai aur process hota hai. Sab kuch aasaan language mein, book ke examples aur diagrams ke saath.

Yeh Martin Kleppmann ki book Designing Data-Intensive Applications (O’Reilly, first edition, March 2017) par based hai.

12 chapters772 min ka readPreface se glossary tak, kuch skip nahi kiya

Yeh readers ke liye likhi gayi ek independent retelling hai, original book nahi. Isme har chapter order mein cover hota hai, book ke apne examples rakhe gaye hain, aur sirf chhoti lines quote ki gayi hain. Diagrams shuru se dobara banaye gaye hain. Kleppmann ki writing kisi bhi summary se zyada careful aur detailed hai, isliye book bhi zaroor padho.

Front matter

Preface

Seedhi baat: data store aur process karne ke tools bahut jaldi badalte hain, lekin unke peeche ke principles zyada time tak chalte hain. Tum woh principles seekh lo, toh kisi bhi tool ko judge kar sakte ho, samajh sakte ho ki woh kahan fit hota hai, aur uski pitfalls pehle hi pakad sakte ho.

Agar tumne pichhle kuch saalon mein software mein kaam kiya hai, khaaskar servers aur backend par, toh tumne data ke baare mein buzzwords ki baarish zaroor dekhi hogi. Preface mein NoSQL, Big Data, web-scale, sharding, eventual consistency, ACID, CAP theorem, cloud services, MapReduce aur real-time ka naam aata hai. Inmein se kaafi cheezein book mein aage dobara aayengi. Chalo, inmein se kuch ka matlab simple words mein dekhte hain:

  • NoSQL un naye database types ka ek loose label hai jo SQL databases ke traditional table model ko follow nahi karte.
  • Sharding ka matlab hai ek bade dataset ko parts mein todna, jo alag-alag machines par rehte hain.
  • Eventual consistency ka matlab hai ki data ki copies kuch der ke liye ek-doosre se alag ho sakti hain, lekin time ke saath sab settle ho jaati hain.
  • ACID un guarantees ka set hai jo database transactions ke liye deta hai. Transaction matlab changes ka ek group, jo ya toh saare succeed honge ya saare fail.
  • CAP theorem kehta hai ki distributed system (jo kai machines par phaila hota hai) mein network split hone par consistency aur availability dono ki poori guarantee nahi di ja sakti.
  • MapReduce bahut saari machines par data ke bade batches process karne ka ek tarika hai.

Pichhle ek dashak mein databases mein, distributed systems mein, aur unke upar applications banane ke tareeke mein kaafi development hua hai. Is development ke peeche kai forces hain. Preface chhe forces ginata hai:

  • Google, Yahoo!, Amazon, Facebook, LinkedIn, Microsoft aur Twitter jaisi internet companies bahut bada data aur traffic handle karti hain. Us scale ke liye unhein naye tools banane pade.
  • Businesses ko agile hona padta hai. Matlab ideas ko sasti tarah test karna, naye market insights par jaldi response dena, aur development cycles chhote aur data models flexible rakhna.
  • Ab commercial ya in-house software ke bajaay free aur open source software ko aksar prefer kiya jaata hai.
  • CPU clock speeds mushkil se badh rahi hain, par multi-core processors (jisme kai processing cores hote hain) ab standard hain, aur networks bhi tez ho rahe hain. Isliye parallelism, yani ek saath kai kaam karna, sirf badhega.
  • Infrastructure as a service (IaaS) ki wajah se, jaise Amazon Web Services, ab ek chhoti team bhi kai machines aur regions mein phaile systems bana sakti hai.
  • Ab bahut saari services se umeed hoti hai ki woh highly available hongi, yani up rahengi. Lamba downtime, chahe outage se ho ya maintenance se, dheere-dheere kam acceptable hota ja raha hai.

Preface kisi application ko data-intensive kehta hai jab data hi uska main challenge ho. Challenge data ki quantity ho sakti hai, uski complexity, ya yeh ki woh kitni tezi se change hota hai. Iska ulta hai compute-intensive kaam, jahan processor ki raw speed bottleneck hoti hai. Data-intensive applications possible ki limits ko push kar rahi hain, aur isme in naye technologies ka use karti hain.

Jo tools aise applications ko data store aur process karne mein help karte hain, woh bhi badal rahe hain. NoSQL databases par kaafi attention jaata hai. Lekin message queues (jahan program ka ek hissa messages bhejta hai aur doosra hissa unhein baad mein handle karta hai), caches, search indexes, aur batch aur stream processing ke frameworks bhi utne hi important hain. Kai applications inmein se kuch ka combination use karti hain.

Buzzwords naye possibilities ke liye enthusiasm ki nishaani hain, aur yeh achhi baat hai. Lekin engineers aur architects ko har technology aur uske trade-offs ki precise, technically sahi samajh bhi chahiye. Woh samajh paane ke liye buzzwords se kaafi gehra jaana padta hai.

Asli idea

Tools aate-jaate rehte hain, lekin unke peeche ke principles aur trade-offs sach rehte hain, chahe tum koi bhi version use karo. Woh seekh lein, toh har naya tool place karna aasaan ho jaata hai.

Book ka goal hai ki data process aur store karne ke alag-alag, tezi se badalte tools ke beech tumhe raasta dikhaye. Yeh kisi ek tool ka tutorial nahi hai, aur theory ki sookhi textbook bhi nahi hai. Yeh successful data systems ko dekhti hai, yani un technologies ko jo kai popular applications ke neeche chalti hain aur jinhein roz scale, speed aur reliability ki demands poori karni padti hain. Yeh unke internals aur key algorithms mein jaati hai, aur sirf yeh nahi poochti ki har cheez kaise kaam karti hai, balki yeh bhi ki woh waise kyun kaam karti hai.

Padhne ke baad tum decide kar paaoge ki kaun si technology kis purpose ke liye sahi hai, aur dekh paaoge ki tools milkar ek achhi application ki foundation kaise bante ho. Tum apna storage engine (database ka woh hissa jo data ko disk par lay out karta hai) scratch se banane ke liye ready nahi honge, aur iski zaroorat bhi kam hi padti hai. Lekin tum yeh zaroor samjhoge ki tumhare systems under the hood kya karte ho, taaki tum unke behavior ke baare mein reason kar sako, achhe design decisions le sakein, aur problems track down kar sakein.

Yeh book kise padhni chahiye?

Agar tum aisi applications banate ho jinme data store ya process karne ke liye server ya backend hai, aur woh applications internet use karti ho (jaise web applications, mobile apps, ya internet se connected sensors), toh yeh book tumhare liye hai.

Yeh software engineers, software architects aur un technical managers ke liye likhi gayi hai jinhein code karna pasand hai. Yeh khaaskar tab kaam aati hai jab tum apne systems ke architecture ke decisions lete ho, jaise kisi problem ke liye tools chunna aur yeh sochna ki unhein kaise apply karo. Agar tools chunne ka tumhare paas choice nahi bhi hai, toh bhi book tumhe unki strengths aur weaknesses samajhne mein help karegi.

Tumhe web applications ya network services banane ka kuch experience hona chahiye, aur relational databases aur SQL se familiar hona chahiye. Non-relational databases aur doosre data tools ka experience bonus hai, par zaroori nahi. TCP aur HTTP jaise network protocols ki general samajh help karti hai. Tum kaun si programming language ya framework use karte ho, isse koi fark nahi padta.

Yeh book tumhare kaam aayegi agar inmein se koi bhi baat sach hai:

  • Tum seekhna chahte ho ki data systems ko scalable kaise banayein, jaise ki millions of users wali web ya mobile apps ko support karne ke liye.
  • Tumhe applications ko highly available banana hai, downtime minimize karke, aur operationally robust rakhna hai.
  • Tum systems ko long run mein maintain karna aasaan banana chahte ho, tab bhi jab woh grow karo aur requirements aur technologies badalti raho.
  • Tumhe cheezein kaise kaam karti hain, is baare mein natural curiosity hai, aur tum jaanna chahte ho ki bade websites aur online services ke andar kya chalta hai. Book kai databases aur data processing systems ke internals todkar samjhati hai.

Kabhi-kabhi log kehte hain, “Tum Google ya Amazon nahi ho. Scale ki chinta chhodo aur bas relational database use karo.” Preface isse kuch hadd tak sehmat hai. Jis scale ki zaroorat nahi, uske liye build karna wasted effort hai, aur isse tum ek inflexible design mein phans bhi sakte ho. Yeh premature optimization ka ek roop hai, matlab speed ya scale ki problem ko tab solve karna jab woh abhi aayi hi nahi.

Lekin kaam ke liye sahi tool chunna phir bhi matter karta hai, aur har technology ki apni strengths aur weaknesses hain. Relational databases important hain, par data handle karne ka aakhri jawab woh nahi hain.

Dhyaan do

Jis scale ki zaroorat nahi, uske liye build mat karo, kyunki woh effort waste jaata hai aur tumhe rigid design mein lock kar sakta hai. Phir bhi, har tool ko uski strengths aur weaknesses dhyaan mein rakhkar chunein.

Book ka scope

Book specific software packages ya APIs (woh interfaces jinse programs aapas mein baat karte hain) install ya use karne ke step-by-step instructions nahi deti. Unke liye documentation pehle se kaafi hai. Iske bajaay, yeh un principles aur trade-offs ki baat karti hai jo data systems ke liye fundamental hain, aur un alag design decisions ki jo alag products lete hain.

Book mainly data systems ke architecture ko dekhti hai, aur yeh ki unhein jodkar data-intensive applications kaise banti hain. Deployment, operations, security, management aur doosre areas cover karne ki jagah usme nahi hai. Preface kehta hai ki yeh complex aur important topics hain, aur unhein side notes ki tarah cover karna unke saath nainsaafi hogi. Unke liye alag books honi chahiye.

Book Big Data term se bhi bachti hai. Preface ke hisaab se yeh term itna overused aur underdefined hai ki serious engineering baat-cheet mein kaam ka nahi. Iske bajaay book zyada clear terms use karti hai, jaise single-node versus distributed systems, ya online versus offline (batch) processing systems.

Book ka jhukaav free aur open source software (FOSS) ki taraf hai. Source code padhna, badalna aur chalana yeh detail mein samajhne ka achha tarika hai ki koi cheez kaise kaam karti hai. Open platforms vendor lock-in ka risk bhi kam karte hain, yani kisi ek company ke product mein phans jaane ka risk. Jahan sahi lage, wahan book proprietary software ki bhi baat karti hai: closed-source products, service ki tarah bechha jaane wala software, aur in-house systems jinke baare mein companies ne literature mein likha hai par kabhi release nahi kiya.

Book ka outline

Book teen parts mein baanti gayi hai.

  • Part I: fundamental ideas jo data-intensive applications ke design ki buniyaad hain.
    • Chapter 1 poochta hai ki hum kya achieve karna chahte hain: reliability, scalability aur maintainability. Isme yeh hai ki har ek ke baare mein kaise sochein aur use kaise achieve karein.
    • Chapter 2 kai data models aur query languages compare karta hai, aur dikhata hai ki kaun si kis situation ke liye sahi hai.
    • Chapter 3 storage engines cover karta hai, jo data ko disk par aise arrange karte hain ki baad mein use efficiently dhoondha ja sake.
    • Chapter 4 data encoding (jise serialization bhi kehte hain) ke formats cover karta hai, aur yeh ki time ke saath schemas kaise change hote hain.
  • Part II: distributed data. Yeh ek machine par rakhe data se kai machines par phaile data ki taraf jaata hai. Scalability ke liye aksar iski zaroorat padti hai, lekin isse apni unique challenges aati hain.
    • Chapter 5 replication cover karta hai, yani data ki copies kai machines par rakhna.
    • Chapter 6 partitioning cover karta hai, jise sharding bhi kehte hain.
    • Chapter 7 transactions cover karta hai.
    • Chapter 8 distributed systems mein aane wali problems cover karta hai.
    • Chapter 9 cover karta hai ki distributed system mein consistency aur consensus (kai machines ko ek baat par agree karwana) achieve karne ke liye kya karna padta hai.
  • Part III: derived data. Yeh un systems ko cover karta hai jo kuch datasets doosre datasets se banate hain. Derived data aksar heterogeneous systems mein dikhta hai, matlab aise systems jo kai alag tools se bane hote hain. Jab koi ek database sab kuch achhe se nahi karta, tab applications kai databases, caches, indexes aur aur bhi cheezein integrate karti hain.
    • Chapter 10 derived data ke liye batch processing approach se shuru hota hai.
    • Chapter 11 uske upar stream processing build karta hai.
    • Chapter 12 sab kuch ek saath jodta hai aur batata hai ki aage reliable, scalable aur maintainable applications kaise banayein.

References aur aage padhne ke liye

Book jo kuch discuss karti hai, uska zyadatar hissa pehle kahin aur kaha ja chuka hai, conference talks, research papers, blog posts, code, mailing lists aur engineering folklore mein. Book un ideas ko summarize karti hai aur poore time original literature ki taraf point karti hai. Har chapter ke end ke references gehra jaane ke liye achhi jagah hain, aur zyadatar online free available hain.

Ebook editions online resources ke full text ke links deti hain, aur publication ke time links check kiye gaye the. Lekin links aksar toot jaate hain. Agar koi link toot jaye, ya tumhare paas print copy ho, toh reference ko naam se search karo. Academic papers ke liye Google Scholar mein title search karein, wahan open-access PDF files mil jaati hain. Authors saare references, up-to-date links ke saath, github.com/ept/ddia-references par bhi rakhte hain.

O’Reilly Safari

Preface mein publisher, O’Reilly Media, ki taraf se Safari ke baare mein ek chhota note hai. Safari ek membership platform hai jisme 250 se zyada publishers ki books, videos, tutorials aur playlists hain. Yeh publisher ki information hai, book ke subject ka hissa nahi.

Hum se kaise contact karein

Try karo

Is preface se ek buzzword chunein, jaise sharding ya ACID. Likho ki tumhare hisaab se woh kaun si problem solve karta hai, aur ek cost jo tum uske saath expect karte ho. Woh note rakh lein, aur jab partitioning (Chapter 6) ya transactions (Chapter 7) ka chapter aaye, toh use book ke saath compare karein.

Acknowledgments, jo book mein preface ke baad aate hain, un reviewers aur collaborators ko thank karte hain jinhone isme help ki. Unhein yahan dobara nahi sunaya gaya hai.

Part I

Data Systems ki Foundations

Chapters 1 se 4 mein woh ideas hain jo har data system par apply hote hain, reliability aur scaling se lekar data models, storage engines aur data encoding tak.

Yeh Kleppmann ke part introduction ka paraphrase hai: pehle chaar chapters tab bhi kaam ke hain jab system ek machine par chale ya kai machines par, aur Part II mein distributed systems ki baat shuru hoti hai.

Part I · Chapter 1

Reliable, Scalable aur Maintainable Applications

Seedhi baat: ek achha data system tab bhi sahi chalta rehta hai jab cheezein galat ho jaati hain. Woh badhte load ko sambhal leta hai, aur logon ke liye chalana aur badalna aasaan rehta hai. Har goal ki apni price hai, free mein kuch nahi milta.

Aajkal ki zyadatar applications compute-intensive nahi, data-intensive hoti hain. Compute-intensive program ko processor ki speed rokti hai. Data-intensive application ko rokta hai data ka size, uski complexity, aur woh kitni tezi se badalta hai. Raw CPU power shayad hi kabhi asli limit hoti hai.

Aisi applications aam taur par kuch standard building blocks se banti hain, aur har block ek common kaam karta hai:

  • Database data store karta hai, taaki application (ya koi doosri application) use baad mein dobara dhoondh sake.
  • Cache kisi expensive operation ka result yaad rakhta hai, taaki agla read tez ho.
  • Search index se users keyword se data dhoondh sakte hain ya alag-alag tarah se filter kar sakte hain.
  • Stream processing ek message doosre process ko bhej deta hai jo use asynchronously handle karta hai, yani sender ko wait nahi karna padta.
  • Batch processing jama hue bade data ko periodically crunch karta hai.

Agar yeh sab bahut obvious lag raha hai, toh wajah yeh hai ki data systems ka idea itna successful raha hai. Naya storage engine (database ka woh hissa jo data ko disk par lay out karta hai) scratch se shayad hi koi likhta hai. Is kaam ke liye database bilkul achha tool hai.

Lekin real life itni simple nahi hoti. Alag-alag strengths wale kaafi database systems hain, kyunki applications ki zarooratein alag hoti hain. Caching ke bhi kai approaches hain, aur search indexes banane ke bhi kai tarike hain. Engineer ko phir bhi apne task ke hisaab se tools aur approaches chunne padte hain. Aur jab ek tool akela poora kaam nahi kar sakta, tab kai tools ko combine karna mushkil ho sakta hai.

Yeh chapter basics se shuru hota hai. Hum define karte hain ki reliable, scalable aur maintainable data systems ka matlab kya hai, har goal ke baare mein sochne ke kuch tarike dekhte hain, aur woh vocabulary set karte hain jo aage ke chapters use karenge. Aage ke chapters layer-by-layer un design decisions se guzarte hain jo data-intensive application banate waqt aate hain.

Data systems ke baare mein sochna

Hum aam taur par databases, queues aur caches ko alag-alag categories mein rakhte hain. Database aur message queue (ek system jismein program ka ek hissa messages daalta hai aur doosra unhe nikaal kar process karta hai) dono kuch der ke liye data hold karte hain. Phir bhi unke access patterns bahut alag hain. Matlab performance characteristics alag hain, aur isliye implementations bhi bahut alag hain.

Toh in sab ko data systems ke ek hi umbrella term mein kyun daalna? Book iske do reasons deti hai.

Pehla reason yeh hai ki categories ke beech ki boundaries dhundhli ho rahi hain. Kuch datastores message queue ki tarah bhi use hote hain, jaise Redis. Kuch message queues mein database jaisi durability hoti hai (yani yeh promise ki likha hua data lost nahi hoga), jaise Apache Kafka. Purane labels ab theek se fit nahi hote.

Doosra reason yeh hai ki ab kai applications ki requirements ek single tool poori nahi kar sakta. Kaam ko aise tasks mein tod diya jaata hai jo ek tool efficiently kar sake, aur application code in tools ko aapas mein jod deta hai. Jaise, ek team main database ke saath application-managed cache (Memcached jaisa server, jo data ko memory mein rakhta hai taaki reads tez hon) ya full-text search server (jaise Elasticsearch ya Solr) chala sakti hai. Aise setup mein caches aur indexes ko main database ke saath sync mein rakhna application code ki zimmedari hoti hai.

Jab tum ek service dene ke liye kai tools combine karte ho, toh service ka interface, yani application programming interface (API), aam taur par clients se yeh details chhupa leta hai. Result ek naya, special-purpose data system hota hai jo chhote general-purpose parts se bana hai. Yeh composite system kuch guarantees de sakta hai, jaise ki writes par cache sahi tarah update ya invalidate ho jaata hai (stale hone par hata diya jaata hai), taaki bahar ke clients ko hamesha consistent results dikhein. Book ka point yeh hai ki jab tum yeh karte ho, toh tum sirf application developer nahi rehte. Tum data system designer bhi ban jaate ho.

Data system design karte waqt mushkil sawaal uthte hain. System ke parts fail ho jaayein, toh data ko correct aur complete kaise rakhein? Jab kuch parts degraded hon, tab clients ke liye performance steady kaise rakhein? Zyada load handle karne ke liye scale up kaise karein? Ek achha API kaisa dikhna chahiye? Aur bhi factors design ko shape karte hain: team ke skills aur experience, purane systems par dependencies, delivery ke liye available time, organization kitna risk accept karti hai, aur legal rules. Yeh factors situation par kaafi depend karte hain.

Book teen concerns par focus karti hai jo zyadatar software systems mein matter karte hain:

  • Reliability: cheezein galat hone par bhi system sahi chalta rehta hai, expected level ki performance ke saath.
  • Scalability: system jab data, traffic ya complexity mein badhta hai, toh us growth se nipatne ke reasonable tarike hote hain.
  • Maintainability: saalon tak kai alag-alag log system par kaam karte hain, aur sab productively kaam kar paate hain.

Yeh words aksar loosely use hote hain, isliye chapter ka baaki hissa inhe zyada carefully define karta hai.

Reliability

Reliable ka matlab kya hai, iska andaaza lagbhag sabko hota hai. Software ke liye typical expectations yeh hoti hain:

  • Application woh function perform karti hai jo user ne expect kiya tha.
  • User se galti ho jaaye ya woh software ko unexpected tarike se use kare, toh bhi woh tolerate kar leti hai.
  • Expected load aur data volume mein, use case ke liye performance kaafi achhi hai.
  • System unauthorized access aur abuse ko rokta hai.

Yeh sab milakar kuch aisa banta hai: cheezein galat hone par bhi sahi kaam karte rehna.

Jo cheezein galat hoti hain, unhe faults kehte hain. Jo system faults ko pehle se soch kar unhe handle karta hai, use fault-tolerant ya resilient kehte hain. Kleppmann kehte hain ki fault-tolerant term thoda misleading hai. Isse lagta hai ki system ko har possible fault ke liye tolerant banaya ja sakta hai, aur yeh realistic nahi hai. Agar poori duniya, har server ke saath, black hole mein chali jaaye, toh bachne ka ek hi tarika space mein hosting hoga, aur aisa budget koi approve nahi karega. Isliye sirf kuch khaas kisam ke faults ko tolerate karne ki baat karna hi sahi hai.

Fault aam taur par system ka ek component hota hai jo apni specification (tay kiya hua behavior) se hat jaata hai. Failure woh hai jab poora system user ko zaroori service dena band kar deta hai. Dono alag hain. Agar system ko fault absorb karne ke liye banaya gaya hai, toh fault bina failure ke bhi ho sakta hai. Fault ki probability kabhi zero nahi ho sakti, isliye book suggest karti hai ki aise fault-tolerance mechanisms design karein jo faults ko failures mein badalne se rokein. Aage ke chapters mein unreliable parts se reliable systems banane ke kai techniques aayenge.

Sunne mein ajeeb lagega, lekin fault-tolerant system ko intentionally faults create karne se fayda ho sakta hai. Jaise, tum bina warning ke random individual processes ko kill kar sakte ho. Kai critical bugs kharab error handling se aate hain. Agar tum deliberately faults trigger karo, toh fault-handling code hamesha chalta rehta hai, aur tumhe zyada bharosa hota hai ki asli fault aane par bhi woh kaam karega. Netflix ka Chaos Monkey is approach ka example hai.

Kabhi-kabhi ilaaj se behtar rokthaam hoti hai. Security ek example hai. Agar attacker pehle hi andar aa chuka hai aur sensitive data padh chuka hai, toh use undo nahi kiya ja sakta. Lekin book zyadatar un faults ki baat karti hai jinka ilaaj ho sakta hai.

Hardware Faults

Jab log sochte hain ki systems fail kyun hote hain, toh sabse pehle hardware yaad aata hai. Hard disks crash hoti hain, memory kharab ho jaati hai, power grid mein blackout ho jaata hai, aur koi galat network cable nikaal deta hai. Jisne bhi bada datacenter chalaya hai, woh jaanta hai ki bahut saari machines hon toh yeh sab hamesha hota rehta hai.

Hard disks ka mean time to failure (MTTF, yani expected average lifetime) lagbhag 10 se 50 saal hota hai. Yeh sunne mein tasalli deta hai, jab tak tum hisaab na lagao. 10,000 disks wale storage cluster par, book ke hisaab se roz lagbhag ek disk marne ki ummeed rakhni chahiye.

Pehla aam response yeh hai ki har hardware component mein redundancy add ki jaaye, yani ek spare rakha jaaye jo kaam sambhal sake. Disks ko RAID configuration mein set kiya ja sakta hai (kai disks ek saath jodi jaati hain taaki ek fail ho toh data na khoye). Servers mein do power supplies ho sakti hain aur aise CPUs jo machine chalte hue badle ja sakte hain. Datacenters mein backup power ke liye batteries aur diesel generators ho sakte hain. Jab ek part mar jaata hai, toh uska spare kaam sambhal leta hai aur kharab part replace hota hai. Redundancy har hardware problem ko failure banne se nahi rok sakti, lekin yeh achhi tarah samjhi hui cheez hai, aur aksar ek machine ko saalon tak bina interruption ke chalaye rakh sakti hai.

Kuch samay pehle tak yeh zyadatar applications ke liye kaafi tha. Agar tum backup ko naye machine par jaldi restore kar sakte the, toh failure ke baad downtime zyadatar applications ke liye disaster nahi tha. Sirf kuch applications ko, jahan high availability zaroori thi, multi-machine redundancy chahiye thi.

Ab yeh badal gaya hai. Data volumes aur computing demands badh gaye hain, isliye zyada applications bahut saari machines par chalti hain. Zyada machines ka matlab hai hardware faults ki rate zyada. Amazon Web Services (AWS) jaise cloud platforms par virtual machines ka bina warning ke unavailable ho jaana bhi kaafi common hai. Yeh platforms kisi ek machine ki reliability se zyada flexibility aur elasticity (capacity ko jaldi add ya remove karne ki ability) ko favor karne ke liye design kiye gaye hain.

Isi wajah se ab aise systems ki taraf move ho raha hai jo poori machine ke loss ko survive kar sakein, aur woh hardware redundancy ki jagah ya uske saath software fault-tolerance techniques use karte hain. Aise systems operations ko bhi aasaan banate hain. Single-server system ko reboot ke liye planned downtime chahiye, jaise operating system ke security patches lagane ke liye. Jo system machine failure tolerate karta hai, use ek time par ek node (cluster ki ek machine) patch kiya ja sakta hai, aur baaki users ko serve karte rehte hain. Ise rolling upgrade kehte hain, aur Chapter 4 mein iske baare mein aur detail hai.

Software Errors

Hum aam taur par hardware faults ko random aur independent maante hain. Ek machine ki disk fail hone ka matlab yeh nahi ki doosri machine ki disk bhi jaldi fail hogi. Kamzor kadiyan ho sakti hain, jaise ek rack ke kai servers ka ek saath bahut garam ho jaana, lekin aam taur par bahut saare hardware parts ke ek hi samay par fail hone ki possibility kam hoti hai.

Software faults alag hote hain. Yeh systematic errors hain, yani aise bugs jo jahan bhi wahi condition aaye, wahan ek hi tarah se dikhte hain. Inhe pehle se anticipate karna zyada mushkil hai, aur kyunki yeh nodes ke beech correlated hote hain, isliye random hardware faults se kaafi zyada failures karte hain. Kuch examples:

  • Ek bug jo har application server instance ko crash kar deta hai jab use koi khaas bad input milta hai. Book mein 30 June 2012 ko add hue leap second ka example hai. Linux kernel ke ek bug ki wajah se kai applications ek hi moment par hang ho gayi thi.
  • Ek runaway process jo koi shared resource khatam kar deta hai, jaise CPU time, memory, disk space ya network bandwidth.
  • Jis service par system depend karta hai, woh slow ho jaati hai, respond karna band kar deti hai, ya corrupted responses return karne lagti hai.
  • Cascading failures, jahan ek component ka chhota fault doosre component mein fault trigger karta hai, aur woh aage aur faults trigger karta hai.

In faults ke peeche ke bugs aksar bahut der tak dormant rehte hain. Woh tabhi dikhte hain jab kuch unusual circumstances ek saath aa jaate hain. Aam taur par software apne environment ke baare mein koi assumption bana rakha hota hai. Yeh assumption zyadatar waqt sach hoti hai, lekin kisi na kisi wajah se aakhir mein sach nahi rehti.

Software ke systematic faults ka koi quick fix nahi hai. Book kuch cheezein batati hai jo madad karti hain: system ke assumptions aur interactions ke baare mein dhyaan se sochna, thoroughly test karna, processes ko ek-doosre se isolate karna, processes ko crash aur restart hone dena, aur production mein behavior ko measure, monitor aur analyze karna. System chalte waqt khud ko check bhi kar sakta hai. Agar use koi guarantee deni hai, jaise ki queue se nikalne wale messages ki ginti andar jaane wale messages ke barabar hai, toh woh ise continuously verify kar sakta hai aur numbers match na hone par alert raise kar sakta hai.

Human Errors

Software insaan design aur build karte hain, aur insaan hi use chalate hain. Sabse achhe irade wale log bhi unreliable hote hain. Book ek study cite karti hai jo bade internet services par thi. Usmein paaya gaya ki operators ki configuration errors outages ki sabse badi wajah thi. Servers ya network ke hardware faults sirf 10 se 25 percent outages mein shaamil the.

Jab system par kaam karne wale log hi reliable nahi hain, toh system ko reliable kaise banayein? Kleppmann kai approaches ko combine karne ka suggestion dete hain.

  • Galtiyan karna mushkil banao. Achhe design ki abstractions, APIs aur admin tools sahi kaam ko aasaan aur galat kaam ko mushkil bana dete hain. Lekin agar interfaces bahut restrictive hon, toh log unka workaround nikaal lete hain, aur fayda khatam ho jaata hai. Yeh balance sahi karna tricky hai.
  • Jahan log galti karte hain aur jahan galti failure banti hai, un jagahon ko alag rakho. Fully featured sandbox environments do jo production nahi hain. Phir log realistic data ke saath explore aur experiment kar sakte hain, bina real users ko affect kiye.
  • Har level par test karo. Isme unit tests, poore system ke integration tests aur manual tests shaamil hain. Automated testing bahut use hoti hai, aur rare corner cases cover karne mein khaas taur par achhi hai.
  • Recovery quick aur aasaan banao. Configuration changes ko jaldi roll back karo. Naya code dheere-dheere release karo, taaki koi unexpected bug sirf chhote group of users ko hit kare. Purani computation galat nikle toh data dobara compute karne ke tools do.
  • Detail mein monitor karo. Performance metrics aur error rates par nazar rakho. Doosri engineering fields ise telemetry kehti hain. Rocket jab zameen chhod deta hai, toh telemetry se hi use track karte hain aur failure samajhte hain. Monitoring early warnings deti hai aur check karti hai ki assumptions abhi bhi sahi hain ya nahi, aur kisi problem ko diagnose karte waqt metrics bahut kaam aate hain.
  • Achha management aur training. Kleppmann ise picture ka ek important hissa maante hain, lekin yeh book ke scope se bahar hai.

Reliability kitni important hai?

Reliability sirf nuclear power stations aur air traffic control software ke liye nahi hai. Aam business applications ko bhi sahi chalna chahiye. Unmein bugs se productivity ka nuksaan hota hai, aur reports mein galat figures se legal risk ban sakta hai. E-commerce site ke outages se lost revenue aur kharab reputation ke roop mein bahut bada nuksaan ho sakta hai.

Example

Book kehti hai ki socho ek parent apne bachchon ki har photo aur video tumhari photo application mein store karta hai. Agar woh database achanak corrupt ho jaaye, toh unhe kaisa lagega? Kya unhe pata hoga ki backup se restore kaise karna hai? Company ke liye application shayad ek noncritical product ho, lekin us parent ke liye woh critical hai.

Kabhi-kabhi paise bachane ke liye reliability ko sacrifice kiya ja sakta hai. Jo team abhi tak prove nahi hui market ke liye prototype bana rahi hai, woh development cost kam karne ke liye zyada risk le sakti hai. Bahut patli profit margin wali service operating cost kam karne ke liye zyada risk le sakti hai. Kleppmann ki salah yeh hai ki corners cut karte waqt tum puri tarah aware raho.

Asli idea

Reliability ka matlab hai cheezein galat hone par bhi sahi kaam karte rehna. Hardware, software aur logon, teeno se faults ki ummeed rakhein, aur design aise karein ki faults failures na ban jaayein.

Scalability

Aaj jo system reliably chal raha hai, zaroori nahi ki kal bhi chalega. Performance girne ki ek common wajah hai load ka badhna. Ho sakta hai system 10,000 concurrent users (jo log ek hi time par use kar rahe hain) se 100,000 par pahunch gaya ho, ya 1 million se 10 million par. Ya phir ab woh pehle se kaafi zyada data process kar raha ho.

Scalability ka matlab hai ki system badhe hue load ko kitni achhi tarah handle kar paata hai. Yeh simple haan ya na wali cheez nahi hai. "X scalable hai" ya "Y scale nahi karta" kehne ka kaafi kam matlab hota hai. Better sawaal yeh hai: agar system ek particular tarike se grow kare, toh hamare paas kya options hain, aur extra load handle karne ke liye computing resources kaise add karein?

Load ko describe karna

Growth ki baat karne se pehle current load ko describe karne ka ek chhota aur precise tarika chahiye. Book in few numbers ko load parameters kehti hai. Sahi parameter architecture par depend karta hai. Yeh web server par requests per second ho sakta hai, database mein reads aur writes ka ratio, chat room mein ek saath active logon ki count, ya cache ka hit rate (yani kitne lookups ka jawab cache de paata hai). Yeh bhi decide karna padta hai ki average case sabse zyada matter karta hai, ya kuch extreme cases hi bottleneck ban rahe hain.

Book Twitter ka example leti hai, aur data woh hai jo Twitter ne November 2012 mein publish kiya tha. Twitter ke do main operations yeh the:

  • Post tweet: user apne followers ko ek naya message publish karta hai. Yeh average 4.6k requests per second tha, aur peak par 12k se zyada.
  • Home timeline: user un logon ke tweets dekhta hai jinhe woh follow karta hai. Yeh 300k requests per second tha.

Tweet post karne ka peak rate 12,000 writes per second hai, aur isse handle karna kaafi aasaan hota. Twitter ki asli scaling problem tweets ki count nahi hai. Asli problem fan-out hai, yani har user bahut logon ko follow karta hai aur bahut log use follow karte hain. Yeh term electronics se aaya hai, jahan yeh count karta hai ki ek output ko kitne inputs drive karne padte hain. Transaction processing systems mein iska matlab hai ki ek incoming request serve karne ke liye tumhe doosre services ko kitni requests bhejni padti hain. Yahan iska matlab hai ki ek tweet ko kitni timelines tak pahunchna hai.

In do operations ko build karne ke broadly do tarike hain.

Example

Approach 1: read time par kaam karo. Tweet post karna bas use ek global collection of tweets mein insert kar dena hai. Jab user apni home timeline maangta hai, toh system yeh steps follow karta hai:

  1. Us user ke follow kiye hue sabhi logon ko dhoondo.
  2. Un sab logon ke likhe hue saare tweets find karo.
  3. Sabko ek list mein merge karo, time ke hisaab se sorted.

Relational database mein book ke mutabiq read kuch aisi query ho sakti hai:

SELECT tweets.*, users.*
FROM tweets
JOIN users ON tweets.sender_id = users.id
JOIN follows ON follows.followee_id = users.id
WHERE follows.follower_id = current_user
Example

Approach 2: write time par kaam karo. System har user ki home timeline ke liye ek cache rakhta hai, jo us user ke liye tweets ke mailbox jaisa kaam karta hai. Jab koi user tweet post karta hai, toh system yeh steps follow karta hai:

  1. Us user ko follow karne wale sabhi logon ko dhoondo.
  2. Naya tweet un sab followers ke home timeline cache mein insert kar do.

Ab home timeline read karna sasta hai, kyunki result pehle se hi compute hua rakha hai. Book ke apne figures approach 1 ka relational schema aur approach 2 ka data pipeline dikhate hain. Neeche ka diagram approach 2 ki ek simplified picture hai.

Twitter ke pehle version mein approach 1 use hua tha. Systems ko home timeline queries ke saath keep up karna mushkil lag raha tha, isliye company approach 2 par switch ho gayi. Iski wajah ek trade-off hai, jo book clearly dikhati hai. Publish hone wale tweets ka average rate home timeline reads ke rate se lagbhag do orders of magnitude kam hai. Isliye better yahi hai ki tweet likhte waqt zyada kaam ho aur timeline read karte waqt kam.

Lekin approach 2 ki ek cost hai. Ab tweet post karne mein kaafi extra kaam lagta hai. Average mein ek tweet lagbhag 75 followers tak deliver hota hai. Toh 4.6k tweets per second badhkar home timeline caches par lagbhag 345k writes per second ban jaate hain. Average ek bada problem chhupa leta hai. Har user ke followers ki count bahut zyada vary karti hai, aur kuch users ke 30 million se zyada followers hain. Aise ek user ka ek tweet 30 million se zyada writes cause kar sakta hai. Twitter tweets ko followers tak paanch seconds ke andar deliver karne ki koshish karta hai, isliye yeh kaam time par karna ek bada engineering challenge hai.

Is example mein followers ki distribution (shayad is hisaab se weighted ki har user kitni baar tweet karta hai) ek key load parameter hai, kyunki yahi fan-out load decide karti hai. Tumhari apni application ke numbers alag honge, par reasoning wahi lagegi.

Aakhri twist yeh hai ki Twitter ab dono approaches ke hybrid ki taraf ja raha hai. Zyaadatar users ke tweets post hote hi ab bhi home timelines mein fan out hote hain. Bahut zyada followers wale chhote se group ke users, yani celebrities, is fan-out se bahar rakhe jaate hain. Jab koi user apni timeline read karta hai, toh jin celebrities ko woh follow karta hai unke tweets alag se fetch hokar merge kiye jaate hain, bilkul approach 1 ki tarah. Yeh hybrid consistently achhi performance deta hai. Book is example par Chapter 12 mein wapas aati hai, jab tak kaafi technical ground cover ho chuka hota hai.

Trade-offs
OptionKahan achha haiCost
Approach 1: read time par combine karnaWrites sasti hain, kyunki tweet ek hi insert haiHar timeline read mein bhaari kaam hota hai. Twitter ka pehla version isi load se struggle kar raha tha.
Approach 2: write time par fan out karnaTimeline reads sasti hain, kyunki result pehle se ready haiHar tweet kaafi saari writes cause karta hai. Celebrity ka ek tweet 30 million se zyada writes cause kar sakta hai.
Hybrid (Twitter ki direction)Consistently achhi performance, zyaadatar users ke liye fan-out aur celebrities ke liye read-time mergingDo mechanisms build aur run karne padte hain, aur read path ko dono sets ke tweets sahi tarah merge karne padte hain.
Try karo

Book ke mutabiq average tweet lagbhag 75 followers tak pahunchta hai, lekin kuch users ke 30 million se zyada followers hain. Maan lo tum approach 2 ke saath ek timeline service chala rahe ho. Tum kin accounts par sabse zyada nazar rakhoge, aur hybrid design unke liye kya badal dega?

Performance ko describe karna

Load describe karne ke baad tum pooch sakte ho ki load badhne par kya hoga. Ise dekhne ke do tarike hain:

  • Agar tum ek load parameter badhao aur system ke resources (CPU, memory, network bandwidth, waghera) wahi rakho, toh performance kaise badlegi?
  • Agar tum ek load parameter badhao, toh performance same rakhne ke liye resources mein kitna add karna padega?

Dono sawaalon ke liye performance numbers chahiye, isliye book pehle yeh dekhti hai ki performance ko kaise describe karein.

Hadoop jaise batch processing system mein key measure usually throughput hota hai. Yani per second kitne records process hue, ya ek given size ke dataset par job chalane mein total kitna time laga. Ideal duniya mein batch job ka running time dataset size ko throughput se divide karne par milta hai. Practice mein yeh aksar zyada hota hai, kyunki data workers mein barabar nahi bantta (ise skew kehte hain), aur job ko apne sabse slow task ke khatam hone ka wait karna padta hai.

Online systems mein usually response time zyada matter karta hai. Yeh woh time hai jo client ke request bhejne aur response milne ke beech lagta hai.

Dhyaan do

Latency aur response time ko aksar ek hi matlab mein use kar liya jaata hai, lekin yeh same nahi hain. Response time woh hai jo client ko dikhta hai. Isme request process karne ka asli time (service time) shaamil hota hai, saath mein network delays aur queueing delays bhi. Latency woh time hai jo request handle hone ke wait mein bitati hai, yani jab woh latent hoti hai, service ka intezaar karte hue.

Response time koi ek fixed number nahi hota. Tum same request baar-baar bhejo, tab bhi har reply thoda alag time leta hai. Jis system mein kai tarah ki requests aati hain, wahan variation kaafi bada ho sakta hai. Isliye response time ko ek single number ki tarah nahi, balki measure kiye hue values ki distribution ki tarah dekhna chahiye.

Response times measure karna

Book ke Figure 1-4 mein ek service ki 100 requests ke response times bars ki ek row ki tarah dikhaye gaye hain, har request ke liye ek bar. Zyaadatar requests kaafi fast hain, lekin kabhi-kabhi kuch outliers aate hain jo bahut zyada time lete hain. Kuch slow requests intrinsically zyada expensive hoti hain, kyunki woh zyada data process karti hain. Lekin jab saari requests ka time same hona chahiye, tab bhi variation dikhta hai. Random extra delay kai wajahon se aa sakta hai: background process par context switch, network packet ka loss aur uske baad TCP retransmission, garbage collection pause (jab language runtime memory clean karne ke liye program ko rok deta hai), page fault jo disk se read karne par majboor karta hai, ya server rack ki mechanical vibrations bhi.

Kisi service ka average response time report karna common hai. Strictly dekhein toh "average" kisi ek formula ka naam nahi hai, lekin practice mein iska matlab arithmetic mean hota hai: saari values ka sum karo aur values ki count se divide karo. Mean typical response time ka achha measure nahi hai, kyunki yeh nahi batata ki kitne users ne actually woh delay experience kiya.

Percentiles usually better hote hain. Apni response times ki list lo aur use fastest se slowest tak sort karo. Median beech ka point hai. Agar median 200 ms (milliseconds) hai, toh aadhi requests 200 ms se kam mein return hoti hain aur aadhi usse zyada time leti hain. Isliye median "users ko typically kitna wait karna padta hai?" ka achha jawab hai. Ise 50th percentile ya p50 bhi kehte hain.

Median ek single request ko describe karta hai. Jo user kai resources wala page load karta hai, ya session mein kai requests karta hai, uske liye kam se kam ek slow request milne ka chance kaafi zyada hota hai. Kai requests mein se kam se kam ek ke median se slow hone ki probability 50 percent se bahut zyada hoti hai.

Outliers kitne bure hain yeh dekhne ke liye higher percentiles dekho. 95th, 99th aur 99.9th percentiles common hain, jinhe p95, p99 aur p999 likha jaata hai. Har ek woh response time hai jisse 95, 99 ya 99.9 percent requests fast hoti hain. Jaise, agar 95th percentile 1.5 seconds hai, toh 100 mein se 95 requests 1.5 seconds se kam leti hain, aur 100 mein se 5 requests 1.5 seconds ya usse zyada leti hain.

Asli idea

Kisi service ko sirf uske average se judge mat karein. Median, p95 aur p99 jaise percentiles dekhein, kyunki yeh dikhate hain ki kitne users ka experience actually slow tha.

Tail latency aur yeh kyun matter karti hai

Sabse high percentiles ko tail latencies kehte hain, aur yeh isliye matter karti hain kyunki yeh users ke experience ko shape karti hain. Amazon internal services ke response time requirements 99.9th percentile se describe karta hai, jabki yeh sirf 1,000 mein se 1 request ko affect karta hai. Wajah yeh hai ki sabse slow requests wale customers aksar woh hote hain jinke accounts mein sabse zyada data hota hai, kyunki unhone bahut purchases ki hain. Yahi sabse valuable customers bhi hain, isliye unka experience fast rakhna zaroori hai.

Slowness ki cost ke baare mein book do aur figures deti hai. Amazon ne paya ki response time mein 100 ms ka increase sales ko 1 percent kam kar deta hai. Doosri reports kehti hain ki 1 second ka slowdown ek customer satisfaction measure ko 16 percent kam kar deta hai. Phir bhi Amazon ne 99.99th percentile, yani sabse slow 10,000 mein se 1 request, optimize na karne ka faisla kiya, kyunki benefit ke mukable cost bahut zyada thi. Bahut high percentiles par response times un random events se asaani se affect ho jaate hain jo tumhare control mein nahi hote, aur har extra improvement ka benefit kam hota jaata hai.

Percentiles service level objectives (SLOs) mein use hote hain, jo internal targets hote hain, aur service level agreements (SLAs) mein bhi, jo contracts hote hain aur service ki expected performance aur availability define karte hain. Ek SLA kuch aisa keh sakta hai ki service tab up maani jaayegi jab uska median response time 200 ms se kam ho aur 99th percentile 1 second se kam ho. (Agar responses isse zyada time lein, toh service down hone jaisi hi hai.) Wahi SLA yeh bhi maang sakta hai ki service kam se kam 99.9 percent time up rahe. Yeh numbers clients ke liye expectations set karte hain, aur SLA meet na hone par customers refund maang sakte hain.

Queueing aur head-of-line blocking

High percentiles par response time ka bada hissa aksar queueing delays ka hota hai. Ek server parallel mein sirf kuch hi cheezein process kar sakta hai, jo jaise uske CPU cores ki count se limited hoti hain. Isliye kuch slow requests apne peeche wali requests ko rok sakti hain. Ise head-of-line blocking kehte hain. Bhale hi baad wali requests server par process hone mein quick hon, client ko overall response slow dikhta hai, kyunki use pehli request ke khatam hone ka wait karna pada.

Isi wajah se book kehti hai ki response times client side par measure karna zaroori hai. Server ki apni timing queue mein bitaya hua wait time miss kar deti hai.

Yahi problem load testing par bhi lagti hai. Scalability test karne ke liye jab tum artificial load generate karte ho, toh load-generating client ko requests bhejte rehna chahiye, chahe responses kitni bhi jaldi aayein. Agar client har response ka wait karke hi agli request bhejta hai, toh test ki queues real life se chhoti rehti hain. Isse measurements skew ho jaate hain.

Percentiles practice mein

High percentiles un backend services mein khaas taur par important ho jaate hain jinhe ek end-user request serve karne ke liye kai baar call kiya jaata hai. Calls parallel mein bhi hon, tab bhi end-user request ko unmein se sabse slow call ke khatam hone ka wait karna padta hai. Ek slow call hi poori request ko slow karne ke liye kaafi hai.

Yeh book ke Figure 1-5 mein dikhaya gaya hai. Slow backend calls ka chhota sa share bhi slow end-user requests ka bada share bana sakta hai, kyunki kam se kam ek slow call milne ka chance calls ki count ke saath badhta hai. Book ise tail latency amplification kehti hai.

Agar tum apni services ke monitoring dashboards mein response time percentiles add karna chahte ho, toh unhe efficiently aur continuously calculate karna padega. Jaise, tum pichhle 10 minutes ki requests ke response times ki ek rolling window rakh sakte ho. Har minute tum us window ki values par median aur doosre percentiles calculate karte ho, aur unhe graph par plot karte ho.

Naive tarika yeh hai ki window ke saare response times ki list rakhein aur har minute use sort karein. Agar yeh bahut slow hai ya bahut zyada memory leta hai, toh aise algorithms hain jo kam CPU aur memory cost mein percentiles ka approximation nikaal dete hain. Book forward decay, t-digest aur HdrHistogram ka naam examples ke taur par leti hai.

Ek common galti se bachein: percentiles ka average lena mathematically meaningless hai, chahe tum time resolution kam karne ke liye karo ya kai machines ka data combine karne ke liye. Iske bajay histograms ko add karein (yani har time range mein kitni requests aayi, uski counts) aur total se percentile compute karein.

Load ko cope karne ke approaches

Ab jab book load describe karna aur performance measure karna cover kar chuki hai, toh woh scalability par aati hai. Jab tumhare load parameters badhein, toh performance achhi kaise rakho?

Jo architecture ek level ke load ke liye theek hai, woh usse das guna load handle kar paaye, yeh unlikely hai. Agar tum fast-growing service par kaam kar rahe ho, toh shayad har baar jab load ek order of magnitude (das guna) badhe, tab architecture ko dobara sochna padega, ya usse bhi zyada baar.

Log aksar do approaches ke beech choice ki baat karte hain:

  • Scaling up (vertical scaling) matlab ek zyada powerful machine par move karna.
  • Scaling out (horizontal scaling) matlab load ko kai chhoti machines mein baant dena. Load ko kai machines mein baantne ko shared-nothing architecture bhi kehte hain, kyunki machines memory ya disks share nahi karti.

Ek machine par chalne wala system aksar simple hota hai. Lekin high-end machines bahut mehngi ho jaati hain, isliye bahut demanding workloads ke liye aksar scaling out se bachna possible nahi hota. Practice mein achhe architectures usually dono ko mix karte hain. Jaise, kaafi powerful kuch machines bahut saari chhoti virtual machines se simple aur sasti ho sakti hain.

Book capacity add karne ke do tarikon mein bhi fark batati hai. Elastic system load badhne ka pata chalte hi computing resources apne aap add kar leta hai. Manually scaled system mein ek insaan ko capacity analyze karke machines add karne ka faisla karna padta hai. Elastic systems tab kaam aate hain jab load predict karna mushkil ho. Manually scaled systems simple hote hain aur operation mein unme surprises kam ho sakte hain. Book is par partitions ko rebalance karne wali baad ki discussion mein wapas aati hai.

Stateless services (jo requests ke beech apna koi data nahi rakhti) ko machines mein distribute karna kaafi straightforward hai. Stateful data systems alag hote hain. Database ko ek single node (ek machine) se distributed setup mein le jaane se complexity kaafi badh jaati hai. Haal tak common wisdom yeh thi ki database ko ek node par rakho, yani scale up karo, jab tak scaling ki cost ya high availability ki zaroorat tumhe distribute karne par majboor na kare. Kleppmann ka kehna hai ki distributed systems ke tools behtar hone par yeh badal sakta hai. Ho sakta hai ek din distributed data systems default ban jaayein, un applications ke liye bhi jo large volumes of data handle nahi karti. Book ka baaki hissa kai tarah ke distributed data systems cover karta hai, aur dekhta hai ki woh sirf scalability mein nahi, balki ease of use aur maintainability mein bhi kaise perform karte hain.

Aisa koi ek scalable architecture nahi hai jo sab par fit ho. Problem reads ki volume ho sakti hai, writes ki volume, store karne wale data ki volume, data ki complexity, response time requirements, access patterns, ya usually in sab ka mixture. 100,000 requests per second handle karne wala system, jisme har request 1 kB ki ho, us system se bahut alag dikhta hai jo 3 requests per minute ke liye bana ho, jisme har request 2 GB ki ho. Phir bhi dono ka data throughput same hai.

Jo architecture kisi particular application ke liye achha scale karta hai, woh is assumption par bana hota hai ki kaunse operations common honge aur kaunse rare. Yahi assumptions load parameters hain. Agar yeh galat nikle, toh scaling par lagi mehnat best case mein waste hai, aur worst case mein counterproductive. Early-stage startup ya unproven product ke liye usually yeh zyada zaroori hai ki features par jaldi iterate karein, bajay kisi hypothetical future load ki taiyari karne ke.

Har scalable architecture apni application ke liye specific hota hai, phir bhi woh usually general-purpose building blocks se bana hota hai jo familiar patterns mein arrange kiye jaate hain. Book ka baaki hissa un building blocks aur patterns ko cover karta hai.

Try karo

Do systems ka data throughput same hai. Ek 100,000 requests per second handle karta hai, har request 1 kB ki. Doosra 3 requests per minute handle karta hai, har request 2 GB ki. Kaunsa chalana zyada mushkil hoga, aur kyun? Socho ki har server ko kitni requests handle karni hain aur har request kitni badi hai.

Maintainability

Software ka zyada cost uske first version mein nahi hota. Asli cost ongoing maintenance mein jaata hai: bugs fix karna, system ko chalte rakhna, failures investigate karna, naye platforms ke liye adapt karna, naye use cases ke liye change karna, technical debt chukana (shortcuts jo aage ka kaam slow kar dete hain), aur features add karna.

Bahut log legacy systems maintain karna pasand nahi karte. Legacy systems purane systems hote hain jinhe change karna mushkil hota hai. Kabhi doosron ki galtiyan theek karni padti hain, kabhi aise platforms par kaam karna padta hai jo ab outdated ho chuke hain, kabhi system se woh kaam karwana padta hai jiske liye usse design hi nahi kiya gaya tha. Har legacy system apne tarike se pareshan karta hai, isliye sabke liye ek general salaah dena mushkil hai.

Lekin hum software ko aise design kar sakte hain ki maintenance kam takleef de, aur hum naye legacy systems na banayein. Book teen design principles par khaas dhyaan deti hai.

  • Operability: operations teams ke liye system ko smoothly chalate rakhna aasaan banao.
  • Simplicity: jitni ho sake complexity hata do, taaki naye engineers system ko aasaani se samajh sakein. Iska matlab user interface ki simplicity nahi hai.
  • Evolvability: requirements badalne par engineers ke liye system ko baad mein change karna aasaan banao. Ise extensibility, modifiability ya plasticity bhi kehte hain.

Reliability aur scalability ki tarah, yahan bhi koi aasaan solution nahi hai. Bas systems ke baare mein operability, simplicity aur evolvability ko dhyaan mein rakhkar sochna hai.

Operability: operations ki life aasaan banana

Ek quote hai ki achhi operations bure software ki limits ke aaspaas kaam nikaal sakti hai, lekin achha software buri operations ke saath reliably nahi chal sakta. Operations ke kuch hisse automate ho sakte hain. Phir bhi automation set up karna aur use chalu rakhna logon ko hi karna padta hai.

Ek achhi operations team kai cheezon ki zimmedaar hoti hai, jaise:

  • System ki health monitor karna, aur jab woh bad state mein chala jaaye toh jaldi service restore karna.
  • Failures ya slow performance ki wajah dhoondhna.
  • Software aur platforms ko up to date rakhna, security patches ke saath.
  • Dekhna ki systems ek doosre ko kaise affect karte hain, taaki koi risky change damage karne se pehle hi roka ja sake.
  • Problems ko hone se pehle anticipate karna, jaise capacity planning ke through.
  • Deployment aur configuration management ke liye achhi practices aur tools set up karna.
  • Complex tasks karna, jaise application ko ek platform se doosre par move karna.
  • Configuration changes hote waqt system ko secure rakhna.
  • Aise processes define karna jo operations ko predictable aur production environment ko stable banayein.
  • System ke baare mein organization ka knowledge bachaye rakhna, chahe log aate-jaate rahein.

Achhi operability ka matlab hai routine tasks ko aasaan banana, taaki team apni energy high-value kaam par laga sake. Data systems kai tarah se madad kar sakte hain:

  • Achhi monitoring ke through runtime behavior aur internals ki visibility dena.
  • Automation ko support karna aur standard tools ke saath achhi tarah integrate hona.
  • Kisi ek machine par depend na karna, taaki maintenance ke liye machines band ki ja sakein aur poora system chalta rahe.
  • Achhi documentation aur samajhne mein aasaan operational model dena, taaki log action ka result predict kar sakein (“agar main X karun, toh Y hoga”).
  • Achha default behavior dena, aur zaroorat padne par administrators ko defaults override karne dena.
  • Jahan sahi ho wahan khud ko heal karna, aur zaroorat padne par administrators ko system state ka manual control dena.
  • Predictably behave karna aur surprises kam se kam rakhna.

Simplicity: complexity ko manage karna

Chhote software projects mein code bahut simple aur expressive ho sakta hai. Lekin project badhne par woh aksar bahut complex aur samajhne mein mushkil ho jaata hai. Yeh complexity system par kaam karne wale sabko slow kar deti hai aur maintenance ka cost badha deti hai. Complexity mein fansa project kabhi-kabhi big ball of mud kehlata hai.

Complexity ke kai symptoms hote hain. State space explode ho sakta hai, modules tightly coupled ho sakte hain, dependencies uljhi hui ho sakti hain, names aur terms inconsistent ho sakte hain, performance hacks ka dher lag jaata hai, aur kahin aur ki problems ke around kaam karne ke liye special cases aa jaate hain. Maintenance mushkil ho toh budget aur schedule dono overrun hote hain. Complex system mein change karte waqt developer se bug aane ka chance bhi zyada hota hai, kyunki jab system par reason karna mushkil ho, tab hidden assumptions, unintended consequences aur unexpected interactions miss ho jaana aasaan hai. Isliye complexity kam karne se maintainability bahut behtar hoti hai, aur simplicity ek key goal honi chahiye.

Simplicity ka matlab hamesha kam features nahi hota. Iska matlab accidental complexity hatana bhi ho sakta hai. Book Moseley aur Marks ki definition use karti hai: complexity accidental tab hai jab woh us problem ka inherent hissa nahi hai jo software solve karta hai (users ki nazar se), aur sirf software ko implement karne ke tarike se paida hui hai.

Accidental complexity hatane ke sabse achhe tools mein se ek abstraction hai. Ek achhi abstraction bahut saari implementation detail ko ek clean, simple façade (simple bahari chehra) ke peeche chhupa deti hai. Use kai applications mein reuse bhi kiya ja sakta hai. Reuse ek hi cheez ko baar-baar banane se zyada efficient hai, aur quality bhi badhata hai, kyunki shared component mein jo bhi improvement hota hai, uska fayda use karne wali sabhi applications ko milta hai.

Book se do examples. High-level programming languages machine code, CPU registers aur system calls ko hide karti hain. SQL complex on-disk aur in-memory data structures, doosre clients ke concurrent requests, aur crash ke baad ki inconsistencies ko hide karta hai. High-level language mein bhi tum machine code hi chala rahe hote ho, bas tumhe uske baare mein sochna nahi padta.

Achhi abstractions dhoondhna bahut mushkil hai. Distributed systems mein kaafi achhe algorithms hain, lekin unhe abstractions mein kaise package karein jo system ko manageable rakhein, yeh kam clear hai. Book promise karti hai ki poori book mein achhi abstractions dhoondhi jayengi, taaki bade system ke parts ko well-defined, reusable components ke roop mein alag kiya ja sake.

Evolvability: change ko aasaan banana

Tumhare system ki requirements lagbhag pakka same nahi rahengi. Woh constantly badalti rehti hain. Tumhe nayi baatein pata chalti hain, aise use cases aa jaate hain jinki umeed nahi thi, business priorities badal jaati hain, users naye features maangte hain, naye platforms purano ki jagah le lete hain, legal rules badal jaate hain, aur growth ki wajah se architecture mein changes karne padte hain.

Agile working patterns organization ke level par change handle karne ka tarika dete hain. Agile community ne technical tools bhi banaye hain, jaise test-driven development (TDD, code se pehle tests likhna) aur refactoring (program ka kaam badle bina uska structure behtar karna). Jab software baar-baar change hota hai, tab yeh kaafi kaam aate hain.

In techniques ki zyada tar discussions kaafi chhote scale par hoti hain, jaise ek hi application ki kuch source files. Book poore data system ke level par agility badhane ke tarike dhoondhti hai, jisme kai applications ya services ho sakti hain. Jaise, Twitter ke home timelines assemble karne wale architecture ko approach 1 se approach 2 par tum kaise refactor karoge? Yeh poore design ka change hai, kisi ek file ka nahi.

Data system ko kitni aasaani se modify kiya ja sakta hai, yeh uski simplicity aur abstractions par bahut depend karta hai. Simple aur samajhne mein aasaan systems ko aam taur par complex systems se change karna aasaan hota hai. Yeh idea bahut zaroori hai, isliye book data system ke level ki agility ke liye alag word use karti hai: evolvability.

Rule of thumb

Achhi abstractions wale simple systems ko chalana bhi aasaan hota hai aur change karna bhi. Accidental complexity ka har extra hissa ek cost hai, jo tumhe aur tumhare colleagues ko aage bharna padega.

Summary

Short mein
  • Requirements. Ek application ki functional requirements hoti hain (woh kya kare, jaise data store karna, retrieve karna, search karna aur process karna) aur nonfunctional requirements (jaise security, reliability, compliance, scalability, compatibility aur maintainability). Is chapter ka focus reliability, scalability aur maintainability par tha.
  • Reliability ka matlab hai ki faults aane par bhi system sahi kaam kare. Faults hardware se aa sakte hain (aam taur par random aur uncorrelated), software se (bugs aam taur par systematic hote hain aur handle karna mushkil), aur humans se (jo kabhi-kabhi galti karte hi hain). Fault-tolerance techniques kuch faults ko end user se hide kar sakti hain.
  • Scalability ka matlab hai load badhne par performance achhi rakhne ki strategies hona. Isse discuss karne ke liye pehle load aur performance describe karne ke quantitative tarike chahiye. Chapter ne load describe karne ke example ke roop mein Twitter ke home timelines use kiye, aur performance measure karne ke liye response time percentiles. Ek scalable system mein tum processing capacity add karke high load mein bhi reliable rah sakte ho.
  • Maintainability ke kai pehlu hain, lekin asal mein yeh un engineering aur operations teams ki life behtar banane ke baare mein hai jo system ke saath kaam karti hain. Achhi abstractions complexity kam karti hain aur system ko naye use cases ke liye modify karna aasaan banati hain. Achhi operability ka matlab hai system ki health ki visibility aur use manage karne ke effective tarike hona.

Applications ko reliable, scalable ya maintainable banane ka koi aasaan fix nahi hai. Lekin kuch patterns aur techniques alag-alag tarah ki applications mein baar-baar dikhte hain. Agle kuch chapters data systems ke examples dekhenge aur analyze karenge ki woh in goals ki taraf kaise kaam karte hain. Phir Part III un systems ke patterns dekhega jo kai components se milkar bante hain, jaise is chapter mein pehle dikhaya gaya composite system.

Chapter ke end mein papers, blog posts aur talks ke 34 references ki numbered list hai jo uske claims ko support karti hai, jaise Chaos Monkey post aur paper The Tail at Scale. Yeh retelling us list ko reproduce nahi karti.

Check yourself

  1. Twitter ke first design mein har home timeline read time par banti thi. Phir woh write time par har tweet ko followers ki timeline caches mein copy karne par kyun move hua?

    Jawab dekho

    Home timeline reads tweet posts se kaafi zyada hote hain, lagbhag do orders of magnitude zyada. Us load ke liye write time par zyada kaam aur read time par kam kaam karna behtar trade tha.

  2. Ek service ka 95th percentile response time 1.5 seconds hai. Har 100 requests mein se kitni requests 1.5 seconds ya usse zyada leti hain?

    Jawab dekho

    Paanch. 95th percentile ka matlab hai ki 100 mein se 95 requests 1.5 seconds se tez hain, toh baaki 5 requests 1.5 seconds ya usse zyada leti hain.

  3. Ek end-user request paanch backend services ko parallel mein call karti hai. Ek slow backend call poori request ko slow kyun bana sakti hai, aur calls ki count badhne par problem zyada kyun hoti hai?

    Jawab dekho

    End-user request ko parallel calls mein se sabse slow call ka wait karna padta hai. Calls zyada hon toh kam se kam ek ke slow hone ka chance badh jaata hai, isliye end-user requests ka bada hissa slow ho jaata hai. Book ise tail latency amplification kehti hai.

  4. Ek RAID set mein ek disk fail ho jaati hai, lekin system bina ruke users ko serve karta rehta hai. Yeh fault hai, failure hai, ya dono?

    Jawab dekho

    Yeh fault hai, kyunki ek component apni specification se hat gaya. Yeh failure nahi hai, kyunki system poora ab bhi service de raha hai. Redundancy ne fault ko failure banne se roka.

Part I · Chapter 2

Data Models and Query Languages

Seedhi baat: data model ek lens jaisa hai, jisse tum apna data dekhte ho. Isi se tay hota hai ki kya likhna aasaan hai, kya slow hai, aur tum problem ke baare mein kaise sochte ho. Relational, document aur graph models, har ek alag shape ke data ke liye fit baithta hai, aur baaki shapes ke liye awkward lagta hai.

Ek data model woh tarika hai jisse information ko describe kiya jaata hai, store kiya jaata hai aur uske baare mein query kiya jaata hai. Software banate waqt data model chunna sabse zaroori faislon mein se ek hai. Isse code kaise likha jaayega, yeh bhi tay hota hai, aur banane wale log problem ke baare mein kaise sochte hain, yeh bhi.

Zyada tar applications ek data model ke upar doosra data model rakhkar bante hain. Har layer par sawaal wahi rehta hai: is layer ko uske neeche wali layer ke terms mein kaise represent karein? Kleppmann chaar levels batate hain:

  1. Application developer real world ko dekhta hai (log, organizations, goods, actions, paise ka flow, sensors) aur use objects ya data structures mein model karta hai, saath mein un par kaam karne wale APIs bhi banata hai.
  2. In structures ko store karne ke liye developer unhe ek general-purpose data model mein express karta hai, jaise JSON ya XML documents, relational database ki tables, ya ek graph.
  3. Database banane wale engineers faisla karte hain ki yeh data memory, disk ya network par bytes ki shakl mein kaise represent hoga. Isi representation se tay hota hai ki data ko kaise query aur process kiya ja sakta hai.
  4. Hardware engineers un bytes ko electrical currents, light ke pulses ya magnetic fields ke roop mein represent karte hain.

Real systems mein aur bhi layers ho sakti hain, jaise ek API ke upar doosra API, par idea wahi rehta hai. Har layer apni neeche wali complexity ko ek clean model ke peeche chhupa deti hai. Isse alag-alag groups saath mein kaam kar paate hain. Database vendor ke engineers aur us database ko use karne wale developers ko har detail share karne ki zaroorat nahi padti.

Har data model ke andar yeh assumptions hote hain ki use kaise use kiya jaayega. Kuch kaam aasaan hote hain, aur kuch support hi nahi hote. Kuch operations fast hote hain, aur kuch ka performance kharab hota hai. Book ke hisaab se sirf relational data modeling par hi kai books bhar sakti hain, yani ek model ko master karna kaafi mehnat ka kaam hai. Model software ki capability par itna gehra asar daalta hai, isliye aisa model chunna sahi rehta hai jo application ke saath fit baithe.

Yeh chapter list ke doosre level ki baat karta hai: data store aur query karne ke general-purpose models. Hum relational model, document model aur kuch graph models ko compare karenge, aur dekhenge ki har ek ke saath kaun si query languages aati hain. Chapter 3 teesre level par jaata hai, yani yeh models storage engines ke roop mein actually kaise implement hote hain.

Chapter ki shuruaat philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein ki ek line se hoti hai: “The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.” Jo models tum jaante ho, wahi tay karte hain ki tum aasaani se kaun se sawaal soch paate ho.

Relational Model Versus Document Model

Aaj ka sabse jaana-maana data model woh hai jo SQL ke peeche hai. Yeh relational model par based hai, jo Edgar Codd ne 1970 mein propose kiya tha. Is model mein data relations mein organize hota hai, jinhe SQL mein tables kehte hain. Har relation tuples ka ek unordered collection hota hai, jinhe SQL mein rows kehte hain.

Jab yeh idea aaya, tab bahut logon ko shak tha ki ise efficiently banaya ja sakta hai. Lekin 1980 ke dashak ke beech tak relational database management systems (RDBMSes, yani woh software jo relational database chalata hai) aur SQL un sab ke liye default tools ban gaye the, jinhe regular structure wala data store karna hota tha. Relational databases takreeban 25 se 30 saal tak chhaaye rahe, jo computing mein bahut lamba time hai.

Inki jadein 1960 aur 1970 ke dashak mein mainframe computers par hone wali business data processing mein hain. Aaj yeh kaam saadharan lagte hain: transaction processing, yani sales, bank transactions, airline reservations aur warehouse stock record karna, aur batch processing, yani customer invoicing, payroll aur reports jaise jobs ek saath bade data par chalana. Pehle ke databases developers ko majboor karte the ki woh sochein data internally kaise layout hua hai. Relational model ka maksad tha us detail ko ek saaf interface ke peeche chhupa dena.

1970 aur 1980 ke shuruaati saalon mein network aur hierarchical models main rivals the, par relational model unpar haavi ho gaya. Object databases 1980 ke aakhir aur 1990 ke shuru mein aaye aur chale gaye. XML databases 2000 ke shuru mein aaye, lekin sirf niche use tak limited rahe. Har challenger ne hype banayi aur phir fade ho gaya. Par relational databases business data se bahut aage tak achhe se kaam karte nikle. Aaj web ka bahut kuch inhi par chalta hai, jaise online publishing, discussion sites, social networks, e-commerce, games aur software-as-a-service products.

The Birth of NoSQL

NoSQL un naye databases ka naam hai jo relational model ke dabdabe ko palatne ki koshish karte hain. Yeh naam thoda unfortunate hai, kyunki yeh kisi ek technology ki taraf point nahi karta. Yeh 2009 ke ek meetup ke liye catchy hashtag ke roop mein shuru hua, jo open source, distributed, nonrelational databases ke baare mein tha. Web startup community mein yeh label tezi se phail gaya, aur baad mein ise Not Only SQL ka matlab de diya gaya.

NoSQL databases apnane ke peeche chaar wajahein hain:

  • Relational databases se zyada scalability ki zaroorat, jaise bahut bade datasets ya bahut high write rates.
  • Commercial products ke mukaable free aur open source software ko zyada pasand karna.
  • Aise specialized query operations jinhe relational model achhe se support nahi karta.
  • Strict relational schemas se frustration (schema yani yeh fixed description ki kaun si tables aur columns hain aur unmein kya hota hai), aur ek zyada dynamic aur expressive model ki chaah.

Alag-alag applications ki zaroorat alag hoti hai, isliye ek kaam ke liye jo tool best hai, woh doosre kaam ke liye best nahi bhi ho sakta. Kleppmann ko lagta hai ki relational databases kai tarah ke nonrelational datastores ke saath-saath chalte rahenge. Is mix ko polyglot persistence kehte hain: kai storage technologies ek saath use karna, har ek wahi kaam karti hai jisme woh sabse achhi hai.

The Object-Relational Mismatch

Zyada tar application code object-oriented languages mein likha jaata hai. SQL par ek aam criticism yeh hai ki agar data relational tables mein store hai, toh code ke objects aur database ki tables, rows, columns ke beech ek awkward translation layer chahiye. In dono models ke beech ke is gap ko impedance mismatch kehte hain. Yeh term electronics se aayi hai, jahan do circuits ka match kharab ho toh power waste hoti hai aur signal reflections aate hain.

Object-relational mapping (ORM) frameworks, jaise ActiveRecord aur Hibernate, us translation layer ka boilerplate kaafi kam kar dete hain. Lekin woh dono models ke saare differences chhupa nahi sakte.

Problem samjhane ke liye book ek résumé ka example leti hai, jaise LinkedIn profile. Uska Figure 2-1 ek relational schema mein profile dikhata hai. Poora profile ek user_id se identify hota hai. First name aur last name jaise fields har person ke liye ek hi baar aate hain, isliye woh users table ke columns ban sakte hain. Lekin zyada tar logon ne kai jobs ki hoti hain, padhai ke kai daur hote hain, aur contact information kitni bhi ho sakti hai. Yeh sab ek one-to-many relationship hain: ek user ki kai positions. Book isse database mein represent karne ke teen tarike batati hai:

  • SQL:1999 se pehle ka traditional normalized tarika: positions, education aur contact information ko alag tables mein rakho. Har table mein ek foreign key hoti hai, yani ek column jo doosri table ki row ka ID rakhta hai, aur users table ki taraf wapas point karti hai.
  • Baad ke SQL standards ne structured types aur XML support jodey. Inse ek row ke andar kai values aa sakti hain, aur unhe query aur index kiya ja sakta hai. Kai major databases yeh alag-alag level tak support karte hain, aur kai JSON type bhi support karte hain.
  • Jobs aur education ko ek JSON ya XML document mein encode karo, use text column mein store karo, aur application ko use interpret karne do. Is setup mein database aam taur par us text ke andar ki values query nahi kar sakta.
Example

Résumé jaise self-contained document ke liye JSON representation kaafi sahi baithta hai. JSON, XML se kaafi simple hai. MongoDB, RethinkDB, CouchDB aur Espresso jaise document databases data isi model mein store karte hain. Book ka Example 2-1 Bill Gates ka profile dikhata hai, jo yahan chhota karke diya gaya hai:

{
  "user_id": 251,
  "first_name": "Bill",
  "last_name": "Gates",
  "positions": [
    {"job_title": "Co-chair", "organization": "Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation"},
    {"job_title": "Co-founder, Chairman", "organization": "Microsoft"}
  ],
  ...
}

Step by step padhein toh document aise kaam karta hai. 251 ka user_id profile ko identify karta hai. Top-level fields mein naam, ek chhota summary, ek region ID aur ek industry ID, aur ek photo URL hai. positions do objects ki list hai: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation mein Co-chair, aur Microsoft mein Co-founder aur Chairman. education ek list hai jisme Harvard University (1973 se 1975) aur Lakeside School, Seattle hai, jiske saath koi dates nahi hain. contact_info ek nested object hai jisme ek blog link aur ek Twitter link hai. Is person ke baare mein sab kuch ek hi document mein hai.

Kuch developers ko lagta hai ki JSON impedance mismatch kam kar deta hai, kyunki document code ke object jaisa dikhta hai. Book yahan do cautions jodti hai. Ek encoding format ke roop mein JSON ki apni problems hain, jinhe Chapter 4 cover karta hai. Aur schema ka na hona, jise aksar advantage bataya jaata hai, us topic par chapter aage dobara aata hai.

JSON form mein locality bhi behtar hoti hai, yani related data paas-paas store hota hai. Relational layout mein profile fetch karne ke liye ya toh tum har table ko user_id se query karte ho, ya users table aur uski related tables par ek messy multi-way join likhte ho. JSON form mein saari relevant information ek jagah hoti hai, aur ek query kaafi hai. One-to-many links ek tree banate hain: profile root hai, aur positions, schools aur contacts uski branches hain. Neeche ka diagram dono layouts ko saath-saath dikhata hai.

Many-to-One and Many-to-Many Relationships

Example 2-1 mein region_id aur industry_id IDs hain, “Greater Seattle Area” ya “Philanthropy” jaisa plain text nahi. Aisa kyun? Agar page par region aur industry ke liye free-text boxes hote, toh plain strings chal jaate. Lekin regions aur industries ki ek standard list, jise drop-down menu ya autocomplete box se chuna jaaye, ke kai fayde hain:

  • Saare profiles mein style aur spelling consistent rehti hai.
  • Koi ambiguity nahi hoti, jaise jab kai cities ka naam same ho.
  • Update aasaan hota hai, kyunki naam sirf ek jagah store hota hai. Agar kisi city ka naam badal jaaye, toh ek change se sab jagah theek ho jaata hai.
  • Localization. Site translate hoti hai toh list bhi translate ho sakti hai, isliye har region viewer ki language mein dikhta hai.
  • Behtar search. Washington State ke philanthropists ki search is profile ko match kar sakti hai, kyunki regions ki list yeh record kar sakti hai ki Seattle Washington mein hai. Yeh baat “Greater Seattle Area” text se nazar nahi aati.
Example

Maan lo woh profile jisme region_id us:91 set hai, jaise book mein hai. Region ka naam regions list ki ek row mein rehta hai. Socho kisi political change ke baad ek city ka naam badal diya gaya. Tum bas ek row update karte ho, aur us par point karne wala har profile ek saath sahi ho jaata hai. Agar har profile ne text store kiya hota, toh us text wale har profile ko alag update chahiye hota. Kuch updates chhoot bhi sakte the, aur phir copies ek-doosre se match nahi karti.

ID store karein ya text string, yeh sawaal duplication ka hai. ID ke saath, insaanon ke liye meaningful information (jaise Philanthropy word) ek jagah store hoti hai, aur baaki sab use ID se refer karte hain. ID ka logon ke liye koi matlab nahi hota, isliye use kabhi badalne ki zaroorat nahi padti, chahe jis cheez ka woh naam hai woh badal jaaye. Text mein information har us record mein copy ho jaati hai jo use use karta hai. Aage koi bhi change ho toh har copy update karni padti hai, jisse writes badhte hain aur copies ke inconsistent hone ka risk rehta hai. Is duplication ko hatana hi normalization ka key idea hai, yani database ko aise organize karna ki har fact sirf ek baar store ho.

Rule of thumb

Agar tum aisi values duplicate kar rahe ho jo sirf ek jagah store ho sakti thi, toh schema normalized nahi hai. Book ke hisaab se literature mein jo formal normal forms hain, practice mein unse zyada yeh rule matter karta hai.

Database administrators aur developers normalization aur uske ulte, denormalization, par debate karna pasand karte hain. Denormalization matlab reads fast karne ke liye intentionally data copy karna. Is baare mein Kleppmann abhi koi faisla nahi dete. Yeh topic Part III mein dobara aayega, jahan caching, denormalization aur derived data ki baat hogi.

Is data ko normalize karne ke liye many-to-one relationships chahiye: kai log ek region mein rehte hain, aur kai log ek industry mein kaam karte hain. Yeh document model mein theek se fit nahi hote. Relational databases mein doosri tables ki rows ko ID se refer karna normal hai, kyunki join, yani ek query mein do tables ki rows ko combine karna, aasaan hota hai. Document databases mein one-to-many tree structures ke liye joins ki zaroorat nahi padti, aur joins ka support aksar kamzor hota hai. Kleppmann ke likhte waqt RethinkDB joins support karta tha, MongoDB nahi karta tha, aur CouchDB sirf predeclared views mein karta tha.

Agar database join nahi kar sakta, toh application ko kai queries se join emulate karna padta hai aur results khud combine karne padte hain. Region aur industry ki lists chhoti hoti hain aur dheere badalti hain, isliye application unhe memory mein rakh sakti hai. Phir bhi, join ka kaam database se nikalkar application code mein aa gaya.

Features jodte jaane par data aur zyada connected hota jaata hai. Book résumé example mein do changes batati hai:

Organizations aur schools ko entities banana. Abhi company aur school sirf strings hain. Ho sakta hai har ek ko apni entity ka reference hona chahiye, apne page, logo aur news feed ke saath. Tab résumé un organizations aur schools se link kar sakta hai jinka usme zikr hai, aur unke logos dikha sakta hai. Book ka Figure 2-3 dikhata hai ki LinkedIn company names ke saath yahi karta hai.

Recommendations. Ek user doosre user ke liye recommendation likh sakta hai. Woh recommended person ke résumé par dikhta hai, likhne wale ke naam aur photo ke saath. Agar author apni photo badal le, toh unki likhi recommendations par nayi photo dikhni chahiye. Isliye recommendation mein author ke profile ka reference hona chahiye, uske naam aur photo ki copy nahi.

Book ka Figure 2-4 dikhata hai ki in features ko many-to-many relationships chahiye. Har dotted box ke andar ka data ek document mein group ho sakta hai. Lekin organizations, schools aur doosre users ke references ko references ki tarah hi store karna padta hai, aur query karte waqt unhe joins chahiye.

Are Document Databases Repeating History?

Relational databases mein many-to-many relationships routine baat hain. Document databases aur NoSQL ne is debate ko dobara khol diya ki unhe sabse achhe tarike se kaise represent karein. Yeh debate NoSQL se bhi purani hai, aur sabse pehle computerized databases tak jaati hai.

1970 ke dashak ka sabse popular business database IBM ka Information Management System (IMS) tha. Ise Apollo space program mein stock-keeping ke liye develop kiya gaya tha, aur 1968 mein pehli baar commercially release hua. Aaj bhi yeh maintain hota hai aur IBM mainframes par chalta hai. IMS ne hierarchical model use kiya, jo saara data records ke andar nested records ke tree ki tarah store karta hai, bilkul Figure 2-2 ke JSON jaisa. Kleppmann kehte hain ki document databases ke JSON model se isme kaafi similarities hain.

Document databases ki tarah IMS one-to-many relationships ke liye achha tha. Lekin many-to-many relationships mushkil the, aur joins the hi nahi. Developers ko ya toh data duplicate karna padta tha (denormalize karna), ya ek record se doosre record ke references haath se resolve karne padte the.
