Book ke hisaab se 1960 aur 1970 ke dashak ki yeh problems kaafi hadd tak wahi hain jo developers aaj document databases ke saath dekhte hain.

Do solutions propose kiye gaye. Pehla relational model tha, jo SQL bana aur poori duniya par chha gaya. Doosra network model tha, jiske shuru mein bahut followers the, par phir woh gayab ho gaya. In dono camps ke beech debate 1970 ke dashak ka kaafi hissa chala. Problem aaj bhi itni relevant hai, isliye book us debate ko aaj ke nazariye se dobara dekhti hai.

The network model. Network model ko CODASYL (Conference on Data Systems Languages) naam ki ek committee ne standardize kiya, aur kai vendors ne use implement kiya. Yeh hierarchical model ka generalization tha. Tree mein har record ka exactly ek parent hota hai. Network model mein ek record ke kai parents ho sakte the. Jaise, Greater Seattle Area region ka ek record wahan rehne wale har user se linked ho sakta tha. Isse many-to-one aur many-to-many relationships possible ho gaye.

Network model ke links foreign keys nahi the. Woh programming language ke pointers jaise the, jo disk par store hote the. Kisi record tak pahunchne ka ek hi tarika tha: ek access path follow karna, yani root record se shuru hone wali links ki chain. Sabse simple case mein yeh linked list par chalne jaisa hai, ek ke baad ek record dekhte hue. Many-to-many links ke saath, kai paths ek hi record tak pahunch sakte hain, aur programmer ko un sabko dimaag mein rakhna padta tha. Committee ke members ne bhi maana ki yeh n-dimensional data space mein navigate karne jaisa tha.

Queries records ki lists mein cursor chalakar aur access paths follow karke kaam karti thi. Paths haath se chunne se 1970 ke dashak ke slow hardware, jaise tape drives, ka achha use hota tha. Lekin isse query aur update code complicated aur inflexible ho jaata tha. Agar tumhe aisa data chahiye jiska koi path nahi hai, toh tum phans jaate the. Tumhe access paths badalne padte the, aur phir haath se likhe bahut saare query code ko dobara likhna padta tha.

The relational model. Relational model ne saara data saamne khol kar rakh diya. Relation bas tuples ka ek collection hai, aur bas. Na koi nested structures hain, na follow karne ke liye access paths. Tum table ki koi bhi ya saari rows padh sakte ho, aur kisi bhi condition se match karne wali rows chun sakte ho. Kuch columns ko key maanke match karke tum koi particular row padh sakte ho. Tum kisi bhi table mein nayi row insert kar sakte ho, bina doosri tables se aane-jaane wali foreign key links ki chinta kiye. (Foreign key constraints optional hain. Relational model unhe require nahi karta. CODASYL mein link effectively insert ke waqt ban jaati thi, jabki relational database mein foreign key par join query ke waqt hota hai.)

Relational database mein ek query optimizer, yani database ka woh hissa jo tay karta hai ki har query kaise chalani hai, steps ka order aur kaun se indexes use karne hain, yeh sab automatically chun leta hai. (Index ek alag structure hai jo database ko rows jaldi dhoondhne mein madad karta hai.) Yeh choices effectively access path hi hain, lekin inhe application developer nahi, database banata hai, isliye hamein inke baare mein kam hi sochna padta hai. Agar tum apne data ko nayi tarah se query karna chahte ho, toh tum ek naya index declare kar sakte ho, aur queries use automatically use kar leti ho. Queries badalni nahi padti. Relational model ne applications mein naye features jodna kaafi aasaan bana diya.

Query optimizers complicated hote hain, aur unpar kai saal ki research aur development lagi hai. Key insight yeh hai ki optimizer sirf ek baar banana padta hai, aur phir database use karne wali har application ko uska fayda milta hai. Optimizer ke bina kisi ek particular query ka access path haath se code karna aasaan lag sakta hai. Par long run mein general-purpose solution hi jeetta hai.

Comparison to document databases. Document databases ek maamle mein hierarchical model par wapas chale gaye: woh nested records, jaise Figure 2-1 ki positions, education aur contact info, ko alag table mein rakhne ke bajaye apne parent record ke andar store karte hain. Lekin many-to-one aur many-to-many relationships ke liye relational aur document databases mein koi fundamental farq nahi hai. Dono mein related item ko ek unique identifier se refer kiya jaata hai. Relational model mein woh identifier foreign key hai. Document model mein woh document reference hai. Dono hi case mein reference read time par resolve hota hai, join ya follow-up queries se. Ab tak document databases CODASYL ke raaste par nahi gaye hain.

Relational Versus Document Databases Today

Relational aur document databases kai maamlon mein alag hain, jaise fault tolerance (Chapter 5) aur concurrency handle karne ka tarika (Chapter 7). Yeh chapter sirf data model dekhta hai. Document model ke favour mein main arguments hain schema flexibility, locality se behtar performance, aur application code ke data structures se closer match. Relational model ka jawab hai joins ka behtar support, aur many-to-one aur many-to-many relationships ka behtar support.

Kaun sa data model simpler application code deta hai? Agar tumhare data ka structure document jaisa hai, yani one-to-many relationships ka ek tree jo aam taur par ek saath load hota hai, toh document model shayad achha idea hai. Relational technique shredding, jo aise structure ko kai tables mein baant deti hai, cumbersome schemas aur bekaar mein complicated application code tak le ja sakti hai.

Document model ki apni limits hain. Tum document ke andar ke nested item ko directly refer nahi kar sakte. Uski jagah tumhe position se point karna padta hai, jaise user 251 ki positions list ki doosri entry. Yeh hierarchical model ke access path se kaafi milta-julta hai. Jab tak documents bahut zyada deeply nested na ho, yeh aam taur par problem nahi hoti.

Joins ka kamzor support matter kar bhi sakta hai, aur nahi bhi. Jo analytics application document database mein record karti hai ki kaun se events kis time par hue, use shayad kabhi many-to-many relationships ki zaroorat na pade. Lekin agar tumhari application unka use karti hai, toh document model kam appealing ho jaata hai. Denormalizing se tum joins ki zaroorat kam kar sakte ho, par phir application code ko copies ko consistent rakhne ke liye mehnat karni padti hai. Tum kai requests karke joins emulate kar sakte ho, lekin isse complexity application mein chali jaati hai, aur yeh aam taur par database ke andar specialized code se hone wale join se slow ho sakta hai. Aise cases mein document model se application code kaafi zyada complex ho sakta hai aur performance bhi kharab.

Isliye book ke hisaab se general mein yeh kehna impossible hai ki kaun sa model simpler code deta hai. Yeh data items ke beech ke relationships par depend karta hai. Bahut zyada interconnected data ke liye document model awkward hai, relational model theek-thaak hai, aur graph models sabse natural hain.

Document model mein schema flexibility. Zyada tar document databases, aur relational databases ka JSON support, documents ke data par koi schema enforce nahi karte. Relational databases mein XML support ke saath aam taur par optional schema validation aata hai. Schema na ho toh document mein koi bhi keys aur values jodi ja sakti hain, aur padhte waqt clients ko koi guarantee nahi hoti ki document mein kaun se fields honge.

Dhyaan do

Document databases ko aksar schemaless kaha jaata hai, lekin book ke hisaab se yeh naam misleading hai. Data padhne wale code ko aam taur par kuch structure assume karna hi padta hai, yani ek implicit schema hota hai. Bas use database enforce nahi karta.

Zyada sahi term hai schema-on-read. Structure implicit hota hai, aur data padhte waqt hi interpret hota hai. Iske opposite hai schema-on-write, yani traditional relational approach, jisme schema explicit hota hai aur database ensure karta hai ki likha gaya har record uske according ho. Pehla programming language ki dynamic type checking jaisa hai, aur doosra static, compile-time type checking jaisa. Programmers dono ke merits par debate karte hain, aur book ke hisaab se database schemas ke saath bhi yahi hota hai. Koi clear sahi ya galat jawab nahi hai.

Yeh difference sabse saaf tab dikhta hai jab application apne data ka format badalna chahti hai. Maan lo abhi tum har user ka full name ek field mein store karte ho, aur first aur last name alag-alag store karna chahte ho. Document database mein tum nayi fields ke saath naye documents likhna shuru kar dete ho, aur aisa code jodte ho jo purane documents ko padhte waqt handle kare. Book ka example yeh hai:

if (user && user.name && !user.first_name) {
  // Documents written before Dec 8, 2013 don't have first_name
  user.first_name = user.name.split(" ")[0];
}

Statically typed relational schema mein tum uski jagah ek migration chalate:

ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN first_name text;
UPDATE users SET first_name = split_part(name, ' ', 1);  -- PostgreSQL
UPDATE users SET first_name = substring_index(name, ' ', 1);  -- MySQL
Example

Book har route ki cost samjhati hai. Schema changes ki reputation kharab hai ki woh slow hote hain aur downtime maangte hain, aur book ke hisaab se yeh poori tarah deserve nahi karte. Zyada tar relational systems ALTER TABLE kuch milliseconds mein chala dete hain. MySQL notable exception hai. Woh ALTER TABLE ke dauran poori table copy karta hai, jisse bade table par minutes ya hours ka downtime ho sakta hai, halanki isse bypass karne ke tools available hain.

UPDATE ki baat alag hai. Yeh kisi bhi database par slow ho sakta hai, kyunki har row dobara likhni padti hai. Agar yeh acceptable nahi hai, toh application first_name ko uski default value NULL (yani koi value nahi) par chhod sakti hai aur read time par fill kar sakti hai, bilkul waise hi jaise document database ke saath karti.

Schema-on-read tab advantage hai jab ek collection ke saare items ka structure same nahi hota. Aisa tab hota hai jab bahut alag-alag types ke objects hote hain aur har type ko apni table mein rakhna practical nahi hota. Aisa tab bhi hota hai jab structure external systems tay karte hain, jin par tumhara control nahi hai aur jo kabhi bhi badal sakte hain. In situations mein schema fayde se zyada nuksaan kar sakta hai, aur schemaless documents zyada natural model ho sakte hain. Lekin jab saare records ka structure same hone ki ummeed ho, tab schema use document aur enforce karne ka ek useful tarika hai. Chapter 4 schemas aur unke time ke saath badalne ki baat karta hai.

Try karo

Kisi aisi application ke baare mein socho jise tum jaante ho. Uska kaun sa data one-to-many items ka tree hai jo hamesha saath padha jaata hai, jaise profile aur uski addresses ki list? Kaun sa data shared hai, jaise region ya product category jise kai records point karte hain? Documents aur references ke beech boundary tum kahan rakhoge?

Queries ke liye data locality. Document aam taur par ek single continuous string ki tarah store hota hai, jo JSON, XML ya MongoDB ke BSON jaise binary variant mein encode hota hai. Agar tumhari application ko aksar poora document chahiye, jaise web page render karne ke liye, toh use ek unit ki tarah store karna performance advantage hai. Figure 2-1 ki tarah tables mein baanta data jama karne ke liye kai index lookups chahiye, jisse zyada disk seeks aur zyada time lag sakta hai.

Locality ka advantage tabhi kaam aata hai jab tumhe document ke bade hisse ek saath chahiye. Database aam taur par poora document load karta hai, chahe tumhe uska chhota sa hissa hi chahiye ho, jo bade documents ke liye wasteful hai. Jab document update hota hai, toh aam taur par poora dobara likha jaata hai. Sirf wahi changes in place aasaani se ho sakte hain jo encoded size ko nahi badalte. In wajahon se Kleppmann documents ko kaafi chhota rakhne aur aise writes se bachne ki salah dete hain jo document ko bada karte hain. In limits ki wajah se un situations ka set kam ho jaata hai jinmein document databases useful hain.

Locality ke liye related data ko saath rakhna sirf document model tak limited nahi hai. Google ka Spanner relational schema mein declare karne deta hai ki ek table ki rows ko parent table ke andar interleave, yani nest, kiya jaaye. Oracle yahi cheez multi-table index cluster tables naam ke feature se deta hai. Bigtable data model ka column-family concept, jo Cassandra aur HBase mein use hota hai, woh bhi locality manage karne ke kaam aata hai. Chapter 3 locality ke baare mein aur batata hai.

Document aur relational databases ka convergence. MySQL ko chhodkar zyada tar relational database systems 2000 ke dashak ke beech se XML support karte aaye hain. Isme XML documents mein local changes karne ke functions, aur unke andar index aur query karne ki ability shaamil hai. Isliye applications aise data models use kar sakti hain jo document database ke models se bahut milte-julte hain. PostgreSQL version 9.3 se, MySQL version 5.7 se, aur IBM DB2 version 10.5 se JSON documents ka milta-julta level ka support dete hain. Web APIs ke liye JSON kitna popular hai, yeh dekhte hue Kleppmann ko lagta hai ki doosre relational databases bhi yahi karenge.

Document side par RethinkDB apni query language mein relational jaise joins support karta hai. Kuch MongoDB drivers database references automatically resolve kar dete hain. Yeh effectively client side par hone wala join hai. Yeh database ke andar hone wale join se slow ho sakta hai, kyunki ismein extra network round trips lagte hain aur yeh kam optimized hota hai.

Book yeh bhi batati hai ki relational pioneer Edgar Codd ke relational model ke original description mein relational schema ke andar JSON documents jaisi cheez ki ijaazat thi. Row ki value ka simple number ya string hona zaroori nahi tha. Woh ek nested table ho sakti thi, jisse arbitrarily nested tree structure ban jaata. Aisa support SQL mein 30 saal se zyada baad aaya, JSON aur XML ke roop mein.

Kleppmann ko lagta hai ki waqt ke saath dono tarah ke databases ek-doosre ke jaise hote jaayenge, aur woh ise achhi baat maante hain, kyunki dono data models ek-doosre ke complement hain. Agar ek database document-like data handle kar sake aur us par relational queries bhi chala sake, toh applications features ka woh combination use kar sakti hain jo unki zaroorat ke liye sabse fit ho. Unka conclusion hai ki relational aur document models ka hybrid databases ke liye future ka achha raasta hai.

Data ke liye Query Languages

Relational model aaya, toh saath mein data maangne ka ek naya tarika bhi aaya. SQL ek declarative query language hai, jabki IMS aur CODASYL apne databases ko imperative code se query karte the. Dono mein fark kya hai?

Zyaadatar common programming languages imperative hoti hain. Inmein computer ko bataya jaata hai ki kaun se steps, kis order mein perform karne hain. Maan lo tumhare paas animal species ki ek list hai aur tumhe sirf sharks chahiye. JavaScript mein tum kuch aisa function likh sakte ho:

function getSharks() {
  var sharks = [];
  for (var i = 0; i < animals.length; i++) {
    if (animals[i].family === "Sharks") {
      sharks.push(animals[i]);
    }
  }
  return sharks;
}

Yeh function pehle ek empty list banata hai. Phir har animal par loop chalata hai. Har animal ke liye check karta hai ki family Sharks hai ya nahi, aur agar hai toh use list mein daal deta hai. Aakhir mein list return kar deta hai. Tum isse line by line step karte hue imagine kar sakte ho: conditions check karna, variables update karna, aur decide karna ki loop ek baar aur ghumana hai ya nahi.

Relational algebra mein yahi result ek single expression se likha jaata hai, jahan σ (Greek letter sigma) selection operator hai. Yeh sirf wahi animals return karta hai jo family = Sharks condition match karte hain. SQL ko design hi aise kiya gaya tha ki woh relational algebra ke structure ko kaafi had tak follow kare. Iska equivalent SQL sirf ek line ka hai:

SELECT * FROM animals WHERE family = 'Sharks';

Declarative language steps nahi batati. Tum bas us data ka pattern batate ho jo tumhe chahiye: results kin conditions ko meet karo, aur unhe kaise transform karna hai, jaise sort, group ya add up. Wahan tak kaise pahunchna hai, yeh tum nahi batate. Database system ka query optimizer decide karta hai ki kaun se indexes aur kaun se join methods use hon, aur query ke parts kis order mein chalein.

Declarative queries ke do bade advantages hain:

  • Yeh aam taur par zyada concise hoti hain aur imperative API se kaam karna aasaan hota hai.
  • Yeh database engine ki details chhupa leti hain. Matlab database queries mein koi change kiye bina performance improvements add kar sakta hai.

Imperative example mein animals ki ordering par dhyaan do. List ek particular order mein wapas aati hai, aur ho sakta hai code us order par depend kare. Maan lo database ko unused disk space reclaim karna hai. Uske liye use records ko idhar-udhar move karna pad sakta hai, jisse yeh order badal jaayega. Kya woh yeh safely kar sakta hai? SQL version mein haan. SQL koi particular order promise nahi karta, isliye database rows ko freely rearrange kar sakta hai. Imperative code mein database ko pata nahi hota ki program order par rely karta hai ya nahi. SQL kam functionality deta hai, aur isi wajah se database ko automatic optimization ke liye kaafi zyada gunjaish milti hai.

Declarative languages parallel execution ke liye bhi achhi hoti hain. Aajkal CPUs zyada cores add karke tez ho rahe hain, clock speed bahut badha kar nahi. Imperative code ko cores aur machines ke across parallelize karna bahut mushkil hai, kyunki usmein instructions ek particular order mein chalne ke liye likhe hote hain. Declarative query sirf results ka pattern batati hai, unhe banane ka algorithm nahi. Isliye agar appropriate ho, toh database use parallel mein chala sakta hai.

Web par Declarative Queries

Declarative languages ke advantages sirf databases tak limited nahi hain. Book web browser mein dono styles ka comparison karti hai. Maan lo tumhare paas ocean animals ka ek page hai jisme navigation list hai. Sharks wala item woh page hai jo abhi dikh raha hai, isliye uske list item par CSS class selected laga hai, aur uska title us item ke andar ek paragraph mein hai. Ab tum chahte ho ki selected page ke title ka background blue ho. CSS mein iske liye bas ek rule kaafi hai:

li.selected > p {
  background-color: blue;
}

Selector li.selected > p ek pattern describe karta hai: har woh paragraph jiska direct parent ek list item ho jis par class selected hai. Sharks ka title match karta hai. Whales ka title match nahi karta, kyunki uske list item par woh class nahi hai. Matching browser khud kar leta hai. XSL (XML ki ek stylesheet language) yahi baat XPath expression li[@class='selected']/p se express kar sakti hai. CSS aur XSL dono declarative styling languages hain.

Yahi kaam JavaScript mein imperative tarike se, core DOM API use karke karna ho, toh har list item par loop chalana padega, uski class check karni padegi, phir uske children par loop chalana padega, dekhna padega ki kaun se paragraphs hain, aur tab jaake matching wale par style set karni padegi. Yeh kaam toh karta hai, lekin kaafi lamba hai aur padhna mushkil. Saath mein isme do serious problems bhi hain:

  • Agar selected class hata di jaaye, jaise user ne koi doosra page click kar diya, toh blue rang waise hi rehta hai. Code dobara chalane se bhi woh nahi hatta, isliye item tab tak highlighted rehta hai jab tak poora page reload na ho. CSS mein browser khud notice kar leta hai ki rule ab apply nahi hota, aur class hatte hi blue hata deta hai.
  • Agar tum koi naya API use karna chahte ho, jaise getElementsByClassName ya document.evaluate, jo shayad faster ho, toh tumhe code rewrite karna padega. Doosri taraf, browser vendors compatibility tode bina CSS aur XPath ko tez kar sakte hain.

Book ka conclusion yeh hai ki JavaScript mein imperative style manipulation se declarative CSS kaafi behtar hai. Isi tarah, databases ke liye SQL jaisi declarative query languages imperative query APIs se kaafi behtar sabit hui. (IMS aur CODASYL dono imperative APIs use karte the. Applications aam taur par COBOL code se records ko ek-ek karke step karte the.)

MapReduce Querying

MapReduce ek programming model hai, jise Google ne popular banaya, aur jo bahut saare machines par badi matra mein data ko bulk mein process karne ke liye hai. Kuch NoSQL datastores, jaise MongoDB aur CouchDB, iska ek limited form support karte hain, taaki bahut saare documents par read-only queries chalayi ja sakein. MapReduce ki general baat Chapter 10 mein hai. Yahan hum bas dekhte hain ki MongoDB ise kaise use karta hai.

MapReduce na declarative query language hai, na poori tarah imperative query API. Yeh dono ke beech kahin baithta hai. Query logic code ke chhote snippets ke roop mein likhi jaati hai, aur processing framework un snippets ko baar-baar call karta hai. Yeh model do functions par based hai jo kai functional programming languages mein milte hain: map (ise collect bhi kehte hain) aur reduce (ise fold ya inject bhi kehte hain).

Example

Maan lo tum ek marine biologist hain. Jab bhi tum ocean mein animals dekhte ho, apne database mein ek observation record add kar dete ho. Ab tumhe ek report chahiye ki har mahine tumne kitne sharks dekhe. PostgreSQL mein tum yeh likh sakte ho:

SELECT date_trunc('month', observation_timestamp) AS observation_month,
       sum(num_animals) AS total_animals
FROM observations
WHERE family = 'Sharks'
GROUP BY observation_month;

Step by step dekhein toh yeh query pehle sirf Sharks family ke observations rakhti hai. Function date_trunc('month', timestamp) woh calendar month nikalta hai jisme timestamp aata hai, aur us month ki starting return karta hai, yani timestamp ko nearest month tak neeche round kar deta hai. Phir query observations ko month ke hisaab se group karti hai aur har group mein animals ki count add up karti hai.

Yahi report MongoDB ke MapReduce feature se bhi likhi ja sakti hai. Is call mein teen cheezein jaati hain: ek map function, ek reduce function, aur options. Options mein ek query hoti hai jo sirf wahi documents rakhti hai jinki family Sharks hai, aur ek out setting hoti hai jo output collection ka naam batati hai, yaani monthlySharkReport. Filter call ka declarative hissa hai, aur yeh MapReduce ka MongoDB-specific extension hai. Phir kaam yeh do functions karte hain:

  • map function har matching document ke liye ek baar chalta hai, aur this us document par set hota hai. Yeh observation ke year aur month se ek key banata hai, jaise “2013-12”, aur us key ko animals ki count ke saath value ke roop mein emit kar deta hai.
  • Emit hue key-value pairs key ke hisaab se group ho jaate hain. Har key ke liye, yani har month ke liye, reduce function ek baar chalta hai aur values ko add up karta hai, jisse us month ke animals ka total milta hai.

Do example documents par yeh aise kaam karta hai. Dono sharks hain. Pehle mein 25 December 1995 ka sighting record hai, species Carcharodon carcharias ke 3 animals. Doosre mein 12 December 1995 ka sighting record hai, species Carcharias taurus ke 4 animals. Map function har document ke liye ek baar chalta hai aur pehle ("1995-12", 3) aur phir ("1995-12", 4) emit karta hai. Dono pairs ki key same hai, isliye reduce function key "1995-12" aur values 3 aur 4 ke saath ek baar chalta hai. Woh 7 return karta hai.

Map aur reduce functions restricted hote hain. Yeh pure functions hone chahiye: yeh sirf wahi data use karte hain jo input mein pass hua hai, additional database queries nahi chala sakte, aur inke koi side effects nahi hone chahiye. In rules ki wajah se database yeh functions kahin bhi, kisi bhi order mein chala sakta hai, aur failure hone par dobara chala sakta hai. Phir bhi yeh powerful hain. Yeh strings parse kar sakte hain, library functions call kar sakte hain, calculations kar sakte hain, aur bhi bahut kuch.

MapReduce machines ke cluster par distributed execution ke liye ek kaafi low-level model hai. SQL jaisi higher-level query languages ko MapReduce operations ki pipeline ke roop mein build kiya ja sakta hai (Chapter 10 mein yeh samjhaya gaya hai). Lekin SQL ke kai distributed implementations aise bhi hain jo MapReduce use nahi karte. SQL mein aisa kuch nahi hai jo single machine zaroori kare, aur distributed query execution par MapReduce ki monopoly nahi hai.

Query ke beech mein JavaScript use karna advanced queries ke liye ek bahut achhi feature hai, aur yeh sirf MapReduce tak limited nahi hai. Kuch SQL databases ko bhi JavaScript functions se extend kiya ja sakta hai.

MapReduce mein ek usability problem hai. Tumhe do carefully coordinated functions likhne padte hain, jo aksar ek single query likhne se mushkil hota hai. Declarative query optimizer ko performance improve karne ke liye zyada gunjaish bhi deti hai. Inhi wajahon se MongoDB 2.2 ne ek declarative query language add ki, jiska naam aggregation pipeline hai. Us language mein shark report aisi dikhti hai:

db.observations.aggregate([
  { $match: { family: "Sharks" } },
  { $group: {
      _id: {
        year: { $year: "$observationTimestamp" },
        month: { $month: "$observationTimestamp" }
      },
      totalAnimals: { $sum: "$numAnimals" }
  } }
]);

Pehla stage sirf shark documents rakhta hai. Doosra stage unhe timestamp ke year aur month ke hisaab se group karta hai, aur har group ke andar numAnimals ko add up karta hai. Aggregation pipeline SQL ke ek subset jitni hi expressive hai. Yeh SQL ke English-jaise sentences ki jagah JSON-based syntax use karti hai, jise book taste ka matter maanti hai. Iska moral yeh hai ki ek NoSQL system ant mein SQL ko hi reinvent kar sakta hai, bas bhes badal kar.

Graph-Like Data Models

Data models mein many-to-many relationships ek bada differentiator hain. Agar tumhari application mein zyada tar one-to-many relationships hain, jaise tree-structured data, ya records ke beech almost koi relationship nahi hai, toh document model fit baithta hai. Lekin jab many-to-many relationships bahut common hon, toh picture badal jaati hai. Simple cases ko relational model achhe se handle kar leta hai. Par data ke connections jaise-jaise complex hote jaate hain, data ko graph ki tarah model karna zyada natural lagne lagta hai.

Graph mein do tarah ke objects hote hain. Vertices (jinhe nodes ya entities bhi kehte hain) woh cheezein hain, aur edges (relationships ya arcs) unke beech ke connections hain. Kaafi tarah ka data is shape mein fit hota hai:

  • Social graphs: vertices log hote hain, aur edges dikhate hain ki kaun kis ko jaanta hai.
  • The web graph: vertices web pages hote hain, aur edges unke beech ke HTML links hote hain.
  • Road ya rail networks: vertices junctions hote hain, aur edges unke beech ki roads ya railway lines hoti hain.

In graphs par kuch well-known algorithms chalte hain. Car navigation system road network mein do points ke beech ka shortest path dhoondhta hai. PageRank web graph par chalta hai aur measure karta hai ki ek page kitna popular hai, jo search results mein uski ranking mein kaam aata hai.

In examples mein saare vertices ek hi tarah ki cheez hain. Lekin graphs ka itna uniform hona zaroori nahi hai. Ek hi datastore mein, ek consistent model ke saath, bilkul alag-alag types ke objects store ho sakte hain. Book Facebook ka example deti hai. Woh ek single graph rakhta hai jisme kai types ke vertices hain: log, locations, events, check-ins aur comments. Uske edges batate hain ki kaun log friends hain, kaun sa check-in kis location par hua, kisne kis post par comment kiya, aur kaun sa person kis event mein gaya.

Chapter ke is hisse mein book ek hi example use karti hai, jo Figure 2-5 mein dikhaya gaya hai. Yeh social network ya family tree se aa sakta hai. Isme do log hain: Lucy, jo Idaho se hai, aur Alain, jo France ke Beaune se hai. Dono married hain aur London mein rehte hain.

Graphs ko structure karne aur query karne ke kai related tarike hain. Chapter property graph model cover karta hai, jo Neo4j, Titan aur InfiniteGraph use karte hain, aur triple-store model, jo Datomic, AllegroGraph aur kuch aur use karte hain. Querying ke liye teen declarative languages hain: Cypher, SPARQL aur Datalog. Imperative graph query languages bhi hain, jaise Gremlin, aur graph processing frameworks bhi, jaise Pregel, jise Chapter 10 cover karta hai.

Property Graphs

Property graph model mein har vertex mein yeh hota hai:

  • Ek unique identifier.
  • Outgoing edges ka ek set.
  • Incoming edges ka ek set.
  • Properties ka collection, jo key-value pairs hote hain.

Har edge mein yeh hota hai:

  • Ek unique identifier.
  • Woh vertex jahan se edge shuru hota hai, jise tail vertex kehte hain.
  • Woh vertex jahan edge khatam hota hai, jise head vertex kehte hain.
  • Ek label jo batata hai ki dono vertices ke beech kis tarah ka relationship hai.
  • Properties ka collection, jo key-value pairs hote hain.

Tum graph ko do relational tables mein store kar sakte ho, ek vertices ke liye aur ek edges ke liye. Book ka Example 2-2 yahi karta hai aur properties ke liye PostgreSQL ka json type use karta hai. Har edge row apna tail aur head vertex record karti hai, aur do indexes, har ek par ek, kisi bhi vertex ke incoming ya outgoing edges jaldi dhoondhne dete hain. Teen features sabse zyada matter karte hain:

  1. Koi bhi vertex kisi bhi doosre vertex se edge bana sakta hai. Koi schema yeh limit nahi karta ki kin cheezon ko connect kiya ja sakta hai.
  2. Kisi bhi vertex ke liye tum uske incoming aur outgoing, dono edges efficiently dhoond sakte ho. Isliye tum graph ko traverse kar sakte ho, yani vertices ki chain mein ek path follow karna, aage bhi aur peeche bhi.
  3. Alag-alag relationships ke liye alag labels use karke, ek hi graph kai tarah ki information rakh sakta hai aur data model clean bhi rehta hai.

In features se graphs mein bahut flexibility aati hai, jaisa book ka Figure 2-5 dikhata hai. Usme aisi cheezein hain jinhe traditional relational schema mein express karna mushkil hoga. Alag countries ke regional structures alag hote hain: France mein départements aur régions hain, jabki US mein counties aur states hain. Ek country kisi doosre region ke andar ho sakti hai, jo history ki ek quirk hai. Data ki granularity bhi alag-alag hai. Lucy ka current residence ek city ke roop mein record hai, jabki uska birthplace sirf state ke level par record hai.

Graph ko aur bhi kaafi extend kiya ja sakta hai. Maan lo tum har food allergen ke liye ek vertex add karte ho, har person se un allergens tak ek edge jinse use reaction hota hai, aur foods ke vertices, jo un substances se linked hon jo unme hain. Phir ek query yeh nikaal sakti hai ki har person ke liye kya khana safe hai. Book ka point hai ki graphs evolvability ke liye achhe hain: application mein features badhne par graph ko badalte data ke hisaab se extend kiya ja sakta hai.

The Cypher Query Language

Cypher property graphs ke liye ek declarative query language hai. Ise Neo4j graph database ke liye banaya gaya tha. Iska naam film The Matrix ke ek character se aaya hai, aur iska cryptography ke ciphers se koi lena-dena nahi hai.

Book ka Example 2-3 ek Cypher statement dikhata hai jo Figure 2-5 ka ek hissa graph database mein insert karta hai. Har vertex ko ek symbolic name milta hai, jaise USA ya Idaho, aur statement ke baad ke hisse in names se arrow notation mein edges banate hain. Notation (Idaho) -[:WITHIN]-> (USA) ek edge banata hai jiska label WITHIN hai, jisme Idaho tail hai aur USA head. Statement ki last lines yeh hain:

(Idaho) -[:WITHIN]-> (USA) -[:WITHIN]-> (NAmerica),
(Lucy) -[:BORN_IN]-> (Idaho)
Example

Ab book ek real sawaal poochti hai: un sab logon ke naam nikaalo jo United States se Europe emigrate hue. Precisely kehein toh, aise har vertex ko dhoondho jisme US ke andar kisi location tak BORN_IN edge ho, aur Europe ke andar kisi location tak LIVES_IN edge bhi ho, phir har ek ka name return karo. Example 2-4 ise Cypher mein aise likhta hai:

MATCH
  (person) -[:BORN_IN]-> () -[:WITHIN*0..]-> (us:Location {name:'United States'}),
  (person) -[:LIVES_IN]-> () -[:WITHIN*0..]-> (eu:Location {name:'Europe'})
RETURN person.name

MATCH clause ka arrow notation graph mein patterns dhoondhta hai. Pattern (person) -[:BORN_IN]-> () aise kisi bhi do vertices ko match karta hai jo BORN_IN edge se jude hon. Tail vertex variable person se bind hota hai, aur head ko unnamed chhod diya jaata hai. Phir query ko ek hi person vertex par do conditions ki tarah padha ja sakta hai:

  1. Person ka kisi vertex tak outgoing BORN_IN edge hai. Us vertex se tum outgoing WITHIN edges ki chain follow kar sakte ho, jab tak aise Location vertex tak na pahunch jaayein jiska name “United States” ho.
  2. Isi person ka ek outgoing LIVES_IN edge bhi hai. Use follow karke, aur phir outgoing WITHIN edges ki chain follow karke, tum aakhir mein aise Location vertex tak pahunchte ho jiska name “Europe” hai.

Jo bhi person dono conditions poori karta hai, uske liye query name property return karti hai. Syntax :WITHIN*0.. ka matlab hai ki WITHIN edge ko zero ya zyada baar follow kiya ja sakta hai. Yeh regular expression ke * operator jaisa kaam karta hai. Zero hops us case ko cover karta hai jab birthplace ya residence khud country ya continent ho.

Is query ko chalane ke kai tarike hain. Ek tarika yeh suggest hota hai ki pehle saare logon ko scan karo, har ek ka birthplace aur residence check karo, aur jo match kare unhe rakh lo. Lekin database ulta kaam bhi kar sakta hai. Agar name property par index hai, toh woh US aur Europe ke vertices jaldi dhoond sakta hai. Un dono se woh saare incoming WITHIN edges follow karke andar ki har location collect karta hai. Aakhir mein woh aise log dhoondhta hai jinka in locations mein se kisi ek tak incoming BORN_IN ya LIVES_IN edge ho.

Declarative language mein jaisa hota hai, query likhte waqt tumhe yeh choice batani nahi padti. Optimizer woh strategy chunta hai jo sabse fast hone ka andaza ho, aur tum application ke baaki kaam par lag sakte ho.

Graph Queries in SQL

Example 2-2 ne dikhaya ki graph data relational database mein store ho sakta hai. Lekin kya ise SQL se query bhi kar sakte hain? Haan, par thodi mushkil se. Relational database mein tumhe aam taur par pehle se pata hota hai ki query ko kaun se joins chahiye. Graph query mein tumhe wanted vertex milne se pehle edges ki variable count follow karni pad sakti hai. Joins ki count pehle se fixed nahi hoti.

Yeh Cypher query ke (...) -[:WITHIN*0..]-> (...) hisse mein hota hai. Kisi person ka LIVES_IN edge kisi bhi tarah ki location par point kar sakta hai: street, city, district, region, state, waghera. Ek city kisi region ke andar ho sakti hai, region state ke andar, aur state country ke andar. LIVES_IN edge seedha us location par point kar sakta hai jo dhoondhi ja rahi hai, ya hierarchy mein woh kai levels door ho sakti hai. Cypher ka :WITHIN*0.. in sab cases ko ek chhote se expression mein cover kar leta hai.

SQL:1999 se ek milta-julta idea recursive common table expressions se likha ja sakta hai, jisme WITH RECURSIVE syntax use hota hai. Isse query ek step ko tab tak repeat kar sakti hai jab tak kuch naya na mile. Book ka Example 2-5 wahi emigration query SQL mein chalata hai. Yeh PostgreSQL, IBM DB2, Oracle aur SQL Server mein chalta hai, lekin Cypher ke comparison mein syntax kaafi clumsy hai.

Example

SQL version vertex IDs ke chaar sets banata hai, phir unhe join karta hai. Step by step:

  1. in_usa. Woh vertex dhoondho jiska name “United States” hai, aur use set in_usa ka pehla member banao. Set mein pehle se present vertices se saare incoming within edges follow karo, aur unke tails ko set mein add karo. Tab tak repeat karo jab tak aur incoming within edges na bachein.
  2. in_europe. Yahi cheez “Europe” naam ke vertex se shuru karke karo, aur set in_europe banao.
  3. born_in_usa. in_usa ke har vertex ke liye incoming born_in edges follow karo. Isse woh log milte hain jo United States ke andar kahin paida hue.
  4. lives_in_europe. in_europe ke har vertex ke liye incoming lives_in edges follow karo. Isse woh log milte hain jo Europe mein kahin rehte hain.
  5. The final join. Logon ke dono sets ko vertex ID par join karke intersect karo, aur jo log dono mein hain unke names return karo.

Book yeh point karti hai ki wahi query ek language mein 4 lines ki hai aur doosri mein 29 lines ki. Isse pata chalta hai ki alag data models alag use cases ke liye design hue hain, aur apni application ke liye sahi model chunna kitna zaroori hai.

Triple-Stores and SPARQL

Triple-store model mostly property graph model ke barabar hai, bas same ideas ke liye alag words use hote hain. Phir bhi ise discuss karna worth hai, kyunki triple-stores ke liye bane tools aur languages tumhare toolbox mein valuable addition ho sakte hain.

Triple-store mein saari information bahut simple teen-hisson wale statements mein store hoti hai: (subject, predicate, object). Triple (Jim, likes, bananas) mein Jim subject hai, likes predicate (verb) hai, aur bananas object hai.

Triple ka subject graph ke ek vertex ke barabar hota hai. Object do cheezon mein se ek hota hai:

  1. Primitive type ki value, jaise string ya number. Tab predicate aur object milkar subject vertex ki property ke key aur value ki tarah kaam karte hain. Jaise (lucy, age, 33) ek aise vertex ki tarah hai jiska naam lucy hai aur properties {"age":33} hain.
  2. Graph ka ek aur vertex. Tab predicate ek edge hota hai, subject uska tail vertex, aur object uska head vertex. Jaise (lucy, marriedTo, alain) mein lucy aur alain dono vertices hain, aur marriedTo unke beech ke edge ka label hai.

Book ka Example 2-6 wahi data jo Example 2-3 mein tha, Turtle mein likhta hai, jo ek human-readable format hai aur Notation3 (N3) ka subset hai. Vertices ko _: se shuru hone wale names se likha jaata hai. In names ka file ke bahar koi matlab nahi hota. Yeh sirf isliye hain ki file bata sake ki kaun se triples same vertex ko refer karte hain. Jab predicate edge ho, toh object vertex hota hai, jaise _:idaho :within _:usa. Jab predicate property ho, toh object string hota hai, jaise _:usa :name "United States".

Har fact ke liye wahi subject baar-baar likhna thakaane wala hai, isliye Turtle semicolons se ek subject ke baare mein kai baatein kehne deta hai. Example 2-7 wahi data zyada concise tarike se dikhata hai:

@prefix : <urn:example:>.
_:lucy a :Person; :name "Lucy"; :bornIn _:idaho.
_:idaho a :Location; :name "Idaho"; :type "state"; :within _:usa.
_:usa a :Location; :name "United States"; :type "country"; :within _:namerica.
_:namerica a :Location; :name "North America"; :type "continent".

The Semantic Web

Agar tum triple-stores ke baare mein padhoge, toh semantic web par likhe gaye bahut saare content mein kheench sakte ho. Triple-store data model semantic web se bilkul independent hai. Jaise Datomic ek triple-store hai jo semantic web se koi connection claim nahi karta. (Technically, Datomic triples ki jagah 5-tuples store karta hai. Do extra fields versioning ke metadata rakhte hain.) Lekin kai logon ke mind mein dono kaafi closely linked hain, isliye book unhe briefly discuss karti hai.

Semantic web ka core idea simple aur reasonable hai. Websites already information text aur pictures ke roop mein publish karti hain jo insaan padhte hain. Toh use computers ke liye machine-readable data ke roop mein bhi kyun na publish karein? Resource Description Framework (RDF) ko isliye banaya gaya tha ki alag-alag websites data ek consistent format mein publish kar sakein. Phir alag sites ka data automatically combine hokar data ka ek web ban sakta tha, yani sab cheezon ka ek internet-wide database.

Unfortunately, semantic web ko early 2000s mein zaroorat se zyada hype mila aur woh abhi tak practice mein realize nahi hua. Isse kai logon ko cynicism ho gaya. Isme acronyms ki bheed, bahut complex standards proposals, aur kaafi hubris bhi raha. Lekin is project se achha kaam bhi nikla hai, aur triples application ke liye achha internal data model ho sakte hain, chahe tumhe web par RDF data publish karne mein koi interest na ho.

The RDF Data Model

Example 2-7 mein jo Turtle language use hui, woh RDF data ka ek human-readable format hai. RDF kabhi-kabhi XML format mein bhi likha jaata hai, jo wahi baat bahut verbose tarike se kehta hai. Example 2-8 Example 2-7 ka data RDF/XML mein dikhata hai. Har location ek nested element ban jaati hai, aur Lucy ek Person element hai jisme bornIn element Idaho par point karta hai. Book Turtle ya N3 ko prefer karti hai kyunki woh padhne mein bahut aasaan hai, aur Apache Jena jaise tools zaroorat padne par RDF formats ke beech convert kar sakte hain.

RDF mein kuch quirks hain kyunki ise poore internet par data exchange ke liye design kiya gaya tha. Triple ke subject, predicate aur object aksar URIs (web addresses jo unique names ki tarah use hote hain) hote hain. Jaise predicate ek aisa URI ho sakta hai jisme kisi company ke domain par namespace ke baad within ya lives_in aaye, plain words WITHIN ya LIVES_IN ki jagah. Wajah yeh hai ki tum apna data kisi aur ke data ke saath combine kar sako. Agar koi doosri organization word within ko alag meaning deti hai, toh uske predicates alag URIs hote hain, isliye koi clash nahi hota. Namespace URL ka kisi real web page par jaana zaroori nahi. Sirf naming matter karti hai. Book ke examples urn:example:within jaise non-resolvable URIs use karte hain taaki confusion na ho, aur woh prefix file ke top par ek hi baar declare karte hain.

The SPARQL Query Language

SPARQL un triple-stores ke liye query language hai jo RDF data model use karte hain. Iska naam SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language ka acronym hai, aur ise “sparkle” bola jaata hai. Yeh Cypher se pehle aayi thi. Cypher ki pattern matching SPARQL se udhaar li gayi hai, isliye dono kaafi similar dikhte hain.

Example

Wahi emigration question, yani un logon ko dhoondhna jo US se Europe gaye, SPARQL mein aur bhi concise hai. Example 2-9 aisa hai:

PREFIX : <urn:example:>
SELECT ?personName WHERE {
  ?person :name ?personName.
  ?person :bornIn / :within* / :name "United States".
  ?person :livesIn / :within* / :name "Europe".
}

Step by step padhein toh query mein ek SELECT hai aur ek hi person ke baare mein teen patterns. Variables question mark se shuru hote hain. Pehla pattern person ka name ?personName se bind karta hai. Doosra kehta hai ki person kisi cheez mein paida hua, jahan se :within steps ki chain (zero ya zyada) United States naam ki cheez tak jaati hai. Teesra kehta hai ki person kisi aisi cheez mein rehta hai jiski :within steps ki chain Europe naam ki cheez tak pahunchti hai.

Structure Cypher query se kaafi milta hai. Cypher pattern (person) -[:BORN_IN]-> () -[:WITHIN*0..]-> (location) SPARQL pattern ?person :bornIn / :within* ?location. ke barabar hai. RDF properties aur edges mein fark nahi karta aur dono ke liye predicates use karta hai, isliye wahi syntax properties ko bhi match karta hai. Cypher pattern (usa {name:'United States'}) SPARQL mein ?usa :name "United States". likha jaata hai, jo variable ko us kisi bhi vertex se bind karta hai jiska name string “United States” ho. Book ka conclusion hai ki SPARQL ek achhi query language hai. Semantic web kabhi na bhi aaye, toh bhi yeh applications ke liye internally use karne ka powerful tool ho sakti hai.

Graph Databases Compared to the Network Model

Chapter mein pehle CODASYL aur relational model many-to-many relationships handle karne ke liye compete kar rahe the. Pehli nazar mein CODASYL ka network model graph model jaisa lagta hai. Toh kya graph databases bhesh badal kar aaya CODASYL ka second coming hain? Book kehti hai nahi, aur chaar differences deti hai:

  • CODASYL mein database ka ek schema hota tha jo batata tha ki kaun sa record type kis doosre type ke andar nest ho sakta hai. Graph database mein aisi koi restriction nahi hai. Koi bhi vertex kisi bhi doosre vertex se edge bana sakta hai, jisse requirements badalne par adapt karna bahut aasaan ho jaata hai.
  • CODASYL mein kisi record tak pahunchne ka ek hi tarika tha: uske access paths mein se kisi ek ko traverse karna. Graph database mein tum kisi bhi vertex ko seedha uski unique ID se refer kar sakte ho, ya index se kisi particular value wale vertices dhoondh sakte ho.
  • CODASYL mein ek record ke children ek ordered set hote the. Database ko woh order maintain karna padta tha, jo storage layout ko affect karta tha, aur records insert karne wali applications ko unki positions ki fikar karni padti thi. Graph database mein vertices aur edges ordered nahi hote. Tum results ko sirf query chalate waqt sort kar sakte ho.
  • CODASYL mein saari queries imperative thi. Unhe likhna mushkil tha aur schema badalne par woh aasaani se tooth jaati thi. Graph database mein agar tum chaho toh traversal imperative code mein likh sakte ho, lekin zyada tar graph databases Cypher ya SPARQL jaisi high-level declarative languages bhi support karte hain.

The Foundation: Datalog

Datalog SPARQL ya Cypher se kaafi purani hai. Academics ne 1980s mein ispar bahut study ki thi. Software engineers mein yeh kam jaani jaati hai, lekin yahi woh foundation deti hai jis par baad ki query languages bani hain. Yeh Datomic ki query language hai, aur Cascalog Datalog ka implementation hai jo Hadoop mein bade datasets query karne ke liye hai. (Datomic aur Cascalog Datalog ke liye Clojure S-expression syntax use karte hain. Yeh chapter Prolog syntax use karta hai, jo padhne mein thoda aasaan hai. Difference sirf notation ka hai.)

Datalog ka data model triple-store model jaisa hi hai, bas thoda generalized. Triple ko (subject, predicate, object) likhne ki jagah tum use predicate(subject, object) likhte hain. Example 2-10 pehle ke examples ka data isi form mein likhta hai:

name(namerica, 'North America').
type(namerica, continent).
name(usa, 'United States').
type(usa, country).
within(usa, namerica).
name(idaho, 'Idaho').
type(idaho, state).
within(idaho, usa).
name(lucy, 'Lucy').
born_in(lucy, idaho).

Example 2-11 emigration query ko Datalog mein likhta hai. Cypher aur SPARQL, jo SELECT se shuru hote hain, unse alag Datalog chhote-chhote steps leti hai. Pehle woh rules define karti hai jo database ko naye predicates ke baare mein batate hain. Rules yeh hain:

within_recursive(Location, Name) :- name(Location, Name).
within_recursive(Location, Name) :- within(Location, Via), within_recursive(Via, Name).
migrated(Name, BornIn, LivingIn) :- name(Person, Name),
    born_in(Person, BornLoc), within_recursive(BornLoc, BornIn),
    lives_in(Person, LivingLoc), within_recursive(LivingLoc, LivingIn).
?- migrated(Who, 'United States', 'Europe').

Pehla rule, jise book rule 1 number deti hai, kehta hai ki naam wali location apne andar hi hoti hai. Doosra, rule 2, kehta hai ki agar koi location kisi jagah ke andar hai, aur woh jagah kisi named location ke andar hai, toh woh location bhi us named location ke andar hai. Rule 3 migrated define karta hai: diya hua naam wala person kisi jagah paida hua aur kisi jagah rehta hai, aur un dono jagahon mein se har ek named regions ke andar hai. Last line sawaal hai. Yeh Who ki har value maangti hai jab birthplace United States ke andar ho aur residence Europe ke andar. Jawab Lucy hai.

Uppercase words variables hain, aur predicates wahi tarah match karte hain jaise Cypher aur SPARQL mein. Jaise name(Location, Name) fact name(namerica, 'North America') se match karta hai, Location ko namerica se aur Name ko 'North America' se bind karke. Rule tab apply hota hai jab system :- symbol ke right ke har predicate ko match kar sake. Apply hone par aisa hota hai jaise left side ko database mein add kar diya gaya ho, variables ko unki matched values se replace karke. Rules doosre rules ko refer kar sakte hain, bilkul waise jaise functions functions ko call karte hain ya khud ko recursively call karte hain. Isliye complex queries ek-ek chhote piece se banayi ja sakti hain.

Book ek tarika dikhati hai ki rules example data par kaise apply hote hain:

  1. name(namerica, 'North America') present hai, isliye rule 1 apply hota hai. Yeh within_recursive(namerica, 'North America') generate karta hai.
  2. within(usa, namerica) present hai, aur pichhle step ne within_recursive(namerica, 'North America') produce kiya tha. Isliye rule 2 apply hota hai aur within_recursive(usa, 'North America') generate karta hai.
  3. within(idaho, usa) present hai, aur pichhle step ne within_recursive(usa, 'North America') produce kiya tha. Isliye rule 2 phir apply hota hai aur within_recursive(idaho, 'North America') generate karta hai.

Rules 1 aur 2 ko baar-baar apply karke within_recursive predicate North America ki, ya kisi bhi aur named location ki, database mein present har location list kar sakta hai. Neeche ka diagram derivations ki yeh chain dikhata hai.

Rule 3 phir wahi derived facts use karta hai. Woh aise log dhoondhta hai jo kisi location mein paida hue, aur kisi location mein rehte hain, jo do named regions ke andar aati ho. United States aur Europe ke saath query karne par person variable Who reh jaata hai, isliye system dhoondhta hai ki ise kaun si values bhar sakti hain. Jawab wahi hai jo Cypher aur SPARQL queries mein tha.

Datalog ke liye is chapter ki doosri languages se alag tarah se sochna padta hai. Lekin yeh powerful hai, kyunki rules ko combine karke kai queries mein reuse kiya ja sakta hai. Simple one-off queries ke liye yeh kam convenient hai, aur data jaise-jaise complex hota hai, yeh uske saath behtar cope karti hai.

Asli idea

Woh model chuno jo tumhare data ki shape se match kare. Tree-shaped, self-contained data documents ke liye theek hai. Shared, many-to-one links relational tables ke liye theek hain. Highly connected data, jahan kuch bhi kisi se bhi related ho sakta hai, graph models ke liye theek hai, jo uske liye sabse natural fit hain.

Try karo

Maan lo tum Idaho ke andar ek city ke liye naya vertex add karte ho. Us city ke liye Datalog database mein tum kaun se naye facts add karoge? Phir North America ke andar kya hai poochne par kaun sa existing rule us city ko dhoondhne dega? Check karein ki rule applications ki chain naye city tak pahunchti hai.

Trade-offs
ModelGood atCosts
Relational (SQL)Joins, many-to-one aur many-to-many links, declarative queries, aur aisa optimizer jo indexes aur join order chunta haiOne-to-many data tables mein bat jaata hai, jiske liye code objects aur rows ke beech translation layer chahiye. Schema changes explicit hote hain, aur MySQL jaise kuch databases ALTER TABLE par poori table copy karte hain.
Document (JSON or XML)Self-contained trees jo ek hi read mein load ho jaate hain, flexible structure, application code ke objects ke kaafi paasJoins kamzor hain, isliye links application code mein ya extra queries se resolve hote hain. Change par poora document load aur rewrite hota hai, aur nested items ko seedha refer nahi kiya ja sakta.
Graph (property graph, triple-store)Highly connected data, koi bhi vertex kisi se bhi linked, unknown depth ke traversals, aur ek hi store mein kai tarah ke objectsSQL mein multi-level traversals clumsy hain (book ke example mein 4 ke against 29 lines). Datalog mein one-off queries ke liye zyada sochna padta hai. Koi schema connections ko restrict nahi karta.

Summary

Short mein
  • History. Data ki shuruaat hierarchical model mein ek bade tree ki tarah hui. Woh many-to-many relationships represent karne mein kamzor tha, isliye relational model invent hua. Baad mein developers ne dekha ki kuch applications relational model mein bhi achhe se fit nahi hoti. Phir naye nonrelational “NoSQL” datastores do main directions mein bat gaye.
  • Document databases un use cases ko target karte hain jahan data self-contained documents mein aata hai, aur ek document aur doosre ke beech relationships kam hote hain.
  • Graph databases ulti direction mein jaate hain. Woh un use cases ko target karte hain jahan kuch bhi potentially sab kuch se related ho sakta hai.
  • Har model apne domain mein achha hai. Document, relational aur graph models, teeno widely use hote hain. Ek model ko doosre mein emulate kiya ja sakta hai, jaise graph data ko relational database mein store karna, lekin result aksar awkward hota hai. Isiliye alag-alag purposes ke liye alag systems hain, aur koi single one-size-fits-all solution nahi hai.
  • Schemas. Document aur graph databases aam taur par schema enforce nahi karte, jisse badalti requirements ke hisaab se applications adapt karna aasaan ho sakta hai. Phir bhi applications maanti hain ki data ka kuch structure hai. Asli sawaal yeh hai ki schema explicit hai (write par enforce hota hai) ya implicit (read par handle hota hai).
  • Query languages. Har model ki apni query language ya framework hai. Chapter ne SQL, MapReduce, MongoDB ki aggregation pipeline, Cypher, SPARQL aur Datalog cover kiye. CSS aur XSL/XPath ko bhi chhua, jo database query languages nahi hain lekin jinme interesting parallels hain.

Kai data models chhod diye gaye. Teen examples yeh hain.

  • Genome data ko sequence-similarity searches chahiye, jo ek bahut lambi string, yani DNA molecule, leti hain aur use strings ke bade database se match karti hain jo similar hain par bilkul same nahi. Yahan bataye gaye databases mein se koi yeh nahi kar sakta, isliye researchers ne GenBank jaisa specialized genome software likha hai.
  • Particle physics mein dashakon se large-scale, big-data-style analysis ho raha hai. Large Hadron Collider jaise projects ab hundreds of petabytes ke saath kaam karte hain. Is scale par hardware cost control se bahar na jaaye, isliye custom solutions chahiye.
  • Full-text search aksar databases ke saath use hota hai. Yeh ek bada specialist field hai jise book deeply cover nahi karti. Chapter 3 aur Part III mein search indexes ka zikr aata hai.

Agla chapter in trade-offs mein se kuch par baat karta hai jo yahan bataye gaye data models implement karte waqt aate hain.

Chapter ke end mein 49 numbered sources ki ek lambi reference list hai, jisme papers, books aur documentation hain. Yeh retelling us list ko reproduce nahi karti.

Check yourself

  1. Ek profile apna region ID ki jagah text “Greater Seattle Area” ki copy ke roop mein store karta hai. Book ke hisaab se isse kya cost aati hai, aur uski jagah kya store karna chahiye?

    Jawab dekho

    Insaano ke liye meaningful text har record mein duplicate ho jaata hai. Agar naam kabhi badle, toh har copy update karni padegi, aur chhooti hui copies data ko inconsistent bana deti hain. Ek region record par point karne wali ID store karne se change sirf ek jagah karna padta hai.

  2. first_name field add karne ke do tarike ho sakte hain. Ek mein naye documents field ke saath likhe jaate hain aur application code purane documents ko read hone par fill karta hai. Doosre mein ALTER TABLE aur phir ek baar UPDATE chalta hai. Kaun sa schema-on-read hai, aur kaun sa schema-on-write?

    Jawab dekho

    Naye documents likhna aur purane documents ko application mein handle karna schema-on-read hai, kyunki structure sirf data read hone par interpret hota hai. ALTER TABLE aur UPDATE wala tarika schema-on-write hai, kyunki schema explicit hai aur database har write par use enforce karta hai.

  3. Database rows ko reorder kar sakta hai ya naya index add kar sakta hai aur SQL queries nahi tootti, lekin wahi change imperative program ko tod sakta hai. Aisa kyun?

    Jawab dekho

    SQL batata hai ki kaun se results chahiye, unhe paane ke steps nahi. Woh kisi row order ka promise nahi deta, aur optimizer indexes aur join order chunta hai. Imperative code steps spell out karta hai aur kisi particular order par depend kar sakta hai, jise database check nahi kar sakta.

  4. US se Europe emigrate hone wale logon ki Cypher query do tarike se chalayi ja sakti hai. Woh kaun se hain?

    Jawab dekho

    Ek tarika saare logon ko scan karta hai, har ek ka birthplace aur residence check karta hai, aur matches rakhta hai. Doosra US aur Europe ke Location vertices se shuru hota hai, jinhe name par index jaldi dhoond sakta hai. Woh incoming WITHIN edges follow karke har region ke andar ki saari locations collect karta hai, phir aise log dhoondhta hai jinke in locations tak incoming BORN_IN ya LIVES_IN edges hon. Strategy optimizer chunta hai.

Part I · Chapter 3

Storage and Retrieval

Seedhi baat: log-structured engines sirf files mein add karte hain aur safai baad mein karte hain, jabki B-trees disk par fixed-size pages ko overwrite karte hain. Analytic systems ko teesra layout chahiye, column storage, kyunki woh bade tables ke sirf kuch columns padhte hain. Har design kuch kaam fast karta hai aur kuch slow.

Database ke do basic kaam hote hain. Jab tum use data dete ho, toh use woh data store karna hota hai. Jab tum baad mein maangte ho, toh use data wapas dena hota hai. Chapter 2 ne ise application ki taraf se dekha tha, data models aur query languages ke zariye. Yeh chapter wahi problem database ki taraf se dekhta hai: data disk par kaise lay out hota hai, aur dobara kaise dhoondha jaata hai.

Application developer ko iski parwah kyun karni chahiye? Hum mein se zyada tar log kabhi storage engine (database ka woh hissa jo decide karta hai ki bytes memory aur disk par kaise arrange hon) nahi likhenge. Lekin hamein kai options mein se ek chunna padta hai, aur use tune karne ke liye andar kya ho raha hai uski mota-moti picture chahiye. Chapter ek German proverb se shuru hota hai, jo kehta hai ki jo log cheezein tidily ordered rakhte hain, woh bas itne aalsi hain ki dhoondhne nahi jaate. Yahi central problem hai. Data ko order mein rakhne se reads aasaan hote hain, lekin ordering ki cost write karte waqt kaam ke roop mein aati hai.

Chapter un storage engines se shuru hota hai jo zyada tar traditional relational databases aur kai NoSQL databases mein use hote hain. Yeh engines do families mein aate hain: log-structured engines, jo files mein sirf append karte hain, aur page-oriented engines jaise B-trees, jo disk ke fixed-size blocks ko overwrite karte hain. Aage chapter analytics ke liye bane engines par aata hai, jinki zarooratein bahut alag hain.

Tumhare database ko power dene wale data structures

Book sabse simple database se shuru hoti hai jo socha ja sakta hai. Yeh do Bash functions se bana hai (Bash ek command-line shell hai jisse scripts run karte hain). Dono milkar ek key-value store banate hain, jo ek value ko ek naam ke neeche rakhta hai, us naam ko key kehte hain. Value lagbhag kuch bhi ho sakti hai, jaise JSON document (structured data ka ek text format).

Example

Pehla function db_set ek file mein ek line append karta hai, jis file ka naam database hai. Us line mein key hoti hai, phir comma, phir value. Doosra function db_get file mein un lines ko dhoondhta hai jo key se shuru hoti hain, aakhri line rakhta hai, aur uski value print kar deta hai. Ek session step by step dekhte hain:

  1. db_set 123456 run karo, London ke baare mein ek JSON value ke saath. File mein ek line aa jaati hai.
  2. db_set 42 run karo, San Francisco ke baare mein value ke saath. File mein doosri line aa jaati hai.
  3. db_get 42 run karo. Function ko woh line milti hai jo 42, se shuru hoti hai, aur woh San Francisco wali value print karta hai.
  4. db_set 42 dobara run karo, is baar Exploratorium ke baare mein value ke saath. File mein teesri line aa jaati hai. Key 42 ki purani line abhi bhi wahin hai.
  5. db_get 42 phir se run karo. Ab function ko do matching lines milti hain, woh aakhri wali rakhta hai, aur Exploratorium wali value print karta hai.
db_set () {
  echo "$1,$2" >> database
}
db_get () {
  grep "^$1," database | sed -e "s/^$1,//" | tail -n 1
}

Storage format ek plain text file hai, jisme har line mein ek key-value pair hota hai. Kuch bhi overwrite nahi hota. Har write end mein ek line add karta hai, aur ek key ki sabse nayi value woh hai jo us key wali aakhri line mein hai. Book ka point hai ki escaping problems ko ignore karein toh yeh lagbhag CSV file jaisa hi hai.

Write side fast hai. File ke end mein add karna disk ke sabse sasti cheezon mein se ek hai. Kaafi real databases isi wajah se andar log use karte hain. Yahan log ka matlab hai append-only sequence of records. Iska matlab application log nahi hai jisme human-readable messages hote hain, aur zaroori nahi ki log insaan padh sake. Real databases ko concurrent writers handle karne padte hain, disk space wapas lena padta hai taaki file hamesha badhti na rahe, aur un records se bhi deal karna padta hai jo sirf aadhe likhe gaye hon. Lekin basic idea wahi hai, aur logs book mein baar-baar aayenge.

Asli problem read side hai. Har db_get poori file ko start se end tak scan karta hai. Algorithm ki language mein, cost records ki count ke saath badhti hai, jise O(n) likhte hain. Records double kar do toh lookup mein double time lagega. Yeh scale nahi karta.

Value jaldi dhoondhne ke liye database ko ek index chahiye. Index side mein rakha gaya extra metadata hai, ek signpost jaisa, jo database ko sab kuch padhe bina data locate karne mein help karta hai. Index primary data se derive hota hai, isliye tum ek index add ya remove kar sakte ho bina is baat ko badle ki database kya store karta hai. Isse sirf queries ki speed badalti hai. Agar tumhe same data ko kai tarah se search karna hai, toh kai indexes chahiye ho sakte hain.

Ek catch hai. Data likhte waqt har index update karna padta hai, isliye woh writes ko slow karta hai. File mein bas append karne ki speed ko kuch beat nahi kar sakta. Soch-samajh ke chune hue indexes reads ko fast karte hain, lekin har index ki har write par kuch cost hoti hai. Isi wajah se databases aam taur par default mein sab kuch index nahi karte. Application developer ya database administrator common queries ko dekhkar indexes chunta hai, taaki fayda overhead se zyada ho.

Hash Indexes

Hash indexes key-value data ke liye hote hain. Sirf yahi ek tarah ka data nahi hai jise index kar sakte hain, lekin yeh common hai, aur zyada complex indexes ke liye ek kaam ka building block hai.

Key-value store kaafi had tak us dictionary type jaisa hai jo zyadatar programming languages mein hota hai, aur jo aam taur par hash map (ya hash table) se bana hota hai. Hash map seedha us jagah kud jaata hai jahan key rehti hai. Toh disk par data index karne ke liye ise kyun na use karein?

Maan lo storage bas pichhle section wali append-only file hai. Sabse simple index yeh hai: memory mein ek hash map rakho jo har key ko ek byte offset se map kare, yani file mein woh position jahan us key ki latest value shuru hoti hai. Jab tum naya key-value pair append karte ho, toh hash map bhi update karte ho taaki woh nayi line ki taraf point kare. Yeh naye keys aur updated keys, dono ke liye kaam karta hai. Value padhne ke liye, hash map mein offset dekho, file mein us position par seek karo (read point ko seedha wahin le jao), aur value padh lo.

Yeh shayad bahut simple lage, lekin yeh ek workable design hai. Bitcask essentially yahi karta hai. Bitcask Riak (ek distributed database) ka default storage engine hai. Bitcask fast reads aur writes deta hai, ek zaroori condition ke saath: saari keys memory mein fit honi chahiye, kyunki poora hash map wahin rehta hai. Values ko fit hona zaroori nahi hai. Value disk se ek single seek mein padh li jaati hai. Agar file ka woh hissa pehle se operating system ke file cache mein hai, toh read ko disk input ya output ki zaroorat hi nahi padti.

Bitcask jaisa design un workloads ke liye sahi baithta hai jahan har key baar-baar update hoti hai, lekin distinct keys zyada nahi hain. Book ka example hai har cat video kitni baar play hua uski count. Har click ek nayi count likhta hai, toh writes bahut hain. Lekin video URLs itne kam hain ki sab memory mein aa jaate hain.

Yahan ek obvious sawaal uthta hai. File sirf badhti hi rehti hai, toh disk space khatam hone se kaise bachein? Jawab hai log ko segments mein todna. Jab segment file ek tay size tak pahunchti hai, toh use close kar dete hain, aur nayi writes ek naye segment mein jaati hain. Closed segments ko phir kabhi change nahi karte. Phir un par compaction run karte hain. Compaction duplicate keys ko hata deta hai aur har key ki sirf sabse recent value rakhta hai.

Example

Ek cat video ka play-count log socho. Maan lo ek closed segment mein us video ki count paanch baar likhi hui hai. Compaction segment padhta hai, paanch counts mein se sirf aakhri rakhta hai, aur ek chhota segment likh deta hai. Yeh tab sabse achha kaam karta hai jab ek key ek hi segment mein kai baar overwrite hui ho, kyunki tab compaction segment ko kaafi chhota kar deta hai.

Compaction segments ko chhota kar deta hai, isliye tum kai segments ko ek hi pass mein merge bhi kar sakte ho. Merged output ek nayi file mein likha jaata hai. Frozen segments kabhi modify nahi hote, isliye yeh safe hai. Merge background thread mein chal sakta hai, jabki database purani segment files se reads aur writes serve karta rehta hai. Merge poora hone par reads naye merged segment par switch ho jaate hain, aur purani files delete kar di jaati hain.

Har segment ka apna in-memory hash map hota hai. Key dhoondhne ke liye pehle sabse naye segment ka hash map check karo. Wahan na mile toh doosre sabse naye segment ka, aur aise hi peeche jaate raho. Merging segments ki count kam rakhti hai, isliye lookup ko kam hi maps check karne padte hain.

Real implementation mein kai details matter karti hain. Book yeh list karti hai:

  • File format. CSV log ke liye sabse achha format nahi hai. Binary format faster aur simple hota hai. Woh har string ki length bytes mein store karta hai, phir raw bytes, isliye escaping ki zaroorat nahi padti.
  • Records delete karna. Key delete karne ke liye database ek special deletion record append karta hai, jise tombstone kehte hain. Segments merge hote waqt tombstone merge ko bata deta hai ki us key ki saari pehle ki values hata do.
  • Crash recovery. Hash maps sirf memory mein rehte hain, isliye restart par kho jaate hain. Tum unhe dobara bana sakte ho: har segment ko shuru se end tak padho aur har key ka latest offset note karte jao. Lekin bade segments mein isme bahut time lag sakta hai. Bitcask isse tez karta hai: woh har segment ke hash map ka snapshot disk par save kar leta hai, jo bahut jaldi load hota hai.
  • Aadhe likhe records. Record append karte-karte beech mein crash ho sakta hai. Bitcask files mein checksums hote hain (data se nikaali gayi ek value, jo corruption pakadne ke kaam aati hai), isliye log ke damaged hisse pakad kar ignore kiye ja sakte hain.
  • Concurrency. Writes strict order mein append hote hain, isliye ek common choice hai sirf ek writer thread rakhna. Segments append-only hain aur kabhi change nahi hote, isliye kai reader threads unhe ek saath padh sakte hain.

Append-only log wasteful lag sakta hai. File ko in place update karke purani value overwrite kyun na kar dein? Book teen wajah deti hai ki append-only design achha kyun hai:

  • Appending aur merging sequential writes hain, yani ek jagah ke baad doosri jagah likhna. Yeh random writes se bahut fast hote hain, jo disk par idhar-udhar kudte hain. Yeh gap spinning hard drives par khaaskar bada hota hai. Flash-based solid state drives (SSDs) par bhi kuch had tak sequential writes ko prefer kiya jaata hai.
  • Jab files kabhi change nahi hoti, toh concurrency aur crash recovery simple ho jaati hain. Tumhe is baat ki fikr nahi karni padti ki value overwrite karte-karte beech mein crash ho gaya, jisse purani aur nayi value ke tukde aapas mein jud kar reh jaate.
  • Purane segments merge karne se data files time ke saath fragmented (chhote bache hue tukdon mein bikhri hui) nahi hotin.

Hash index ki do limits bhi hain:

  • Hash map ko memory mein fit hona padta hai. Keys bahut zyada hon toh kuch nahi kar sakte. Tum hash map disk par rakh sakte ho, lekin wahan use achhi performance dilana mushkil hai. Usme bahut random reads aur writes lagte hain, bhar jaane par use badhana mehnga padta hai, aur collisions (do keys ka ek hi slot mein aa jaana) ke liye fiddly logic chahiye.
  • Range queries slow hoti hain. Tum kitty00000 aur kitty99999 ke beech ki saari keys aasaani se scan nahi kar sakte. Tumhe har possible key ko hash map mein ek-ek karke lookup karna padega.

Agla section ek aisi indexing structure dekhta hai jisme yeh limits nahi hain.

SSTables aur LSM-Trees

Upar ke segments mein har segment key-value pairs ki list hai, us order mein jis order mein woh likhe gaye. Same key ke liye baad ki entries pehle wali par jeet jaati hain. Ab ek simple change karo: har segment ke pairs ko key ke hisaab se sorted hona zaroori kar do. Book is format ko Sorted String Table ya SSTable kehti hai. Merged segment mein har key sirf ek baar aati hai, jo compaction pehle se guarantee karta hai.

Pehli nazar mein lagta hai ki sorting sequential-write wale idea ko tod deti hai. Book kehti hai ki aisa nahi hota, aur wajah bhi samjhati hai. Hash indexes wale log segments ke muqable SSTables ke teen bade advantages hain.

1. Merging simple aur efficient hai, files memory se badi hon tab bhi. Merge bilkul mergesort algorithm ke merge step jaisa kaam karta hai. Tum input files ko side by side kholte ho aur har ek ki pehli key dekhte ho. Sabse chhoti key ko output mein copy karte hain aur us file mein aage badhte hain. Yeh kaam khatam hone tak dohrate raho. Result ek naya sorted segment hota hai.

Example

Maan lo do segments mein key kiwi dono mein hai. Har segment mein kisi ek period ki saari writes hoti hain, aur segments time order mein merge hote hain. Isliye naye segment ki har value purane segment ki har value se zyada recent hai. Jab koi key dono mein dikhe, toh naye segment ki value rakho aur purani hata do. Neeche ka figure yeh simple made-up keys ke saath dikhata hai.

2. Ab tumhe har key ka index memory mein rakhne ki zaroorat nahi. Maan lo tum key handiwork dhoondh rahe ho, lekin segment file mein uska exact offset tumhe nahi pata. Tumhe handbag aur handsome ke offsets pata hain. File sorted hai, isliye handiwork in dono ke beech mein hi hoga. Toh tum handbag ke offset par jump karte ho aur aage scan karte ho jab tak handiwork mil na jaaye, ya woh jagah nikal jaaye jahan use hona chahiye tha, aur tum samajh jaate ho ki woh hai hi nahi.

Kuch offsets jaanne ke liye tumhe phir bhi in-memory index chahiye. Lekin woh sparse ho sakta hai, yani file ke har kuch kilobytes ke liye ek key rakhe, har key ke liye nahi. Kuch kilobytes bahut jaldi scan ho jaate hain. (Agar saari keys aur values ka size fixed hota, toh index ke bina file par binary search use kar sakte the. Practice mein lengths alag-alag hoti hain, isliye index ke bina pata nahi chalta ki ek record kahan khatam hota hai.)

3. Reads ko blocks mein compress kiya ja sakta hai. Keys ki range padhne mein waise bhi kai records scan karne padte hain. Isliye records ko ek block mein group karke disk par likhne se pehle compress kiya ja sakta hai. Sparse index ki har entry phir ek compressed block ki shuruaat ki taraf point karti hai. Isse disk space bachta hai aur disk se padha jaane wala data bhi kam hota hai.

SSTables banana aur maintain karna

Sorted files kaam ki hain, lekin data sorted hota kaise hai? Writes kisi bhi order mein aati hain. Disk par sorted structure rakhna possible hai (B-tree section ek tarika batata hai). Lekin memory mein rakhna kaafi aasaan hai. Standard balanced trees, jaise red-black trees ya AVL trees, tumhe keys kisi bhi order mein insert karne dete hain aur sorted order mein wapas padhne dete hain.

Storage engine phir chaar steps mein kaam karta hai:

  • Write aane par use in-memory balanced tree mein add karo. Is tree ko memtable kehte hain.
  • Jab memtable ek threshold se bada ho jaaye, aam taur par kuch megabytes, use SSTable ke roop mein disk par likh do. Yeh sasta hai, kyunki tree mein pairs pehle se sorted order mein hain. Naya SSTable sabse naya segment ban jaata hai. Purana likhte waqt writes ek fresh memtable mein jaati reh sakti hain.
  • Read serve karne ke liye pehle memtable check karo, phir disk ka sabse naya segment, phir uske peeche wala purana, aur aise hi aage.
  • Time-time par background mein merge aur compaction chalao. Yeh segments ko combine karta hai aur overwritten ya deleted values hata deta hai.

Ek weakness hai. Database crash ho jaaye toh sabse recent writes kho jaati hain. Woh memtable mein thin lekin abhi disk par nahi likhi gayi thin. Isse bachne ke liye disk par ek alag log rakho, aur har write ko turant usme append karo, bilkul pehle wale log design ki tarah. Yeh log sorted nahi hota, aur hona bhi nahi chahiye. Iska sirf ek kaam hai: crash ke baad memtable ko dobara banana. Memtable ke SSTable ke roop mein save ho jaane ke baad, uska matching log discard kiya ja sakta hai.

SSTables se LSM-tree banana

Yeh algorithm essentially wahi hai jo LevelDB aur RocksDB use karte hain. Dono key-value storage libraries hain jo doosri applications ke andar embed hone ke liye bani hain. LevelDB ko Riak mein Bitcask ke alternative ke taur par use kiya ja sakta hai. Milte-julte engines Cassandra aur HBase mein use hote hain, jo dono Google ke Bigtable paper se inspired the. Us paper ne hi SSTable aur memtable terms introduce kiye.

Is index structure ko sabse pehle Patrick O'Neil aur unke saathiyon ne describe kiya, aur use Log-Structured Merge-Tree ya LSM-tree naam diya. Yeh log-structured filesystems par pehle ke kaam par bana hai. Sorted files ko merge aur compact karne wale is idea par based storage engines ko aksar LSM storage engines kehte hain.

Lucene, jo full-text search library Elasticsearch aur Solr use karte hain, apni term dictionary ke liye milta-julta tarika use karti hai. Full-text search key-value lookup se mushkil hai, lekin yeh milte-jule idea par tika hai. Search mein ek word diya ho, toh un sab documents ko dhoondho jisme woh word hai. Index har word (term) ko ek postings list se map karta hai, jo un documents ke IDs ki list hai jisme woh word aata hai. Lucene mein yeh mapping SSTable-jaisi sorted files mein rakhi jaati hai, jinhe zaroorat padne par background mein merge kiya jaata hai.

Performance optimizations

Hamesha ki tarah, storage engine ko fast banane mein bahut saari details lagti hain. LSM-tree un keys ke liye slow hai jo exist hi nahi karti. Key absent hai yeh pakka karne se pehle tumhe memtable check karna padta hai, phir sabse purane tak har segment, aur shayad har ek ke liye disk se padhna bhi padta hai. Ise tez karne ke liye storage engines aksar Bloom filters add karte hain. Bloom filter ek compact structure hai jo approximately batata hai ki set mein kaun se items hain. Woh bata sakta hai ki key database mein definitely nahi hai, jisse bahut saare unnecessary disk reads bach jaate hain.

Segments kab aur kaise merge hon, iske bhi alag-alag rules hain. Do sabse common hain size-tiered aur leveled compaction. LevelDB aur RocksDB leveled compaction use karte hain, aur LevelDB ka naam wahin se aaya hai. HBase size-tiered compaction use karta hai, aur Cassandra dono support karta hai. Size-tiered compaction mein naye aur chhote SSTables ko purane aur bade SSTables mein merge kiya jaata hai. Leveled compaction mein key range ko chhote SSTables mein baant diya jaata hai, aur purana data alag “levels” mein move hota hai. Isse compaction chhote steps mein ho paata hai aur disk space kam lagta hai.

In sab details ke baad bhi core idea simple hai: SSTables ka ek cascade rakho aur unhe background mein merge karte raho. Yeh tab bhi achha kaam karta hai jab data memory se kaafi bada ho. Data sorted order mein store hota hai, isliye range queries efficient hoti hain. Disk writes sequential hoti hain, isliye LSM-tree kaafi high write throughput sustain kar sakta hai.

B-Trees

Log-structured indexes ko acceptance mil rahi hai, lekin sabse common index woh nahi hain. Sabse zyada use hone wala structure B-tree hai. Yeh 1970 mein introduce hua tha, aur das saal se kam mein hi ise ubiquitous bataya ja chuka tha. B-trees lagbhag saare relational databases mein aaj bhi standard index hain, aur kai nonrelational databases bhi unhe use karte hain.

SSTables ki tarah B-trees bhi key-value pairs ko key ke hisaab se sorted rakhte hain, isliye fast lookups aur range queries support karte hain. Iske alawa dono designs bahut alag hain. Log-structured indexes database ko variable-size segments mein todte hain, aam taur par kai megabytes ya usse zyada ke, aur segment ko hamesha ek sequential pass mein likhte hain. B-trees database ko fixed-size blocks mein todte hain jinhe pages kehte hain. Page traditionally 4 KB (kilobytes) ka hota hai, kabhi zyada. Database ek baar mein ek page padhta ya likhta hai. Yeh hardware se behtar match karta hai, kyunki disks bhi fixed-size blocks mein laid out hoti hain.

Har page ka ek address hota hai, jisse ek page doosre page ko refer kar sakta hai. Yeh pointer jaisa hai, lekin yeh memory ki jagah disk par ek location ki taraf point karta hai. Page references milkar pages ka ek tree banate hain. Ek page root hota hai. Key dhoondhne ke liye tum root se shuru karte ho. Root mein kai keys aur child pages ke references hote hain. Har child keys ki ek continuous range cover karta hai, aur references ke beech ki keys batati hain ki ranges ki boundaries kahan hain.

Example

Book ek B-tree mein key 251 ko lookup karti hai. Steps yeh hain:

  1. Root se shuru karo. Uski boundaries batati hain ki kaun sa child kaun si range cover karta hai. Key 251 boundaries 200 aur 300 ke beech aati hai, toh us range wala reference follow karo.
  2. Woh child page 200 se 300 ki range ko chhote subranges mein todta hai. Woh subrange dhoondho jisme 251 hai aur uska reference follow karo.
  3. Aise hi chalte raho jab tak leaf page na aa jaaye, jo sabse neeche ka level hai aur individual keys hold karta hai. Leaf ya toh har value inline store karta hai, ya un jagahon ke references jahan values rakhi hain.

Existing key ki value update karne ke liye, us leaf page ko dhoondho jisme woh hai, wahan value badlo, aur page ko wapas likh do. Page references valid rehte hain kyunki page ka address wahi rehta hai. Nayi key add karne ke liye woh page dhoondho jiski range us key ko cover karti hai aur use wahan add kar do. Agar page mein jagah kam hai, toh use split karke do half-full pages bana dete hain. Phir parent page ko update karte hain taaki woh dono halves ko point kare, aur isse parent bhi split ho sakta hai.

Isse tree balanced rehta hai. n keys wale B-tree ki depth hamesha O(log n) hoti hai, matlab data badhne par depth bahut dheere badhti hai. Zyadatar databases ek aise B-tree mein fit ho jaate hain jo teen ya chaar levels gehra ho, isliye page tak pahunchne ke liye tumhe kam hi references follow karne padte hain. Book ka example: 4 KB pages ka chaar-level tree, jiska branching factor 500 hai, 256 TB tak store kar sakta hai. Branching factor ek page mein child references ki count hai. Upar ke figure mein yeh teen hai, aur practice mein aam taur par kai sau hota hai. (B-tree mein insert karna kaafi intuitive hai. Tree ko balanced rakhte hue delete karna zyada involved hai.)

B-trees ko reliable banana

B-tree ka basic write operation hai disk par ek page ko naye data se overwrite karna, uski location wahi rakhte hue taaki uske saare references valid rahein. Yeh log-structured indexes se bahut alag hai, jo files mein sirf append karte hain aur obsolete files delete karte hain.

Page overwrite karna ek real hardware action hai. Magnetic hard drive par disk head ko sahi jagah jaana padta hai, platter ke ghoomkar sahi spot ko uske neeche laane ka wait karna padta hai, aur phir sector overwrite karna padta hai. SSDs zyada complicated hain, kyunki unhe storage chip ke kaafi bade blocks ek baar mein erase aur rewrite karne padte hain.

Kuch operations mein kai pages ek saath change karne padte hain. Page split hone par tumhe do naye pages likhne padte hain aur parent ko bhi overwrite karna padta hai taaki woh dono ko point kare.
