Agar in mein se sirf kuch writes ke baad database crash ho jaaye, toh index corrupt ho jaata hai. Tumhare paas ek orphan page reh sakta hai, yani aisa page jise koi parent point nahi karta.

B-trees ko crash-resistant banane ke liye zyadatar implementations ek write-ahead log add karti hain, jise redo log bhi kehte hain. Yeh ek append-only file hai. B-tree mein har change ko tree ke pages par apply karne se pehle is log mein likhna padta hai. Database crash ho jaaye toh log ko replay karke tree ko consistent state mein wapas laaya jaata hai. Yeh wahi idea hai jo upar memtable ke log mein use hua, lekin yahan log tree ke pages ko protect karta hai.

Pages ko in place update karne ke liye careful concurrency control bhi chahiye, yani woh rules jo kai threads ko ek doosre ke raste mein aane se rokte hain. Agar kai threads ek saath tree use karein, toh koi ek use inconsistent state mein dekh sakta hai. Aam fix hai tree ko latches se protect karna, jo lightweight locks hain. Log-structured designs yahan simple hain. Woh merging background mein karte hain, incoming queries mein dakhal diye bina, aur purane segments ko naye segments se ek saath swap kar dete hain.

B-tree optimizations

B-trees kai dashakon se hain, aur kai optimizations develop ho chuke hain. Book kuch ka zikr karti hai:

  • Copy-on-write. Kuch databases, jaise LMDB, pages overwrite karne aur write-ahead log se bachte hain. Changed page ko ek nayi location par likha jaata hai, aur uske parent pages ke naye versions banaye jaate hain jo uski taraf point karein. Yeh concurrency control mein bhi help karta hai, jo book aage cover karti hai.
  • Abbreviated keys. Pages ko poori keys store karne ki zaroorat nahi. Tree ke andar keys ko sirf ranges ke beech boundaries ka kaam karna hota hai, isliye unhe chhota kiya ja sakta hai. Isse har page mein zyada keys aa jaati hain, jisse branching factor badhta hai aur levels kam ho jaate hain.
  • Disk par layout. Pages disk par kahin bhi ho sakte hain. Paas-paas ki key ranges ek doosre ke paas store nahi hoti. Key range ke bade hisse par scan karne mein har page ke liye disk seek lag sakta hai. Kuch implementations leaf pages ko sequential order mein rakhne ki koshish karti hain, lekin tree badhne par ise maintain karna mushkil hai. LSM-trees ke liye yeh aasaan hai, kyunki merges storage ke bade chunks ko ek hi baar mein rewrite karte hain aur neighboring keys ko paas rakhte hain.
  • Sibling pointers. Har leaf page apne left aur right neighbors ko point kar sakta hai. Isse scan parent pages tak wapas chadhe bina keys ke saath order mein aage badh sakta hai.
  • Fractal trees. Kuch B-tree variants disk seeks kam karne ke liye log-structured designs se ideas udhaar leti hain. Naam chahe jo ho, unka fractals se koi lena-dena nahi hai.

B-Trees aur LSM-Trees ki tulna

B-tree implementations aam taur par LSM-tree implementations se zyada mature hain. Phir bhi LSM-trees apni performance ki wajah se interesting hain. Rule of thumb ke taur par, LSM-trees aam taur par writes ke liye faster hain, aur B-trees ko reads ke liye faster maana jaata hai. LSM-trees par reads slow isliye hain kyunki unhe compaction ke alag-alag stages par kai structures aur SSTables check karne pad sakte hain.

Book ek warning bhi deti hai. Benchmarks aksar inconclusive hote hain aur workload ki details par depend karte hain. Valid comparison ke liye har system ko apne workload ke saath test karo. Phir book kuch cheezein list karti hai jo storage engine measure karte waqt dekhne layak hain.

LSM-trees ke advantages

B-tree ko data ka har hissa kam se kam do baar likhna padta hai. Ek baar write-ahead log mein, aur ek baar tree page mein. Split hone par pages dobara bhi likhe ja sakte hain. Poora page likhne ka overhead bhi hota hai, chahe usme sirf kuch bytes badle hon. Kuch storage engines ek hi page do baar overwrite karte hain, taaki power failure page ko aadha updated na chhod de.

LSM-trees bhi data kai baar rewrite karte hain, kyunki compaction aur merging SSTables ko baar-baar copy karte hain. Database ki life mein ek logical write kai physical disk writes ban sakta hai. Ise write amplification kehte hain. Yeh SSDs par sabse zyada matter karta hai, jo wear out hone se pehle blocks ko sirf limited baar overwrite kar sakte hain.

Write-heavy application mein bottleneck yeh ho sakta hai ki database disk par kitni tez likh paata hai. Yahan write amplification ki seedhi cost hoti hai. Storage engine jitna zyada likhta hai, available disk bandwidth mein utni kam writes per second handle kar paata hai. LSM-trees aam taur par B-trees se zyada write throughput sustain karte hain. Iska ek hissa yeh hai ki unka write amplification kabhi-kabhi kam hota hai, lekin yeh configuration aur workload par depend karta hai. Dusra hissa yeh hai ki woh compact SSTable files sequence mein likhte hain, kai bikhre hue pages ko overwrite karne ke bajaye. Magnetic disks par yeh fark bada hai, kyunki wahan sequential writes random se kaafi fast hoti hain.

LSM-trees ko behtar compress bhi kiya ja sakta hai, isliye woh aksar B-trees se chhoti files banate hain. B-tree storage mein kuch disk space unused reh jaata hai. Page split hone par, ya row ke page mein fit na hone par jagah bachi hone par bhi, page ka kuch hissa khaali reh jaata hai. LSM-trees page-oriented nahi hote, aur woh is fragmentation ko hatane ke liye SSTables ko periodically rewrite karte hain. Isliye unka storage overhead kam hota hai, khaaskar leveled compaction ke saath.

Kai SSDs mein firmware andar se log-structured tarika use karta hai taaki random writes chips par sequential writes ban jaayein. Isliye wahan storage engine ka write pattern kam matter karta hai. Phir bhi, SSDs par lower write amplification aur kam fragmentation kaam aate hain, kyunki compact data se zyada reads aur writes available I/O bandwidth mein aa jaate hain. (I/O ka matlab input aur output, yani CPU aur storage ke beech ka traffic.)

LSM-trees ke downsides

Log-structured storage ka downside yeh hai ki compaction chalte hue reads aur writes mein dakhal de sakta hai. Storage engines chhote steps mein compact karne ki koshish karte hain taaki concurrent access par asar na pade. Lekin disks ke resources limited hain, isliye request ko wait karna pad sakta hai jab tak disk ek bada compaction khatam na kar le. Average response time par effect aam taur par chhota hota hai. Lekin higher percentiles par (sabse slow requests, jaisa Chapter 1 mein bataya gaya), log-structured engines par queries kaafi slow ho sakti hain, aur B-trees zyada predictable hain.

Doosra issue high write throughput par aata hai. Disk ki write bandwidth finite hoti hai, jise nayi writes (unhe log karna aur memtable flush karna) aur background compaction ke beech share karna padta hai. Fresh, empty database poori disk bandwidth nayi writes ke liye use kar sakta hai. Lekin database badhne par compaction ko us bandwidth ka zyada hissa chahiye. Agar writes heavy hain aur compaction careful tarike se configure nahi hai, toh compaction peeche reh sakta hai. Phir unmerged segments disk par jama hote jaate hain jab tak space khatam na ho jaaye, aur reads slow ho jaate hain kyunki unhe zyada files check karni padti hain. SSTable-based engines aam taur par incoming writes ko throttle nahi karte jab compaction saath na de paaye. Isliye yeh notice karne ke liye tumhe explicit monitoring chahiye.

Yahan B-trees ka ek advantage hai. Har key index mein exactly ek jagah hoti hai. Log-structured engine ek hi key ki kai copies alag-alag segments mein rakh sakta hai. Isse B-trees un databases ke liye attractive ban jaate hain jo strong transactional guarantees chahte hain. Kai relational databases mein transaction isolation keys ki ranges par locks se hota hai, aur B-tree mein woh locks seedhe tree se jud sakte hain. Chapter 7 is point par wapas aata hai.

B-trees database architecture mein gehre baithe hain aur kai workloads ke liye consistently achhi performance dete hain, isliye woh jaldi gayab hone wale nahi hain. Naye datastores mein log-structured indexes ki popularity badh rahi hai. Dono mein se ek chunne ka koi quick rule nahi hai, isliye book dono ko empirically test karne ki salah deti hai. Neeche ki table trade-offs ka summary deti hai.

Trade-offs
OptionKis mein achhaCosts
LSM-trees (log-structured)Fast writes aur high write throughput. Compact files, kam fragmentation. Sequential disk writes.Slower reads, kyunki kai structures check karne pad sakte hain. Compaction se high percentiles par slow requests ho sakti hain aur woh heavy writes se peeche reh sakta hai. Write amplification.
B-trees (page-oriented)Fast reads aur predictable response times. Har key ek hi jagah rehti hai, isliye transaction locks tree se aasaani se jud jaate hain.Har write kam se kam do jagah touch karta hai (log aur page), aur poore pages rewrite hote hain. Fragmentation se kuch space waste hota hai.

Doosre indexing structures

Ab tak humne sirf key-value indexes ki baat ki hai. Yeh relational model ke primary key index jaise hain. Primary key table mein ek row, ek document, ya graph mein ek vertex ko uniquely identify karti hai. Doosre records us row ko uski primary key se refer kar sakte hain, aur un references ko resolve karne ke liye index use hota hai.

Databases mein aam taur par secondary indexes bhi hote hain. Relational database mein tum CREATE INDEX command se kai bana sakte ho, aur efficient joins ke liye woh aksar crucial hote ho. Jaise Chapter 2 ke figure mein, tumhare paas shayad user_id columns par secondary index hota, taaki tum har table mein ek user ki saari rows dhoondh sako.

Secondary index ko key-value index se banaya ja sakta hai. Fark yeh hai ki keys unique nahi hoti. Kai rows ki same key ho sakti hai. Isse deal karne ke do tarike hain. Ek, har index value ko matching row identifiers ki list bana do, full-text index ki postings list ki tarah. Doosra, har key ke aage row identifier jodkar use unique bana do. Dono tarike se B-trees aur log-structured indexes, dono secondary indexes ka kaam kar sakte hain.

Index ke andar values store karna

Key woh hai jise queries search karti hain. Value do cheezon mein se ek ho sakti hai. Ya toh actual row, document, ya vertex. Ya row ka ek reference, jo kahin aur store hoti hai. Doosre case mein jahan rows store hoti hain us jagah ko heap file kehte hain. Heap file data ko kisi khaas order mein nahi rakhti. Woh append-only ho sakti hai, ya deleted rows ko track kar sakti hai taaki unki jagah reuse ho sake.

Heap file approach se data copy karne se bachte hain jab kai secondary indexes hon. Har index bas heap ki ek location ko point karta hai, aur row ek hi jagah store hoti hai. Jab update key nahi badalta, tab heap file achha kaam karti hai. Agar nayi value purani se badi nahi hai, toh record wahin overwrite ho jaata hai. Agar badi hai, toh use aisi jagah move karna padta hai jahan zyada room ho. Phir ya toh har index ko update karna padta hai taaki woh nayi location ko point kare, ya purani location par ek forwarding pointer chhod diya jaata hai.

Kabhi-kabhi index se heap tak ka extra hop reads ke liye bahut slow hota hai. Tab tum indexed row ko seedha index ke andar store kar sakte ho. Isse clustered index kehte hain. MySQL ke InnoDB engine mein table ki primary key hamesha clustered index hoti hai, aur secondary indexes heap location ki jagah primary key ko point karte hain. SQL Server tumhe har table par ek clustered index rakhne deta hai.

Ek beech ka option bhi hai. Covering index, ya included columns wala index, table ke kuch columns index ke andar store karta hai, sab nahi. Agar query ko sirf wahi columns chahiye jo index mein store hain, toh index akela hi use answer kar sakta hai. Tab kehte hain ki index query ko cover karta hai.

Kisi bhi duplicated data ki tarah, clustered aur covering indexes reads ko fast karte hain lekin extra storage lete hain aur writes ko slow karte hain. Database ko transaction guarantees enforce karne mein bhi zyada mehnat karni padti hai, kyunki applications ko duplication se hui inconsistencies kabhi nazar nahi aani chahiye.

Multi-column indexes

Ab tak ke indexes ek single key ko value se map karte hain. Jab tumhe kai columns (ya document ke kai fields) ek saath search karne hon, toh yeh kaafi nahi hota.

Sabse common multi-column index concatenated index hai. Yeh kai fields ko ek key mein jodta hai, ek column ke baad doosra append karke, us order mein jo index definition tay karti hai. Purani paper phone book aise hi kaam karti hai. Woh last name aur first name ko ek saath index karti hai, aur tumhe phone number deti hai. Sort order ki wajah se tum kisi ek last name wale sab log, ya kisi last name aur first name ke pair wale sab log dhoondh sakte ho. Lekin book dhyaan dilati hai ki sirf kisi particular first name wale sab log dhoondhne ke liye yeh index bekaar hai.

Multi-dimensional indexes kai columns ko ek saath zyada general tarike se search karte hain. Yeh geographic data ke liye sabse zyada matter karte hain. Maan lo ek restaurant-search website har restaurant ka latitude aur longitude store karti hai. Jab user map dekhta hai, toh site ko wo saare restaurants dhoondhne padte hain jo user ko dikhne wale rectangle ke andar hain. Yeh ek two-dimensional range query hai.

Example

Neeche ki query user ke map ke ek rectangle ke andar ke restaurants maangti hai. Rectangle latitudes ki ek range aur longitudes ki ek range se tay hota hai:

SELECT * FROM restaurants WHERE latitude > 51.4946 AND latitude < 51.5079
AND longitude > -0.1162 AND longitude < -0.1004;

Standard B-tree ya LSM-tree ise efficiently answer nahi kar sakta. Woh tumhe latitudes ke ek band ke saare restaurants de sakta hai, kisi bhi longitude par, ya longitudes ke ek band ke saare restaurants, kisi bhi latitude par. Woh dono ek saath nahi kar sakta. Rectangle ke liye dono conditions ek saath apply honi chahiye.

Ek option hai two-dimensional location ko ek single number mein badalna, space-filling curve se, jo ek aisa path hai jo grid ke har cell se guzarta hai. Phir normal B-tree index use kiya ja sakta hai. Zyada common tarika specialized spatial indexes hain jinhe R-trees kehte hain. PostGIS, jo PostgreSQL ka geographic extension hai, apne spatial indexes R-trees ke roop mein implement karta hai. Book R-trees ko detail mein describe nahi karti.

Multi-dimensional indexes sirf maps ke liye nahi hain. Ek online shop products ko teen dimensions, red, green aur blue, par index kar sakti hai, taaki colors ki ek range ke items mil sakein. Weather observations ka database date aur temperature ko ek saath index kar sakta hai. Tab 2013 ke woh saare observations jahan temperature 25 se 30 degrees Celsius ke beech tha, seedhe answer ho sakte hain. One-dimensional index ke saath tumhe 2013 ke har record ko scan karke phir temperature se filter karna padta, ya ulta karna padta. Two-dimensional index dono ko ek saath narrow kar sakta hai. HyperDex system yeh technique use karta hai.

Full-text search aur fuzzy indexes

Ab tak ke saare indexes exact data maante hain. Woh exact lookups support karte hain, aur sort order ke saath key ki ranges. Woh milti-julti keys, jaise galat spelling wale words, nahi dhoondh sakte. Uske liye alag techniques chahiye.

Full-text search engines search word ko uske synonyms tak expand kar sakte hain, plurals aur tenses jaise grammatical variations ko ignore kar sakte hain, aur document mein ek-doosre ke paas aaye words dhoondh sakte hain. Woh language ke analysis par based aur features bhi support karte hain. Typos se nipatne ke liye Lucene ek certain edit distance ke andar ke words search kar sakta hai. Edit distance 1 ka matlab hai ek letter add, remove ya replace hua hai.

Lucene ki term dictionary SSTable-jaisi hai, jaisa pehle bataya gaya. Queries ko ek chhota in-memory index chahiye jo batata hai ki sorted file mein key kahan dhoondhni hai. LevelDB mein woh index keys ka ek sparse set hai. Lucene mein yeh keys ke characters par ek finite state automaton hai, trie (ek tree jo characters par branch karta hai) jaisa. Us automaton ko Levenshtein automaton mein convert kiya ja sakta hai, jo ek diye gaye edit distance ke andar ke words efficiently search karta hai.

Doosre fuzzy search methods document classification aur machine learning ki taraf jaate hain. Book aur jaanne ke liye information retrieval ki ek textbook suggest karti hai.

Sab kuch memory mein rakhna

Ab tak ke structures disks ki limits solve karte hain. Disks awkward hoti hain. Magnetic ho ya SSD, disk par data ko achhi read aur write speed ke liye dhyaan se layout karna padta hai. Hum yeh sehte hain kyunki disks ke do bade advantages hain. Woh durable hoti hain, matlab power cut ke baad bhi unka content bacha rehta hai. Aur woh RAM (main memory) se per gigabyte sasti padti hain.

RAM sasti hone par cost wali dalil kamzor padti hai. Kai datasets itne bade nahi hote, isliye woh poore memory mein fit ho sakte hain, shayad kai machines mein baant kar. Isi se in-memory databases aaye.

Kuch in-memory key-value stores, jaise Memcached, sirf caching ke liye hain. Machine restart par unka data kho jaana theek hai. Doosre in-memory databases durability chahte hain. Woh yeh special hardware se pa sakte hain, jaise battery-backed RAM. Ya woh changes ka log disk par likh sakte hain, disk par periodic snapshots likh sakte hain, ya in-memory state ko doosri machines par copy kar sakte hain. Aisa database restart hone par apni state disk se reload karta hai, ya network par replica se (doosri machine par data ki ek aur copy), jab tak special hardware use na ho.

Disk par likhna in-memory database ka phir bhi ek real hissa hai. Yahan disk sirf durability ke liye append-only log ki tarah use hoti hai, aur reads poori tarah memory se serve hote hain. Disk files ke operational advantages bhi hain. Unka backup aasaani se liya ja sakta hai, aur bahar ke tools unhe inspect aur analyze kar sakte hain.

VoltDB, MemSQL aur Oracle TimesTen jaise products in-memory relational databases hain. Unke vendors ka claim hai ki disk ke liye data structures manage karne ka saara overhead hata dene se badi speed gains milti hain. RAMCloud ek open source in-memory key-value store hai jo durable rehta hai, aur memory aur disk, dono par log-structured approach use karta hai. Redis aur Couchbase kamzor durability dete hain, kyunki woh disk par asynchronously likhte hain (background mein, write acknowledge hone ke baad).

Book ek surprising point rakhti hai. In-memory databases ki speed advantage disk reads se bachne se nahi aati. Disk-based engine bhi, agar kaafi memory ho, toh shayad kabhi disk se na padhe, kyunki operating system recently use hue disk blocks ko cache kar leta hai. Asli advantage yeh hai ki in-memory databases ko in-memory structures ko aise form mein encode karne ki cost nahi chukani padti jo disk par likha ja sake.

In-memory databases aise data models bhi de sakte hain jo disk par banana mushkil hai. Redis, jaise, priority queues aur sets jaise data structures ko database-jaisa interface deta hai. Sab kuch memory mein hone ki wajah se uska implementation relatively simple hai.

Recent research batati hai ki in-memory design memory se bade data ko bhi handle kar sakta hai. Anti-caching approach memory kam padne par sabse kam recently use hua data memory se disk par evict kar deti hai. Jab woh data dobara chahiye hota hai, use wapas load kar liya jaata hai. Yeh waisa hi hai jaisa operating systems virtual memory aur swap files ke saath karte hain. Database ise behtar kar sakta hai, kyunki woh poore memory pages ki jagah individual records par kaam karta hai. Lekin indexes ko phir bhi memory mein fit hona padta hai, chapter ki shuruaat ke Bitcask example ki tarah.

Agar non-volatile memory (NVM) common ho gayi, toh future storage engines mein bhi changes ki zaroorat pad sakti hai. Yeh abhi ek naya research area hai, lekin dhyaan dene layak hai.

Transaction processing ya analytics?

Business data processing ke shuruaati din mein database write aksar kisi commercial transaction se match karta tha: ek sale, supplier ko diya gaya order, ya di gayi salary. Phir databases un jagahon par bhi use hone lage jahan paise ka lena-dena nahi hota, lekin transaction word waise hi raha. Ab iska matlab hai reads aur writes ka ek group, jo ek logical unit banata hai. Transaction mein poori ACID properties (atomicity, consistency, isolation aur durability) hona zaroori nahi hai, jinhe Chapter 7 cover karta hai. Yahan transaction processing ka matlab bas itna hai ki clients low-latency reads aur writes kar sakein, na ki batch jobs jo periodically chalti hain, jaise din mein ek baar. Batch processing Chapter 10 mein cover hoti hai.

Databases blog comments, game actions, address book contacts jaise kaafi tarah ke data ke liye use hote the. Lekin access pattern lagbhag ek jaisa hi raha. Application kisi key se index use karke thode se records dhoondhti hai. User ke input ke hisaab se records insert ya update karti hai. Yeh apps interactive hoti hain, isliye is pattern ko online transaction processing, yani OLTP kehte hain.

Phir databases data analytics ke liye bhi zyada use hone lage, jiska access pattern bilkul alag hota hai. Ek analytic query aam taur par bahut saare records scan karti hai, har record ke sirf kuch columns padhti hai, aur count, sum ya average jaise aggregate statistics nikaalti hai. Woh raw records return nahi karti. Sales transactions ki table ke liye typical analytic sawaal kuch aise honge:

  • January mein har store ka total revenue kitna tha?
  • Latest promotion ke dauraan humne aam se kitne zyada bananas bechein?
  • Baby food ka kaunsa brand brand X ke diapers ke saath sabse zyada kharida jaata hai?

Yeh queries aksar business analysts likhte hain, aur inse reports banti hain jo management ko faisle lene mein madad karti hain. Ise business intelligence kehte hain. Is pattern ko transaction processing se alag batane ke liye ise online analytic processing, yani OLAP kehte hain. (Book ka kehna hai ki yahan “online” word saaf nahi hai. Shayad iska matlab hai ki analysts system ko interactively use karte hain, sirf fixed reports nahi, balki exploratory queries bhi chalate hain.)

Trade-offs

OLTP aur OLAP ka fark hamesha bilkul saaf nahi hota, lekin book ki table typical characteristics deti hai.

PropertyTransaction processing (OLTP)Analytic systems (OLAP)
Main read patternHar query mein thode records, key se fetch hote hainBahut saare records par aggregate
Main write patternUser input se random-access, low-latency writesBulk import (ETL) ya event stream
Mainly kaun use karta haiEnd users aur customers, web application ke throughInternal analysts, decision support ke liye
Data kya dikhata haiIs waqt data ki latest stateTime ke saath hue events ki history
Dataset sizeGigabytes se terabytesTerabytes se petabytes

Data Warehousing

Ek badi company mein dozens of transaction systems ho sakte hain. Ek customer website ke liye, ek physical stores ke checkout systems ke liye, ek warehouse inventory ke liye, ek vehicle routes ke liye, ek suppliers ke liye, aur ek employees ke liye. Har system complex hota hai aur uski apni team chahiye, isliye yeh zyadatar ek-doosre se independent chalte hain.

In OLTP systems se umeed hoti hai ki woh highly available aur fast honge, kyunki business unpar depend karta hai. Database administrators inhe bahut protect karte hain. Woh analysts ko inpar ad hoc analytic queries chalane dena nahi chahte, kyunki aisi queries expensive ho sakti hain. Jo query dataset ke bade hisse ko scan karti hai, woh saath mein chal rahi transactions ko slow kar sakti hai.

Iska jawab hai data warehouse: ek alag database, jispar analysts bina OLTP systems ko affect kiye freely query kar sakein. Isme company ke saare OLTP systems ke data ki read-only copy hoti hai. Data OLTP databases se extract hota hai, ya periodic dumps se ya changes ke continuous stream se. Phir use analysis ke layak schema mein transform kiya jaata hai, clean kiya jaata hai, aur warehouse mein load kar diya jaata hai. Is process ko Extract–Transform–Load, yani ETL kehte hain.

Data warehouses ab lagbhag har badi enterprise mein milte hain, lekin chhoti companies mein kam hote hain. Chhoti companies mein OLTP systems kam hote hain aur data bhi bahut kam hota hai. Us data ko ek aam SQL database mein, ya spreadsheet mein bhi query kiya ja sakta hai. Badi company mein woh kaam karne ke liye kaafi heavy lifting karni padti hai, jo chhoti company mein aasaan hota hai.

Alag warehouse ka ek bada fayda yeh hai ki use analytic access patterns ke liye optimize kiya ja sakta hai. Is chapter mein pehle jo indexing algorithms dekhe, woh OLTP ke liye achhe hain, lekin analytic queries ke liye bahut achhe nahi hain.

OLTP databases aur data warehouses ka alag hona

Data warehouse aksar relational hota hai, kyunki SQL analytic queries ke liye achha fit hai. Kaafi graphical tools SQL generate karte hain, results draw karte hain, aur analysts ko drill-down (zyada detail mein jaana) aur slicing and dicing (alag dimensions par filter karna) jaise operations se data explore karne dete hain.

Upar se dekhein toh warehouse aur OLTP database ek jaise lagte hain, kyunki dono mein SQL interface hota hai. Andar se woh bahut alag ho sakte hain, kyunki unhe bahut alag queries ke liye tune kiya gaya hota hai. Ab kaafi vendors ek hi workload par focus karte hain, dono par nahi.

Microsoft SQL Server aur SAP HANA jaise kuch products transaction processing aur warehousing dono support karte hain. Lekin woh dheere-dheere do alag storage aur query engines ban rahe hain, jo ek common SQL interface share karte hain.

Teradata, Vertica, SAP HANA aur ParAccel jaise data warehouse vendors aam taur par expensive commercial licenses bechte hain. Amazon Redshift ParAccel ka hosted version hai. Haal hi mein kaafi open-source SQL-on-Hadoop projects aaye hain. Woh abhi naye hain, lekin commercial warehouses se compete karna chahte hain. Examples mein Apache Hive, Spark SQL, Cloudera Impala, Facebook Presto, Apache Tajo aur Apache Drill shaamil hain. Kuch Google ke Dremel paper par based hain.

Stars aur Snowflakes: analytics ke liye schemas

Transaction processing mein kaafi data models use hote hain, jo har application ke hisaab se chune jaate hain. Analytics mein bahut kam models hote hain. Kaafi warehouses ek formulaic layout follow karte hain jise star schema kehte hain, ya dimensional modeling bhi.

Star schema ke center mein ek fact table hoti hai. Fact table ki har row kisi particular time par hua ek event record karti hai. Grocery store mein har row ek customer ka ek product kharidna ho sakti hai. Website traffic ke liye har row ek page view ya click ho sakti hai. Aam taur par facts individual events ki tarah rakhe jaate hain, kyunki isse baad mein sabse zyada flexibility milti hai. Nuksaan yeh hai ki fact tables bahut bade ho jaate hain. Book ke hisaab se ek badi enterprise ke warehouse mein tens of petabytes ki transaction history ho sakti hai, jiska zyadatar hissa fact tables mein hota hai.

Fact table ke kuch columns plain values hote hain, jaise product kis price par bika aur use kharidne mein kitna cost aaya, taaki profit margin nikaala ja sake. Baaki columns foreign keys hote hain, jo dimension tables ke references hain. Fact table ki har row ek event hai, aur uski dimensions us event ke who, what, where, when, how aur why batati hain.

Book ka ek worked example grocery retailer ka hai. Uski fact table ka naam fact_sales hai. Ek dimension hai bika hua product. dim_product ki har row bikri ke liye available ek kism ka product hai, jisme stock-keeping unit (SKU, product ka unique code), description, brand, category, fat content, package size aur aur bhi cheezein hoti hain. fact_sales ki row foreign key se batati hai ki kaunsa product bika. Agar customer ek saath kai products kharidta hai, toh har product fact table mein alag row ban jaata hai.

Dates aur times bhi aksar dimension tables hote hain. Isse warehouse kisi date ke baare mein extra facts record kar sakta hai, jaise woh public holiday thi ya nahi, taaki queries holidays aur aam dinon ki sales compare kar sakein.

Naam picture se aaya hai. Table relationships draw karein toh fact table beech mein hoti hai aur uske charon taraf dimension tables, bilkul star ki rays ki tarah.

Snowflake schema ek variant hai jisme dimensions ko aur chhoti subdimensions mein tod diya jaata hai. Jaise brands aur product categories ki apni-apni table ban sakti hai, aur dim_product unhe text ki tarah store karne ke bajaye unke foreign keys rakhegi. Snowflake schemas zyada normalized hote hain (zyada tables mein bante hue, repetition kam). Phir bhi star schemas aksar pasand kiye jaate hain, kyunki analysts ko unke saath kaam karna aasaan lagta hai.

Warehouse tables aksar bahut wide hoti hain. Fact tables mein aksar 100 se zyada columns hote hain, kabhi-kabhi kai sau. Dimension tables bhi wide hoti hain, kyunki unme har woh detail hoti hai jo analysis ke liye matter kar sakti hai. Store dimension mein record ho sakta hai ki store kaunsi services deta hai, in-store bakery hai ya nahi, floor area kitna hai, kab khula, last baar kab remodel hua, aur nearest highway kitni door hai.

Column-oriented storage

Agar tumhare paas trillions of rows aur petabytes ke facts hain, toh unhe efficiently store aur query karna mushkil hai. Dimension tables kaafi chhoti hoti hain, aksar millions of rows ki. Isliye book is par focus karti hai ki facts kaise store hote hain.

Fact table 100 se zyada columns wide ho sakti hai, lekin ek typical warehouse query ek baar mein sirf chaar-paanch columns use karti hai. Queries ko shayad hi kabhi SELECT * chahiye. Book ka example dekhte hain, jo poochta hai ki hafte ke alag-alag dinon par log fresh fruit zyada kharidte hain ya candy.

Example

Neeche wali query 2013 mein fresh fruit ya candy ki har sale dekhti hai, aur har weekday aur category ke liye count karti hai ki kitna bika. Yeh bahut saari rows touch karti hai, lekin fact_sales ke sirf teen columns: date_key, product_sk aur quantity. Baaki saare columns ignore ho jaate hain.

SELECT
  dim_date.weekday, dim_product.category,
  SUM(fact_sales.quantity) AS quantity_sold
FROM fact_sales
JOIN dim_date ON fact_sales.date_key = dim_date.date_key
JOIN dim_product ON fact_sales.product_sk = dim_product.product_sk
WHERE dim_date.year = 2013 AND
  dim_product.category IN ('Fresh fruit', 'Candy')
GROUP BY dim_date.weekday, dim_product.category;

Yeh efficiently kaise chalegi? Zyadatar OLTP databases mein storage row-oriented hota hai. Ek row ki saari values ek-doosre ke bagal mein store hoti hain. Document databases bhi kuch aise hi kaam karte hain, jo poore document ko bytes ke ek contiguous run ki tarah store karte hain, jaise chapter ke shuru wala CSV log.

Tum fact_sales.date_key ya fact_sales.product_sk par indexes laga sakte ho, taaki engine ek date ki ya ek product ki saari sales dhoondh sake. Lekin row-oriented engine ko phir bhi har matching row disk se load karni padti hai, uske saare 100-plus columns ke saath, har ek ko parse karna padta hai, aur phir jo match nahi karti unhe filter karna padta hai. Isme kaafi time lagta hai.

Column-oriented storage ka idea simple hai. Ek row ki values ek saath store nahi karte. Har column ki saari values ek saath store karte hain. Agar har column apni alag file mein rakhi ho, toh query sirf wahi columns padhti aur parse karti hai jo use chahiye. Baaki ko kabhi touch nahi kiya jaata. Book ise apne Figure 3-10 mein dikhati hai, jo neeche diya hai.

Column layout is par depend karta hai ki har column file mein rows ek hi order mein hon. Isliye poori row dobara banane ke liye har column file se 23rd entry uthayein aur unhe jod dein. Isse table ki 23rd row mil jaati hai.

Column storage ko relational tables ke saath samjhana sabse aasaan hai, lekin yeh idea doosre data models ke liye bhi kaam karta hai. Parquet ek columnar format hai jo document model support karta hai, aur woh Google ke Dremel system par based hai.

Column compression

Kam columns padhne se disk par load kam hota hai. Data ko compress karke load aur kam kiya ja sakta hai. Column storage aksar bahut achha compress hota hai. Ek column ki values ke sequences dekhein. Woh repetitive hote hain, jo compression ke liye achhi baat hai. Alag-alag columns par alag techniques fit baithti hain. Warehouses mein ek technique khaas taur par achha kaam karti hai, bitmap encoding.

Aksar column mein rows ke comparison mein distinct values kam hoti hain. Ek retailer ke paas billions of sales transactions ho sakte hain, lekin sirf 100,000 distinct products. Bitmap encoding ek column ko, jisme n distinct values hain, n alag bitmaps mein badal deta hai, har value ke liye ek. Har bitmap mein har row ke liye ek bit hota hai. Agar us row mein woh value hai toh bit 1 hota hai, nahi hai toh 0.

Agar n chhota hai, jaise country column mein lagbhag 200 values, toh har bitmap ko har row ke liye ek bit se store kiya ja sakta hai. Agar n bada hai, toh zyadatar bitmaps mein zyadatar bits zero hote hain. Aise bitmaps ko sparse kehte hain. Sparse bitmap ko run-length encoded bhi kiya ja sakta hai, matlab har bit store karne ke bajaye barabar bits ke har run ki length store karna. Isse column kaafi compact ho sakta hai.

Bitmap indexes common warehouse queries ke liye bahut achhe hain. In do examples ko dekhte hain.

Example

Products ki list. Query WHERE product_sk IN (30, 68, 69) ko teen products mein se kisi ek ki rows chahiye. Engine teen bitmaps load karta hai, product 30 ka, 68 ka aur 69 ka. Phir un teeno ka bitwise OR nikaalta hai, matlab agar kisi bhi bitmap mein us position par 1 hai toh row include hoti hai. Yeh bahut efficient hai.

Do conditions ek saath. Query WHERE product_sk = 31 AND store_sk = 3 ko woh rows chahiye jo dono conditions match karti hain. Engine product 31 ka bitmap aur store 3 ka bitmap load karta hai, aur bitwise AND nikaalta hai. Yeh isliye kaam karta hai kyunki columns rows ko ek hi order mein store karte hain. Isliye ek bitmap ka kth bit doosre bitmap ke kth bit ki same row ko refer karta hai.

Doosre kism ke data ke liye aur bhi compression schemes hain. Book unke overview ki taraf point karti hai.

Dhyaan do

Cassandra aur HBase mein “column families” hoti hain, jo Bigtable se aaya concept hai. Naam kuch bhi ho, woh sach mein column-oriented nahi hain. Har column family ke andar woh ek row ke saare columns row key ke saath ek jagah store karte hain, aur column compression use nahi karte. Isliye Bigtable model abhi bhi zyadatar row-oriented hai.

Memory bandwidth aur vectorized processing

Jin warehouse queries mein millions of rows scan hoti hain, unke liye ek bada bottleneck disk se memory tak data laane ki bandwidth hai. Lekin yahi akela bottleneck nahi hai. Analytic databases ke developers main memory se CPU cache (processor ke paas ki ek chhoti, bahut fast memory) tak ki bandwidth par bhi kaam karte hain. Woh branch mispredictions (jab CPU galat guess karta hai ki program kaunsa raasta lega) aur instruction pipeline mein stalls se bachne ki bhi koshish karte hain. Modern CPUs par woh SIMD instructions (ek hi instruction jo kai data items ko ek saath process karti hai) use karte hain.

Column layout CPU ki bhi madad karta hai, sirf disk ki nahi. Query engine compressed column data ka ek chunk utha sakta hai jo L1 cache (sabse chhota aur sabse fast cache) mein fit ho jaye, aur uspar bina function calls ke tight loop chala sakta hai. CPU aisa loop un code se kaafi tez chalata hai jo bahut saare function calls karta hai aur har record ke liye checks lagata hai. Compression se same cache space mein zyada rows fit hoti hain. Bitwise AND aur OR jaise operators in compressed chunks par seedhe kaam kar sakte hain. Ise vectorized processing kehte hain.

Column storage mein sort order

Column store mein rows ka order matter karna zaroori nahi hai. Sabse simple choice hai rows ko insert hone ke order mein store karna, kyunki tab nayi row bas har column file mein ek value append karti hai. Lekin tum ek order impose bhi kar sakte ho, jaise pehle SSTables mein dekha, aur use indexing method ki tarah use kar sakte ho.

Tum har column ko alag se sort nahi kar sakte. Tab values row ke hisaab se line up nahi rahengi. Row tabhi dobara ban sakti hai jab har column ki kth value usi row ki ho. Isliye rows ko poori rows ki tarah sort karna padta hai, bhale hi woh column ke hisaab se store hoti hain. Sort columns database administrator common queries ke hisaab se chunta hai.

Example

Maan lo queries aksar date ranges ko target karti hain, jaise pichhla mahina. Tab date_key pehli sort key ho sakti hai. Phir query optimizer sirf pichhle mahine ki rows scan karta hai, jo har row scan karne se kaafi tez hai.

Doosri sort key un rows ka order decide karti hai jinki pehli key ki value same hai. Agar date_key pehli hai, toh product_sk doosri ho sakti hai. Tab ek din mein ek hi product ki saari sales saath baithti hain, jo un queries ki madad karta hai jo date range ke andar product se group ya filter karti hain.

Sorting compression mein bhi madad karti hai. Agar pehle sort column mein distinct values kam hain, toh sort ke baad usme ek hi value ke lambe runs ban jaate hain. Simple run-length encoding us column ko kuch kilobytes tak dabaa sakta hai, chahe table mein billions of rows hon. Yeh asar pehli sort key par sabse zyada hota hai. Doosri aur teesri keys zyada jumbled hoti hain, isliye unke runs chhote hote hain. Sort order mein aur neeche wale columns random dikhte hain aur kam compress hote hain. Phir bhi pehle kuch columns ko sort karna kul milakar fayde ka sauda hai.

Kai alag sort orders

C-Store se ek clever extension aaya, jise commercial warehouse Vertica ne apnaya. Alag queries ko alag sort orders se fayda hota hai. Toh same data ko kai alag tarah sort karke store kyun na kiya jaye? Data ko waise bhi kai machines par copy karna padta hai, taaki ek machine kho jaye toh data na jaye. Toh un copies ko alag-alag tarah sort karke rakh lein. Phir har query woh copy use kar sakti hai jo uske liye sabse achhi ho.

Yeh kuch-kuch row-oriented store mein kai secondary indexes rakhne jaisa hai. Lekin ek bada fark hai. Row-oriented store har row ko ek jagah rakhta hai, heap file ya clustered index mein, aur secondary indexes sirf uske pointers rakhte hain. Column store mein normally data ke doosri jagah pointers nahi hote. Usme sirf values ke columns hote hain.

Column-oriented storage mein writing

Yeh optimizations warehouses ke liye fit hain, jahan zyadatar load analysts ki badi read-only queries ka hota hai. Lekin compression, sorting aur column layout se writes mushkil ho jaati hain. Compressed columns ke saath B-tree jaisa update in place possible nahi hai. Sorted table ke beech mein row insert karne ke liye saari column files rewrite karni pad sakti hain, kyunki rows ki pehchaan har column mein unki position se hoti hai. Insert ko har column consistently update karna padta hai.

Pehle wala solution yahan bhi kaam karta hai: LSM-trees. Saari writes pehle ek in-memory store mein jaati hain, jahan woh ek sorted structure mein add hoti hain aur disk ke liye taiyaar hoti hain. Yeh store row-oriented ho ya column-oriented, koi fark nahi padta. Jab kaafi writes jama ho jaati hain, toh unhe disk ki column files ke saath merge kiya jaata hai aur bulk mein nayi files mein likh diya jaata hai. Book ke hisaab se Vertica essentially yahi karta hai.

Queries ko disk ka column data aur memory ki recent writes, dono dekhne padte hain aur unhe combine karna padta hai. Lekin query optimizer yeh split chhupa deta hai. Analyst ke point of view se inserts, updates aur deletes agli queries mein turant dikhte hain.

Aggregation: data cubes aur materialized views

Har warehouse column store nahi hota. Traditional row-oriented databases aur kuch doosre designs bhi use hote hain. Lekin ad hoc analytic queries ke liye columnar storage kaafi tez ho sakta hai, isliye woh tezi se popular ho raha hai.

Warehouse queries aksar COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN ya MAX jaise aggregate functions use karti hain. Agar kai queries same aggregates use karti hain, toh har baar raw data crunch karna waste hai. Jo counts ya sums queries sabse zyada use karti hain, unhe cache kyun na kar liya jaye?

Ek tarika hai materialized view. Normal (virtual) view ek table jaisi cheez hai jiska content ek query se aata hai. View khud kuch store nahi karta. Use padhne ka matlab query chalana hai. Materialized view query results ki asli copy hai, jo disk par likhi hoti hai. Virtual view padhte waqt SQL engine use on the fly uski underlying query mein expand kar deta hai. Materialized view padhte waqt tum stored results padhte ho.

Jab underlying data badalta hai, toh materialized view ko update karna padta hai, kyunki woh ek denormalized copy hai (aisi copy jo woh information repeat karti hai jo pehle se kahin aur stored hai). Database yeh automatically kar sakta hai, lekin isse writes expensive ho jaati hain. Isi wajah se OLTP databases mein materialized views kam use hote hain. Read-heavy warehouses mein woh zyada sense bana sakte hain, halaanki woh reads ko sach mein tez karte hain ya nahi, yeh case par depend karta hai.

Ek common special case hai data cube, jise OLAP cube bhi kehte hain. Yeh aggregates ka ek grid hai, jo alag dimensions ke hisaab se group kiya hota hai.

Abhi ke liye maan lo ki har fact ki sirf do dimension tables ki foreign keys hain, date aur product. Ek two-dimensional table banayein jisme ek axis par dates aur doosre par products hon. Har cell mein aggregate hota hai, jaise net price jaisi attribute ka SUM, un saare facts ke liye jinki woh date aur product hai. Phir tum same aggregate ek row ya ek column ke saath laga sakte ho. Isse ek dimension kam karke summary milti hai: date ki parwah kiye bina product ke hisaab se sales, ya product ki parwah kiye bina date ke hisaab se sales.

Facts mein aksar do se zyada dimensions hoti hain. Grocery example mein paanch hain: date, product, store, promotion aur customer. Tab har cell mein paanchon ke ek combination ki sales hoti hain. Paanch-dimensional cube ko imagine karna mushkil hai, lekin idea wahi hai. Har cell ko kisi bhi dimension ke saath summarize kiya ja sakta hai.

Example

Date aur store par bana cube “kal har store ki total sales” ka jawab de sakta hai, store dimension ke saath kal ke totals padhkar. Millions of rows scan karne ki zaroorat nahi. Kuch queries bahut fast ho jaati hain, kyunki unke jawab pehle se compute kiye hue hote hain.

Nuksaan yeh hai ki flexibility kam ho jaati hai. Cube sirf apni dimensions ke baare mein sawaalon ka jawab deta hai. Jaise, jis cube mein price dimension nahi hai, woh yeh nahi bata sakta ki $100 se mehnge items se sales ka kitna hissa aaya. Raw data bata sakta hai, isliye zyadatar warehouses jitna ho sake raw data rakhte hain, aur cubes aur aggregates ko sirf kuch queries ke liye speed boost ki tarah use karte hain.

Summary

Short mein
  • Do tarah ke workload. Storage engines do bade groups mein aate hain: jo transaction processing (OLTP) ke liye optimized hain, aur jo analytics (OLAP) ke liye. OLTP systems user-facing hote hain aur har query mein thode records touch karte hain, jo key aur index se dhoondhe jaate hain. Disk seek time aksar bottleneck hota hai. Analytic systems mein queries kam aati hain, lekin har ek millions of records scan karti hai. Disk bandwidth aksar bottleneck hoti hai, aur column storage uska ek tezi se popular hota jawab hai.
  • Log-structured school. Yeh family sirf files mein append karti hai aur obsolete files delete karti hai. Ek baar likhi file ko woh kabhi badalti nahi. Bitcask, SSTables, LSM-trees, LevelDB, Cassandra, HBase aur Lucene isi mein aate hain. Iska key idea random writes ko sequential writes mein badalna hai, jisse hard drives aur SSDs par write throughput zyada milta hai. Yeh engines comparatively naya development hain.
  • Update-in-place school. Yeh family disk ko fixed-size pages ki tarah treat karti hai jinhe overwrite kiya ja sakta hai. B-trees sabse bada example hain. Woh saare major relational databases mein aur kai nonrelational databases mein use hote hain.
  • Doosri structures. Secondary indexes, clustered aur covering indexes, multi-column aur multi-dimensional indexes, aur fuzzy full-text indexes, sab basic idea ko aage badhate hain. In-memory databases saara data RAM mein rakhte hain, aur durability ke liye logs ya snapshots use karte hain.
  • Warehouses aur column storage. Data warehouse analysts ke liye ek alag database hai, jo OLTP systems se ETL ke zariye bhara jaata hai. Star schemas use fact tables aur dimension tables ke around organize karte hain. Column-oriented storage, compression aur sort orders ke saath, har query ke liye sirf zaroori columns padhta hai. Materialized views aur data cubes common aggregates pehle se precompute kar lete hain.
  • Apna engine jaanein. Yeh internals jaanne se application developer sahi tool chun sakta hai, aur andaza laga sakta hai ki koi tuning parameter kya badlega. Isse tumhe jo bhi database use karte hain, uska documentation padhne mein bhi madad milti hai.

Chapter ke end mein 64 references hain, papers, documentation aur articles ke, jin par uske claims tike hain. Yeh retelling us list ko reproduce nahi karti.

Check yourself

  1. Hash index har key memory mein rakhta hai. Isse yeh approach kaise limit hoti hai, aur values ko bhi memory mein rakhne ke baare mein book kya kehti hai?

    Jawab dekho

    Poora hash map RAM mein fit hona chahiye, isliye bahut saari keys hon toh design toot jaata hai. Values ko memory mein fit hona zaroori nahi, kyunki har ek ko disk se ek seek mein padha ja sakta hai.

  2. B-tree update jo page split karta hai, kai pages likhta hai. Zyadatar B-tree implementations write-ahead log bhi kyun rakhti hain?

    Jawab dekho

    Agar un mein se sirf kuch pages likhe jaane ke baad database crash ho jaye, toh tree corrupt ho sakta hai, jaise ek orphan page jisko koi parent point nahi karta. Log har change ko apply hone se pehle record karta hai, taaki crash ke baad tree ko consistent state mein wapas laaya ja sake.

  3. LSM-tree par heavy writes aati hain, lekin compaction saath nahi de paata. Kya galat hota hai, aur book monitoring ki zaroorat kyun batati hai?

    Jawab dekho

    Unmerged segments disk par jama hote jaate hain jab tak space khatam na ho jaye, aur reads slow ho jaati hain kyunki unhe zyada files check karni padti hain. SSTable engines aam taur par incoming writes ko throttle nahi karte, isliye agar tum dhyaan na rakho toh problem silently badh sakti hai.

  4. Fact table mein 100 se zyada columns hain, aur query sirf teen padhti hai. Column storage kaam kaise kam karta hai, aur column files se poori row kaise dobara banti hai?

    Jawab dekho

    Sirf teen column files load aur parse hoti hain, isliye disk se kaafi kam data padha jaata hai. Har column file rows ko same order mein rakhti hai, isliye row dobara banane ke liye har column file se same position (jaise 23rd entry) uthayi jaati hai.

Part I · Chapter 4

Encoding aur Evolution

Seedhi baat: programs time ke saath change hote rehte hain, lekin unka likha hua data saalon tak zinda rehta hai. Isliye data ka encoding aisa hona chahiye ki purana aur naya code ek-doosre ka data padh sakein, deployment adhoora ho tab bhi aur uske kaafi baad bhi.

Applications hamesha change hoti rehti hain. Naye features ship hote hain, business rules badalte hain, aur teams ko dheere-dheere pata chalta hai ki users ko asal mein kya chahiye. Zyaadatar feature changes mein application ka stored data bhi change hota hai. Ho sakta hai tumhe ek naya field capture karna pade, ya existing data ko naye tarike se dikhana pade. Chapter 1 mein is adapt karne ki ability ko evolvability kaha tha.

Databases change ko alag-alag tarike se handle karte hain. Relational database aam taur par maanta hai ki ek time par ek hi schema (data ka agreed structure, jaise tables aur columns) hoga. Tum migration se schema badal sakte ho, matlab ALTER statement jo structure ko rewrite kar deta hai, lekin kisi bhi moment par exactly ek schema hi lagu hota hai. Schema-on-read database, jise schemaless bhi kehte hain, schema enforce nahi karta. Usme alag-alag time par likhe gaye purane aur naye formats ka mix ho sakta hai. Dono approaches Chapter 2 mein cover hue hain.

Code badalna schema badalne se mushkil hai, kyunki code har jagah ek saath change nahi hota. Server-side applications mein aksar rolling upgrade hota hai, jise staged rollout bhi kehte hain. Naya version pehle kuch nodes (cluster ki machines ya processes) par jaata hai. Team check karti hai ki sab smoothly chal raha hai, phir baaki nodes par ek-ek group karke jaati hai. Matlab naya version bina downtime ke release ho sakta hai, aur isse releases zyada frequently hone lagte hain. Client-side applications mein yeh aur mushkil hai. Update kab install karna hai, yeh user decide karta hai, toh purana version mahino tak chalta reh sakta hai.

Toh ek hi system mein code ke purane aur naye versions, aur data ke purane aur naye formats, sab saath-saath ho sakte hain. Sab smoothly chalta rahe, isliye system ko dono directions mein compatibility chahiye:

  • Backward compatibility: naya code woh data padh sakta hai jo purane code ne likha tha.
  • Forward compatibility: purana code woh data padh sakta hai jo naye code ne likha tha.
Asli idea

Backward compatibility ka matlab hai naya code purana data padh le, aur forward compatibility ka matlab hai purana code naya data padh le. Rolling upgrade ke dauraan dono chahiye, kyunki dono versions ek saath live hote hain.

Backward compatibility aam taur par mushkil nahi hoti. Naya code tumne likha hai, toh purane data ka format tumhe pata hai. Tum use explicitly handle kar sakte ho, chahe purane records padhne ke liye purana code hi rakhna pade. Forward compatibility thodi tricky hai. Purane code ko naye version ke add kiye hue parts ko bina toote ignore karna padta hai.

Is chapter mein data encode karne ke kai formats dekhte hain: JSON, XML, Protocol Buffers, Thrift aur Avro. Dekhte hain ki har format schema changes ko kaise handle karta hai, aur purane-naye data aur code ko saath chalane mein kitna achha hai. Phir dekhenge ki yeh formats kahan use hote hain: databases mein data store karne ke liye, web services aur remote procedure calls mein communication ke liye (RPC, jahan ek program doosri machine ka function aise call karta hai jaise woh local ho), aur queues aur actor systems ke through message passing ke liye.

Data encode karne ke formats

Programs aam taur par data ke saath do forms mein kaam karte hain. Memory mein data objects, structs, lists, arrays, hash tables aur trees mein rehta hai. Yeh structures CPU ke fast access ke liye bane hote hain, aur parts ko jodne ke liye aksar pointers (memory addresses) use karte hain. Jab tumhe data file mein likhna ho ya network par bhejna ho, toh use ek self-contained bytes ki sequence mein badalna padta hai, jaise JSON document. Pointer kisi doosre process ke liye bekaar hota hai, isliye bytes wala form in-memory form se kaafi alag dikhta hai.

In-memory form se bytes mein translate karne ko encoding kehte hain, jise serialization ya marshalling bhi bolte hain. Ulta translation decoding hai, jise parsing, deserialization ya unmarshalling bhi kehte hain.

Dhyaan do

Serialization word transactions ke context mein bhi aata hai, aur wahan uska matlab bilkul alag hai. Dono mein confusion na ho, isliye book encoding word hi use karti hai. Encoding ka encryption se bhi koi lena-dena nahi hai, aur encryption ko book cover nahi karti.

Yeh problem itni common hai ki chunne ke liye bahut saari libraries aur formats hain. Book unhe lagbhag isi order mein dekhti hai.

Language-specific formats

Kai programming languages mein memory ke objects ko bytes mein encode karne ka built-in support hota hai. Java mein java.io.Serializable hai, Ruby mein Marshal hai, aur Python mein pickle hai. Third-party libraries bhi hain, jaise Java ke liye Kryo. Yeh built-in tools convenient hain, kyunki bahut kam extra code mein objects save aur restore ho jaate hain. Lekin Kleppmann kuch gehri problems point karte hain:

  • Format ek hi language se bandha hota hai. Doosri language se yeh data padhna bahut mushkil hai. Is tarah data store karenge, toh tum kaafi time tak apni current language se bandh jaate ho, aur doosri languages use karne wale organizations ke saath data share karna mushkil ho jaata hai.
  • Security. Object restore karne ke liye decoder ko arbitrary classes ke instances banane padte hain. Agar attacker tumhari application se apni choose ki hui byte sequence decode karwa le, toh woh arbitrary classes bana sakta hai. Remote code execution ka yeh ek common raasta hai, matlab woh apna code tumhari machine par chala sakta hai.
  • Versioning baad mein socha jaata hai. Yeh libraries quick aur easy encoding ke liye bani hain, isliye forward aur backward compatibility ki jhanjhat wali problems aksar ignore ho jaati hain.
  • Efficiency bhi baad mein sochi jaati hai. Matlab encode ya decode karne ka CPU time bhi, aur result ka size bhi. Jaise Java ki built-in serialization poor performance aur bloated encoding ke liye jaani jaati hai.

Inhi wajahon se book ka kehna hai ki language ki built-in encoding ko bahut short-lived kaamon ke alawa kisi aur cheez ke liye use karna generally bura idea hai.

JSON, XML aur binary variants

Aisi standardized encodings jinhe kai languages likh aur padh sakein, agla obvious choice hain. JSON aur XML main contenders hain. Yeh dono bahut jaane-pehchaane aur widely supported hain, aur lagbhag utne hi widely naapasand bhi. XML ko aksar bahut verbose aur zaroorat se zyada complicated kaha jaata hai. JSON mainly isliye popular hua ki web browsers ise natively support karte hain (yeh JavaScript ka subset hai) aur yeh XML se simple hai. CSV, jo comma-separated values ki plain table hoti hai, ek aur popular format hai, par kam powerful hai.

JSON, XML aur CSV textual hain, isliye insaan kuch had tak unhe padh sakte hain, halaanki unki syntax debate ka favorite topic hai. Upar-upar ki baaton ke alawa inme kuch subtle problems hain:

  • Numbers ambiguous hote hain. XML aur CSV mein external schema ke bina number aur digits ki string mein farak nahi bata sakte. JSON strings aur numbers ko alag karta hai, lekin integers aur floating-point numbers (decimal part wale numbers, jo approximately store hote hain) mein farak nahi karta, aur precision bhi specify nahi karta. Yeh bade integers ke liye matter karta hai. 253 se bada koi bhi integer IEEE 754 double-precision float mein exactly store nahi ho sakta, jo JavaScript samet kai languages ka standard number format hai. Parse karne ke baad numbers inaccurate ho jaate hain. Twitter har tweet ko identify karne ke liye 64-bit numbers use karta hai, isliye uski API har tweet ID do baar return karti hai: ek baar JSON number ki tarah aur ek baar decimal string ki tarah. Is workaround se JavaScript applications ko sahi value mil jaati hai.
  • Binary strings support nahi hoti. JSON aur XML Unicode text achhe se handle karte hain, lekin character encoding ke bina plain bytes ki sequence hold nahi kar sakte. Log iska jugaad yeh karte hain ki bytes ko Base64 se text mein encode kar dete hain, aur schema bata deta hai ki us text ko bytes ki tarah decode karna hai. Kaam toh karta hai, par hacky hai, aur data lagbhag 33 percent bada ho jaata hai.
  • Schema support optional hai. XML aur JSON dono ki optional schema languages hain. Yeh powerful hain, lekin seekhna aur implement karna complicated hai. XML schemas kaafi common hain, par kai JSON-based tools schemas ko poori tarah skip kar dete hain. Numbers aur binary strings ka sahi matlab schema par depend karta hai, isliye jin applications mein schema nahi hota, unhe decoding logic hardcode karna padta hai.
  • CSV mein schema hota hi nahi. Har row aur column ka matlab application ko define karna padta hai. Agar kisi change se row ya column add ho jaye, toh use haath se handle karna padega. CSV vague bhi hai. Agar kisi value mein comma ya newline ho toh kya hoga? Uske escaping rules formally likhe ja chuke hain, lekin har parser unhe sahi implement nahi karta.

In flaws ke baad bhi JSON, XML aur CSV kai use cases ke liye kaafi achhe hain, aur shayad popular bane rahenge. Yeh data interchange formats ke roop mein khaas taur par achhe kaam karte hain, yani ek organization se doosre ko data bhejne ke liye. Is setting mein asli mushkil dono sides ko format par agree karwana hai. Ek baar agree ho gaye, toh format kitna sundar ya efficient hai, yeh bahut kam matter karta hai.

Binary encoding

Jo data sirf tumhare apne organization ke andar use hota hai, usme lowest-common-denominator format use karne ka pressure kam hota hai. Tum koi zyada compact ya parse karne mein fast format chun sakte ho. Chhote dataset mein gain na ke barabar hota hai. Terabytes tak pahunchte hi format ka choice bahut bada farak dal sakta hai.

JSON XML se kam verbose hai, lekin dono binary formats se kaafi zyada space lete hain. Isi observation se JSON ke liye binary encodings ka bada family bana, jisme MessagePack, BSON, BJSON, UBJSON, BISON aur Smile aate hain, aur XML ke liye WBXML aur Fast Infoset. In formats ko apni-apni niches mili hain, par koi bhi textual versions jitna widely adopt nahi hua. Inme se kuch datatypes add karte hain, jaise integers aur floating-point numbers ko alag batana ya binary strings jodna. Baaki sab mein JSON ya XML ka data model waisa hi rehta hai. Kyunki yeh schema use nahi karte, inhe har object ke field names encoded data ke andar hi rakhne padte hain.

Chapter ke baaki hisse mein formats compare karne ke liye book yeh record use karti hai:

{
  "userName": "Martin",
  "favoriteNumber": 1337,
  "interests": ["daydreaming", "hacking"]
}
Example

Book is record ko MessagePack se encode karti hai, jo JSON ke liye ek binary encoding hai. Pehle kuch bytes aise kaam karte hain:

  1. Pehla byte, 0x83, batata hai ki ek object aa raha hai (top four bits 0x80 hain) jisme teen fields hain (bottom four bits 0x03 hain). Agar object mein 15 se zyada fields hon, toh alag type marker use hota, aur field count ke liye do ya chaar bytes lagte.
  2. Doosra byte, 0xa8, batata hai ki ek string aa rahi hai (top four bits 0xa0 hain) jo aath bytes lambi hai (bottom four bits 0x08 hain).
  3. Agle aath bytes field name userName hain, ASCII mein. Length pehle hi di ja chuki hai, isliye end marker ya escaping ki zaroorat nahi.
  4. Agle saat bytes mein chhe letters ki value Martin hai, prefix byte 0xa6 ke saath, aur record ke baaki hisse ke liye bhi aise hi chalta hai.

Poori binary encoding 66 bytes ki hai. Whitespace hata kar textual JSON 81 bytes ka hai. Saving chhoti hai, aur book poochti hai ki itni saving ke liye human readability khona sahi hai ya nahi. Saari binary JSON encodings lagbhag aise hi behave karti hain. Phir book dikhati hai ki wahi record 32 bytes mein kaise encode ho sakta hai.

Thrift aur Protocol Buffers

Apache Thrift aur Protocol Buffers (jinhe aam taur par protobuf kehte hain) ek hi principle par bani binary encoding libraries hain. Protocol Buffers pehle Google mein develop hua tha, aur Thrift Facebook mein. Dono 2007 aur 2008 mein open source kiye gaye.

Dono ko encode kiye jaane wale har data ke liye schema chahiye. Schema tum ek chhoti language mein describe karte ho jise interface definition language (IDL) kehte hain, matlab data ki shape likhne ka aisa tarika jise tools padh sakein. Thrift ke IDL mein example record aisa dikhta hai:

struct Person {
  1: required string userName,
  2: optional i64 favoriteNumber,
  3: optional list<string> interests
}

Protocol Buffers ka schema bahut similar dikhta hai:

message Person {
  required string user_name = 1;
  optional int64 favorite_number = 2;
  repeated string interests = 3;
}

Dono tools ke saath code generator aata hai. Woh aise schema ko leta hai aur tumhari chuni hui language mein classes bana deta hai jo us schema ko implement karti hain. Application code records encode ya decode karne ke liye in generated classes ko call karta hai.

Thrift mein actually ek se zyada binary formats hain. Uske do main formats BinaryProtocol aur CompactProtocol hain. Kleppmann note karte hain ki teesra, DenseProtocol, sirf C++ version mein hai, isliye woh cross-language nahi maana jaata. BinaryProtocol example record ko 59 bytes mein encode karta hai. Har field ko type annotation milti hai, aur jahan zaroori ho wahan length bhi, jaise string ki length ya list ke items ki count. Strings, jaise “Martin”, UTF-8 mein store hoti hain. JSON se bada farak yeh hai ki field names hote hi nahi. Unki jagah har field ke saath ek field tag hota hai, schema ka ek number (yahan 1, 2 aur 3). Field tag field name ke chhote alias jaisa kaam karta hai.

Example

Thrift ka CompactProtocol wahi information 34 bytes mein rakh deta hai. Woh field type aur tag number ko ek hi byte mein pack kar deta hai, aur variable-length integers use karta hai. Number 1337 ke liye poore aath bytes ki jagah sirf do bytes lagte hain. Har byte ka top bit batata hai ki aur bytes aage aa rahe hain ya nahi. –64 se 63 tak ke numbers ek byte mein fit ho jaate hain, –8192 se 8191 tak ke do bytes mein, aur bade numbers mein zyada bytes lagte hain.

Protocol Buffers ka sirf ek binary format hai. Woh bits ko CompactProtocol se thoda alag tarike se pack karta hai, lekin baaki sab lagbhag same hai, aur wahi record 33 bytes mein fit kar deta hai.

Ek detail dhyaan dene wali hai. Dono schemas fields ko required ya optional mark karte hain, lekin is marker se encoded bytes change nahi hote. Binary data mein kahin nahi likha hota ki field required tha ya nahi. Farak bas itna hai ki required ek runtime check add kar deta hai, jo field set na ho toh fail ho jaata hai. Yeh check bugs pakadne mein madad kar sakta hai.

Field tags aur schema evolution

Schemas time ke saath badalte hi hain. Book ise schema evolution kehti hai. Thrift aur Protocol Buffers backward aur forward dono compatibility bacha ke changes kaise handle karte hain?

Encoded record bas apne encoded fields ka concatenation hota hai. Har field apne tag number se identify hota hai aur uske datatype ki annotation hoti hai, jaise string ya integer. Jo field set nahi hai, use record se bas hata diya jaata hai. Isse field tags data ke matlab ke liye critical ho jaate hain. Schema mein tum field ka naam badal sakte ho, kyunki encoded data mein field names kabhi use hi nahi hote. Lekin field ka tag nahi badal sakte, kyunki isse saara existing encoded data invalid ho jaayega.

Field add karna safe hai agar naye field ko naya tag number mile. Maan lo purana code, jo naye tag ko nahi jaanta, naye code ka likha data padhta hai. Use ek aisa tag dikhta hai jo woh pehchanta nahi, toh woh us field ko skip kar sakta hai. Datatype annotation parser ko batati hai ki kitne bytes skip karne hain. Isse forward compatibility bani rehti hai: purana code naye code ke likhe records padh sakta hai.

Backward compatibility bhi kaam karti hai. Jab tak har field ka tag unique hai, naya code purana data hamesha padh sakta hai, kyunki tags ka matlab waisa hi rehta hai. Ek catch hai. Naya add kiya hua field required nahi ho sakta. Agar hota, toh purana data padhte waqt naya code check mein fail ho jaata, kyunki purane code ne woh field kabhi likha hi nahi. Isliye schema ke first deployment ke baad add kiya gaya har field optional hona chahiye ya uski default value honi chahiye.

Field remove karna wahi change hai bas compatibility ki concerns ulti ho jaati hain. Tum sirf optional field remove kar sakte ho, kyunki required field kabhi remove nahi ho sakta. Aur kabhi tag number reuse nahi karna chahiye. Purane data mein kahin purana tag ab bhi ho sakta hai, aur naye code ko us field ko ignore karna hoga, use kuch naya samajhne ki galti nahi karni.

Try karo

Maan lo Protocol Buffers service ke naye version mein ek required field add hota hai, aur use rolling upgrade se roll out kiya jaata hai. Sabse pehle kaun sa code apna required-field check fail karega, aur kis data par? Socho ki kaun se records naye field ke aane se pehle likhe gaye the.

Datatypes aur schema evolution

Field ka datatype badalna kaisa rahega? Ho sakta hai yeh possible ho, lekin details har tool ki documentation mein hain. Risk yeh hai ki values ki precision kam ho sakti hai ya woh truncate ho sakti hain. Maan lo 32-bit integer ko 64-bit integer mein badalna hai. Naya code purane code ka likha data padh sakta hai, kyunki parser missing bits ko zeros se bhar sakta hai. Lekin agar purana code naye code ka likha data padhe, toh purana code value ko abhi bhi 32-bit variable mein hi store karta hai. Decoded value agar 32 bits mein fit nahi hoti, toh woh truncate ho jaati hai.

Protocol Buffers mein list ya array datatype nahi hai. Uski jagah field ko repeated mark kar sakte hain, jo required aur optional ke saath teesra option hai. Repeated field ek hi tag ke record mein kai baar aane ke roop mein encode hota hai. Isse optional, single-valued field ko repeated, multi-valued field mein badalna safe ho jaata hai. Purana data padhta naya code ek list dekhta hai jisme zero ya ek element hota hai, is par depend karke ki field present tha ya nahi. Naya data padhta purana code list ka sirf last element dekhta hai.

Thrift mein dedicated list datatype hai, jo element type se parameterize hota hai. Isse single value se many values wala wahi change nahi ho paata jo Protocol Buffers mein hota hai. Badle mein Thrift nested lists support karta hai.

Avro

Apache Avro ek aur binary encoding format hai, aur woh Protocol Buffers aur Thrift se kaafi alag tarike se kaam karta hai. Yeh 2009 mein Hadoop (big data framework) ke subproject ke roop mein shuru hua, kyunki Hadoop ke use cases ke liye Thrift achha fit nahi tha.

Avro bhi apne encode kiye data ko describe karne ke liye schema use karta hai. Uski do schema languages hain. Ek, Avro IDL, insaanon ke edit karne ke liye hai. Doosri JSON par based hai aur machines ke liye padhna aasaan hai. Avro IDL mein example record aisa dikhta hai:

record Person {
  string userName;
  union { null, long } favoriteNumber = null;
  array<string> interests;
}

Wahi schema JSON form mein aisa hai:

{
  "type": "record",
  "name": "Person",
  "fields": [
    {"name": "userName", "type": "string"},
    {"name": "favoriteNumber", "type": ["null", "long"], "default": null},
    {"name": "interests", "type": {"type": "array", "items": "string"}}
  ]
}

Dhyaan dein ki Avro schema mein tag numbers hain hi nahi. Is schema se example record encode karne par 32 bytes bante hain, jo chapter mein ab tak dekhi saari encodings mein sabse chhota hai. Iska breakdown book ke ek figure mein hai, jo yahan dobara nahi banaya gaya.

Example

In 32 bytes mein kya hai, dekhte hain. Bytes mein kahin nahi likha ki kaun sa field kaun sa hai, ya har value ka type kya hai. Encoding bas values hain, ek ke baad ek. String matlab length aur uske baad uske UTF-8 bytes. Data mein kahin nahi likha ki woh string hai. Wahi bytes integer ya bilkul kuch aur bhi ho sakte the. Integers variable-length encoding use karte hain, wahi jo Thrift ka CompactProtocol use karta hai.

Data parse karne ke liye tum schema mein fields ke order mein ek-ek karke chalte ho, aur schema har field ka type bata deta hai. Iska ek nateeja hai. Data sirf wahi code sahi decode kar sakta hai jo bilkul wahi schema use kare jo likhne wale code ne use kiya tha. Mismatch hua toh data galat decode hoga, aur warn karne ke liye koi error bhi nahi aayega.

Toh agar dono sides ko schema par agree karna zaroori hai, phir Avro schema evolution kaise support karta hai?

Writer’s schema aur reader’s schema

Jab application data encode karti hai, file ya database mein likhne ke liye ya network par bhejne ke liye, woh schema ka wahi version use karti hai jo use pata hai. Maan lo woh schema application mein compile hua hai. Yeh writer’s schema hai.

Jab application data decode karti hai, woh expect karti hai ki data kisi schema se match karega. Yeh reader’s schema hai. Application ka code isi schema par depend karta hai, aur ho sakta hai code build ke dauraan isi se generate hua ho.

Avro ka key idea yeh hai ki writer’s schema aur reader’s schema ka same hona zaroori nahi. Bas unka compatible hona kaafi hai. Data decode hote waqt Avro library writer’s schema aur reader’s schema ko side by side dekhti hai, aur data ko writer ke form se reader ke form mein translate kar deti hai. Yeh resolution exactly kaise kaam karta hai, yeh Avro specification mein define hai.

Fields name se match hote hain, isliye dono schemas apne fields alag order mein list kar sakte hain. Agar reader ko aisa field mile jo writer’s schema mein hai par reader’s schema mein nahi, toh woh us field ko ignore kar deta hai. Agar reader aisa field expect kare jo writer’s schema mein nahi hai, toh reader apne schema mein declare ki hui default value bhar deta hai.

Schema evolution ke rules

Avro mein forward compatibility ka matlab hai ki schema ka naya version writer ho sakta hai aur purana version reader. Backward compatibility ka matlab hai ki naya version reader ho sakta hai aur purana version writer.

Compatible rehne ke liye tum sirf wahi field add ya remove kar sakte ho jiski default value ho. Example schema mein field favoriteNumber ka default null hai. Maan lo tum default wala field add karte ho. Naya field naye schema mein hai par purane mein nahi. Jab naye schema wala reader purane schema se likha record padhta hai, toh default missing field ko bhar deta hai.

Agar tum bina default ka field add karte ho, toh naye readers purane writers ka data nahi padh sakte, isliye backward compatibility toot jaati hai. Agar tum bina default ka field remove karte ho, toh purane readers naye writers ka data nahi padh sakte, isliye forward compatibility toot jaati hai.

Avro nulls ko kai languages se alag tarike se handle karta hai. Avro mein null har variable ke liye acceptable default nahi hai. Agar koi field null ho sakta hai, toh use union type se batana padta hai, matlab field listed kai types mein se koi ek hold kar sakta hai. Jaise union { null, long, string } field; ka matlab hai ki field number, string ya null ho sakta hai. Null ko default tabhi bana sakte hain jab null union ki branches mein se ek ho. (Book yeh bhi jodti hai ki default union ki pehli branch ke type se match karna chahiye. Yeh Avro ki ek specific limitation hai, unions ka general rule nahi.) Yeh sab kuch nullable bana dene se thoda zyada verbose hai, lekin yeh explicit karke bugs rokta hai ki kya null ho sakta hai. Isi wajah se Avro mein Protocol Buffers aur Thrift jaise optional aur required markers nahi hain. Uski jagah woh union types aur default values use karta hai.

Field ka datatype badalna tab possible hai jab Avro purane type ko naye type mein convert kar sake. Field ka naam badalna possible hai, par thoda tricky hai. Reader’s schema aliases list kar sakta hai, yani field ke purane naam. Isse woh purane writer ke field name ko alias se match kar sakta hai. Toh rename backward compatible hai par forward compatible nahi. Union type mein branch add karna bhi backward compatible hai par forward compatible nahi.

Lekin writer’s schema hai kya?

Ab tak ek zaroori sawaal unanswered raha hai. Reader ko kaise pata chale ki kisi particular data ke liye kaun sa writer’s schema use hua tha? Har record ke saath poora schema include nahi kar sakte. Schema aksar encoded data se kaafi bada hota hai, aur isse binary format ki saari saving khatam ho jaayegi. Iska jawab context par depend karta hai. Book chaar examples deti hai.

  • Bahut saare records wali badi file. Avro ka ek common use, khaas kar Hadoop ke saath, aisi badi file hai jisme lakhon records hote hain aur sab ek hi schema share karte hain. Writer schema ko file ke shuru mein ek baar include kar deta hai. Avro ek file format define karta hai, object container files, jo exactly yahi karta hai.
  • Aisa database jisme records alag-alag time par likhe gaye. Records alag time points par alag writer’s schemas se likhe ja sakte hain, isliye yeh maan nahi sakte ki sab records ek hi schema share karte hain. Sabse simple approach yeh hai ki har encoded record ke shuru mein version number daal do aur database mein schema versions ki list rakho. Reader record fetch karta hai, uska version number padhta hai, matching writer’s schema dhundta hai, aur phir record ka baaki hissa decode karta hai. Book ke hisaab se LinkedIn ka Espresso aise hi kaam karta hai. Version number simple incrementing integer ho sakta hai ya schema ka hash.
  • Network connection par bheje gaye records. Jab do processes two-way connection par baat karte hain, woh connection set up karte waqt schema version par agree kar sakte hain, aur connection chalne tak wahi schema use karte hain. Avro RPC protocol aise hi kaam karta hai.
  • Aam taur par schema version database. Schema versions ki list rakhna kisi bhi case mein kaam ka hai. Yeh documentation ka kaam karta hai, aur tumhe check karne ka mauka deta hai ki schemas ek-doosre se compatible hain ya nahi.

Dynamically generated schemas

Avro ka Protocol Buffers aur Thrift par ek advantage hai: uske schema mein tag numbers nahi hote. Yeh kyun matter karta hai? Schema mein kuch numbers rakhna harmless lag sakta hai.

Farak dynamically generated schemas mein dikhta hai. Socho tumhe relational database ka content ek file mein dump karna hai. Binary format JSON, CSV ya SQL jaise textual formats ki problems se bacha deta hai. Avro ke saath tum relational schema se Avro schema generate kar sakte ho, wahi JSON form mein jo pehle dikhaya, aur usse content ko Avro object container file mein encode kar sakte ho. Har database table ek record schema ban jaata hai. Har column ek field ban jaata hai, aur column name field name ban jaata hai.

Example

Ab maan lo database schema badal gaya. Ek table mein ek column add hua aur ek hat gaya. Tum updated database schema se naya Avro schema generate karte ho, aur usi se data export karte ho. Export process ko change par dhyaan dene ki zaroorat nahi. Woh har baar chalne par schema convert kar deta hai. Jo bhi naye files padhta hai, use dikhta hai ki record ke fields badal gaye hain. Kyunki fields name se identify hote hain, naya writer’s schema purane reader’s schema se ab bhi match ho sakta hai.

Thrift ya Protocol Buffers mein field tags aam taur par haath se assign karne padte. Database schema badalne par har baar administrator ko column names se field tags ka mapping update karna padta. Isse automate kiya ja sakta hai, lekin generator ko bahut careful rehna padta ki pehle use hua koi tag kabhi reuse na ho. Dynamically generated schemas Thrift ya Protocol Buffers ka design goal kabhi the hi nahi. Avro ka design goal woh the.

Code generation aur dynamically typed languages

Thrift aur Protocol Buffers code generation par depend karte hain. Schema define karne ke baad tum apni language mein usse implement karne wala code generate karte ho. Yeh Java, C++ ya C# jaisi statically typed languages mein kaam ka hai. Isse decoded data efficient in-memory structures use kar paata hai. Compiler types check kar leta hai, aur data use karne wala code likhte waqt editor autocompletion de sakta hai.

JavaScript, Ruby ya Python jaisi dynamically typed languages mein code generate karne se kuch khaas fayda nahi hota, kyunki wahan koi compile-time type checker hai hi nahi jise khush karna ho. In languages mein code generation ko aksar pasand nahi kiya jaata, kyunki yeh waise bhi explicit compilation step se bachti hain. Dynamically generated schema ke liye, jaise database table se bana schema, code generation tumhare aur data ke beech ek faltu rukawat hai.

Avro statically typed languages ke liye code generation ko option ke roop mein deta hai, lekin uske bina bhi utna hi achha kaam karta hai. Object container file writer’s schema ko apne andar embed rakhti hai, isliye tum use Avro library se khol kar data waise hi dekh sakte ho jaise JSON file dekhte ho. File khud ko describe karti hai. Yeh Apache Pig jaise dynamically typed data processing tools ke saath khaas kaam ka hai. Pig mein tum kuch Avro files kholkar analyze karna shuru kar sakte ho, aur derived datasets ko Avro format mein wapas likh sakte ho, schemas ke baare mein soche bina.

Ab dekhte hain ki chaaron encodings same example record par kaise compare hoti hain. Avro ke bytes sabse kam hain, kyunki schema field names aur types rakhta hai, aur data mein sirf values hoti hain.

Schemas ke fayde

Protocol Buffers, Thrift aur Avro teeno binary encoding describe karne ke liye schema use karte hain. Inki schema languages XML Schema ya JSON Schema se kaafi simple hain. Woh dono detailed validation rules support karte hain, jaise “yeh string is regular expression se match kare” ya “yeh integer 0 se 100 ke beech ho.” Protocol Buffers, Thrift aur Avro implement aur use karne mein simple hain, isliye woh programming languages ki kaafi badi range ko support karne lage hain.

Yeh ideas naye nahi hain. Inme ASN.1 se kaafi cheezein milti hain, jo 1984 mein pehli baar standardize hui ek schema language hai. ASN.1 se alag-alag network protocols define kiye gaye, aur uski binary encoding DER aaj bhi SSL certificates (X.509) encode karne mein use hoti hai. ASN.1 tag numbers se schema evolution support karta hai, bilkul Protocol Buffers aur Thrift ki tarah. Lekin yeh bahut complex bhi hai aur uski documentation kharab hai, isliye Kleppmann ko lagta hai ki naye applications ke liye yeh shayad achha choice nahi hai.

Kai data systems ka apna proprietary binary encoding bhi hota hai. Zyaadatar relational databases mein queries bhejne aur responses wapas paane ka network protocol hota hai. Yeh protocols aam taur par kisi ek database ke liye specific hote hain. Vendor ek driver deta hai, jaise ODBC ya JDBC interfaces par bana, jo responses ko in-memory data structures mein decode kar deta hai.

Toh JSON, XML aur CSV jaise textual formats widespread hain, phir bhi schema-based binary encodings bhi ek viable option hain. Inki kai achhi properties hain:

  • Yeh binary JSON variants se bhi kaafi zyada compact ho sakte hain, kyunki encoded data se field names hata sakte hain.
  • Schema ek keemti documentation hai. Decoding ke liye schema chahiye, isliye tum pakka kar sakte ho ki woh up to date hai. Haath se maintain ki hui documentation aasaani se reality se door ho jaati hai.
  • Schemas ka database rakhne se tum deploy karne se pehle hi kisi change ki forward aur backward compatibility check kar sakte ho.
  • Statically typed languages ke liye schema se code generate karne par compile time par type checking mil jaati hai.

Summary yeh hai ki schema evolution schemaless JSON databases jaisi hi flexibility deta hai, aur saath mein tumhare data par mazboot guarantees aur behtar tools bhi deta hai.

Trade-offs
OptionKismein achhaKya cost hai
Language-specific encodings (Java serialization, Ruby Marshal, Python pickle)Bahut kam code mein objects save aur restore karnaEk hi language se bandhe hain. Untrusted bytes decode karna risky hai. Versioning aur size baad mein socha jaata hai.
JSON, XML, CSVReadable, widely supported, aur organizations ke beech share karna aasaanAmbiguous numbers, Base64 ke bina binary strings nahi, optional schemas, aur bada size.
Binary JSON variants (MessagePack aur baaki)JSON se thode chhote aur parse karne mein thode fastBook ke example mein chhoti saving (66 bytes vs 81). Field names data mein hi rehte hain, aur data aankhon se padhne layak nahi rehta.
Thrift aur Protocol BuffersCompact. Field tags par based clear compatibility rules. Static languages ke liye code generation.Schemas sambhal kar rakhne padte hain, aur tags haath se manage karne padte hain. Padhne se pehle data decode karna padta hai.
