Asal mein log ek bounded buffer hai jo bhar jaane par sabse purane messages phenk deta hai. Ise circular buffer ya ring buffer kehte hain. Buffer disk par hai, isliye woh phir bhi bahut bada ho sakta hai.

Example

Kleppmann ek quick estimate karte hain. Book likhte waqt ek typical large hard drive 6 TB ki thi aur 150 MB per second par write kar sakti thi. Agar messages utni tezi se aayein jitni tezi se disk le sakti hai, toh drive lagbhag 11 ghante mein bhar jaati hai. Uske baad woh sabse purane messages ko overwrite karna shuru kar deti hai.

  1. 6 TB lo, jo lagbhag 6,000,000 MB hai.
  2. 150 MB per second se divide karo. Yeh 40,000 seconds hai.
  3. 40,000 seconds lagbhag 11 ghante hote hain.

Yeh ratio wahi rehta hai chahe tum ek drive use karo ya kai machines. Practice mein deployments disk ki poori write speed shayad hi use karte hain, isliye ek log aam taur par kai din, ya hafte bhar ke messages rakh sakta hai.

Log ka throughput lagbhag constant rehta hai chahe woh kitni bhi history rakhe, kyunki har message waise bhi disk par likha jaata hai. Yeh un messaging systems se alag hai jo messages memory mein rakhte hain aur queue bahut lambi hone par hi disk par likhte hain. Woh systems queues chhoti hone tak fast hote hain, lekin disk par spill karna shuru karte hi bahut slow ho jaate hain. Unka throughput is par depend karta hai ki woh kitni history rakhte hain.

Jab consumers producers ke saath keep up nahi kar paate

Pehle chapter ne teen cheezein ginayi thi jo consumers ke peeche rehne par system kar sakta hai: messages drop karna, buffer karna, ya backpressure lagana. Log-based broker buffering ka hi ek roop hai, ek bade buffer ke saath. Buffer ka size fixed hai, lekin woh sirf available disk space se limited hai.

Agar koi consumer itna peeche reh jaaye ki use jo messages chahiye woh disk ke retain kiye hue data se purane hain, toh woh unhe padh nahi sakta. Broker ne effectively un messages ko drop kar diya jo buffer ke hold karne se zyada purane the. Tum dekh sakte ho ki har consumer log ke head se kitna peeche hai, aur gap bahut badhne par alert utha sakte ho. Buffer bada hai, isliye human operator ke paas aam taur par bahut time hota hai ki woh slow consumer ko theek kare aur koi message lose hone se pehle use catch up karne de.

Consumer peeche reh jaaye toh sirf wahi slow consumer affect hota hai. Woh doosre consumers ki service ko disturb nahi karta. Kleppmann ise ek bada operational advantage kehte hain. Tum development, testing ya debugging ke liye production log ko experimentally padh sakte ho, production ko zyada risk ke bina. Jab consumer shut down ya crash hota hai, toh woh resources use karna band kar deta hai. Peeche sirf uska offset bachta hai.

Traditional message brokers alag tarah se kaam karte hain. Wahan tumhe dhyaan rakhna padta hai ki jis queue ka consumer shut down ho gaya ho, use delete kar do. Warna queue messages se bharti rehti hai aur jo consumers abhi chal rahe hain unki memory kha leti hai.

Purane messages ko replay karna

AMQP- aur JMS-style brokers ke saath message process aur acknowledge karna destructive hai, kyunki isse message delete ho jaata hai. Log-based broker alag hai. Log se consume karna file padhne jaisa hai. Woh read-only hai aur log ko change nahi karta. Consumer jo output likhta hai uske alawa iska bas ek side effect hai ki consumer ka offset aage badh jaata hai. Aur consumer apna offset khud control karta hai, isliye use intentionally move kiya ja sakta hai.

Jaise, tum kal ke offsets ke saath consumer ki ek copy start kar sakte ho aur uska output kisi alag jagah bhej sakte ho. Is tarah woh pichhle din ke messages dobara process karta hai. Tum yeh jitni baar chaho dohra sakte ho, har baar processing code badalkar. Isse log-based messaging pichhle chapter ki batch processing jaisi lagti hai, jahan derived data ko input se ek repeatable transformation ke zariye alag rakha jaata hai. Isse experiments aasaan ho jaate hain, aur errors aur bugs se recovery bhi aasaan ho jaati hai. Kleppmann ise organization bhar mein data flows jodne ka achha tool kehte hain.

Try karo

Maan lo tumhare consumer ke bug ne pichhle teen din ke totals galat likhe. Agar message queue acknowledgment par delete kar deti hai, toh tumhe kya karna padega? Aur agar log hafte bhar ki history rakhta hai, toh tum ise kaise fix karoge? Kaunsa design tumhe experiment karne ki zyada gunjaish deta hai?

Databases aur Streams

Is chapter mein hum message brokers aur databases ko kai baar compare kar chuke hain, aur dekha ki dono kaafi alag hain. Phir bhi log-based brokers ne databases se kuch ideas liye hain, aur yeh rishta doosri taraf bhi chalta hai. Messaging aur streams ke ideas databases par bhi apply ho sakte hain.

Pehle ke sections mein bataya tha ki event ek record hota hai ki kisi point in time par kuch hua. Woh kuch user ka action ho sakta hai, jaise search query type karna. Sensor reading bhi ho sakti hai. Database mein ek write hona bhi ho sakta hai. Database mein kuch likha gaya, yeh baat khud ek event hai, aur ise capture, store aur process kiya ja sakta hai. Matlab databases aur streams ka link sirf disk par logs ke physical storage tak limited nahi hai. Yeh ek basic relationship hai.

Chapter 5 ka replication log dekho. Yeh database write events ka stream hai, jo leader transactions process karte time produce karta hai. Followers is writes ke stream ko apni database copy par apply karte hain, aur isliye unke paas same data ki accurate copy ban jaati hai. Replication log ke events data mein hue changes ko describe karte hain.

Chapter 9 mein state machine replication ka principle bhi aaya tha. Isme baat yeh hai ki agar har event database ka ek write hai, aur har replica wahi events same order mein process karta hai, toh saare replicas same final state par pahunchte hain. Yahan maana jaata hai ki event ka processing deterministic hai, yani same input se hamesha same result milta hai. Yeh bhi event streams ka ek case hai.

Is section mein hum pehle ek aisi problem dekhenge jo kai alag data stores se bane systems mein aati hai. Phir dekhenge ki event streams ke ideas databases mein laane se woh problem kaise solve ho sakti hai.

Systems ko sync mein rakhna

Koi ek system data store, query aur process karne ki saari zarooratein poori nahi kar sakta. Zyadatar real applications kai technologies ko combine karti hain. Ek typical setup mein OLTP database (jo users ke bahut saare chhote reads aur writes handle karta hai), common requests ko tez karne ke liye cache, search queries ka jawab dene ke liye full-text index, aur analytics ke liye data warehouse ho sakta hai. Har ek ke paas data ki apni copy hoti hai, us format mein jo uske apne kaam ke liye chuna gaya ho.

Jab same data kai jagah rakha ho, toh copies ko sync mein rakhna padta hai. Agar database mein koi item update hua, toh use cache, search index aur warehouse mein bhi update karna hoga. Data warehouse ke liye yeh synchronization aam taur par ETL processes (extract, transform aur load, jo Chapter 3 mein cover hua) se hoti hai. ETL aksar database ki poori copy leta hai, use transform karta hai, aur warehouse mein bulk-load kar deta hai. Yeh ek batch process hai. Book yeh bhi batati hai ki search indexes aur recommendation systems bhi aksar isi tarah, batch jobs se bante hain.

Agar roz poori copy lena bahut slow ho, toh teams kabhi-kabhi dual writes ki taraf jaati hain. Data badalne par application code har system mein seedha write karta hai. Jaise, pehle database mein write kiya, phir search index update kiya, phir cache entries invalidate kar di. Ya phir yeh writes ek saath kar diye.

Dual writes mein serious problems hain. Pehli problem race condition hai, jo Kleppmann Figure 11-4 mein dikhate hain. Chalo example step by step dekhte hain.

Example

Do clients ek hi item X ko update karna chahte hain. Client 1 use A set karna chahta hai. Client 2 use B set karna chahta hai. Dono clients pehle database mein write karte hain, phir search index mein. Kharab timing ki wajah se unki requests aapas mein interleave ho jaati hain.

  1. Database ko pehle client 1 ka write milta hai, jo X ko A set karta hai.
  2. Phir use client 2 ka write milta hai, jo X ko B set karta hai. Database mein final value B hai.
  3. Search index ko pehle client 2 ka write milta hai, jo X ko B set karta hai.
  4. Phir use client 1 ka write milta hai, jo X ko A set karta hai. Search index mein final value A hai.

Ab dono systems aapas mein hamesha ke liye disagree karte hain. Kahin bhi koi error raise nahi hua.

Concurrent writes detect karne ka koi extra mechanism na ho, jaise Chapter 5 ke version vectors, toh tumhe pata hi nahi chalega ki writes overlap hue the. Ek value silently doosri value ko overwrite kar deti hai.

Doosri problem yeh hai ki do writes mein se ek fail ho sakta hai aur doosra succeed. Yeh concurrency ki nahi, fault-tolerance ki problem hai. Lekin isse bhi dono systems inconsistent ho jaate hain. Yeh pakka karna ki dono writes succeed hon ya dono fail hon, atomic commit problem ka ek instance hai, aur ise solve karna mehnga hai (Chapter 9).

Teesri problem structural hai. Agar tumhare paas ek replicated database hai jisme single leader hai, toh woh leader writes ka order tay karta hai, isliye database replicas ke beech state machine replication chalti hai. Lekin upar ke example mein koi single leader nahi hai. Database ka apna leader hai, search index ka apna leader hai, aur koi kisi ko follow nahi karta. Isliye conflicts ho sakte hain (multi-leader replication Chapter 5 mein hai). Cheezein kaafi behtar hongi agar ek hi leader ho, yani database, aur search index bas uska follower ho. Kya yeh practice mein possible hai? Agla section kehta hai ki haan, thodi mehnat se.

Dhyaan do

Do systems mein bina coordination ke ek saath write karne se woh hamesha ke liye alag ho sakte hain, aur koi error bhi nahi aata. Ordering problems aur partial failures, dono isse cause karte hain.

Change Data Capture

Zyadatar databases ke replication logs ki problem yeh hai ki unhe bahut samay se database ki internal detail maana gaya, public interface nahi. Clients se umeed hai ki woh database ko uske data model aur query language se query karein. Replication log padhkar usse data nikalna unka kaam nahi maana gaya.

Kai decades tak bahut se databases mein apne par hue changes ka log nikalne ka koi documented tarika hi nahi tha. Isliye database mein hua har change lekar use kisi doosre storage system, jaise search index, cache ya data warehouse mein copy karna mushkil tha.

Haal hi mein change data capture mein interest badha hai, jise aam taur par CDC kehte hain. CDC ka matlab hai database mein likhe gaye saare data changes ko observe karna, aur unhe aise form mein nikalna jo doosre systems mein copy ho sake. Yeh khaas taur par tab kaam aata hai jab changes ek stream ke roop mein, likhte hi turant publish hote hain.

Jaise, tum database ke changes capture karke wahi changes, usi order mein, ek search index par apply kar sakte ho. Agar changes usi order mein apply hue jis order mein likhe gaye the, toh search index ka data database se match karega. Phir search index aur koi bhi doosra derived data system bas change stream ke consumers hain. Book ki Figure 11-5 mein yeh layout dikhaya gaya hai.

Change data capture implement karna

Source database leader ban jaata hai, jisse changes capture hote hain. Baaki systems followers ban jaate hain. Change events carry karne ke liye log-based message broker achha tarika hai, kyunki woh messages ko order mein rakhta hai. Isse Figure 11-2 wali reordering problem avoid ho jaati hai. Derived data systems ko derived isliye kehte hain ki unka data system of record ke data par ek view hota hai, aur system of record authoritative source hai.

Changes capture karne ke kai tarike hain. Ek hai database trigger, yani chhota sa logic jo table mein har change par chalta hai. Triggers changelog table mein ek matching entry likhte hain. Chapter 5 mein ise trigger-based replication kaha tha. Book ke hisaab se triggers fragile hote hain aur kaafi overhead add karte hain. Ek zyada robust option database ka replication log parse karna hai. Isme bhi challenges hain, jaise schema changes handle karna.

Kai bade companies ne is tarah CDC systems banaye hain. LinkedIn ka Databus, Facebook ka Wormhole aur Yahoo! ka Sherpa, sab yahi idea bade scale par use karte hain. Kuch open source tools alag-alag databases ke liye yahi karte hain. Bottled Water PostgreSQL ka write-ahead log decode karta hai. Maxwell aur Debezium MySQL ka binlog parse karte hain. Mongoriver MongoDB ka oplog padhta hai. GoldenGate Oracle ke liye milti-julti facilities deta hai.

Message brokers ki tarah CDC bhi aam taur par asynchronous hota hai. Source database commit karne se pehle yeh wait nahi karta ki change consumers par apply ho gaya ya nahi. Operations ke liye yeh achha hai, kyunki ek slow consumer add karne se source database ko zyada farak nahi padta. Nuksan yeh hai ki replication lag ki saari problems yahan bhi lagu hoti hain (Chapter 5).

Initial snapshot

Agar tumhare paas database mein hue har change ka poora log hai, toh log ko shuru se replay karke poori state dobara bana sakte hain. Lekin zyadatar cases mein har change ko hamesha rakhne mein bahut disk space lagega, aur replay mein bahut time lagega. Isliye log ko chhota, yani truncate, karna padta hai.

Isse naye derived systems ke liye problem ho jaati hai. Maan lo naya full-text index banana hai, toh uske liye poore database ki full copy chahiye. Sirf recent changes apply karna kaafi nahi hai, kyunki jo items haal mein change nahi hue woh index mein missing rahenge. Isliye agar tumhare paas poori log history nahi hai, toh database ke ek consistent snapshot se shuru karna padega. Chapter 5 mein naye followers set up karne ke liye yeh bataya tha.

Snapshot change log ki kisi known position, yani offset, se match hona chahiye. Isse pata chalta hai ki snapshot load hone ke baad changes kahan se apply karne hain. Kuch CDC tools mein yeh snapshot step included hota hai. Baaki ise manual kaam chhod dete hain.

Log compaction

Agar tum sirf limited log history rakh sakte ho, toh jab bhi naya derived system add karna ho, naya snapshot lena padega. Log compaction ek behtar option deta hai. Chapter 3 mein hash indexes aur log-structured storage engines ke context mein yeh idea aaya tha, aur book ki Figure 3-2 mein example hai.

Principle simple hai. Storage engine regularly aise log records dhundhta hai jinka key same ho, purane duplicates phenk deta hai, aur har key ka sirf sabse recent update rakhta hai. Compaction aur merging background mein chalte hain. Log-structured storage engine mein null value wala ek special update, jise tombstone kehte hain, key ko deleted mark karta hai. Compaction tombstone dekhkar key hata deta hai. Jab tak koi key overwrite ya delete nahi hoti, woh log mein hamesha rehti hai.

Compacted log ko jitni space chahiye woh sirf database ke current contents par depend karti hai, is par nahi ki ab tak kitne writes hue. Agar ek hi key kai baar overwrite hui, toh uski purani values aakhir mein garbage-collect ho jaati hain, aur sirf latest value bachti hai.

Yahi idea log-based message brokers aur CDC ke liye bhi chalta hai. Agar har change ki ek primary key hai, aur ek key ka har update us key ki pichhli value ko replace karta hai, toh har key ka sirf sabse recent write rakhna kaafi hai. Phir tum search index jaise derived system ko dobara bana sakte ho: compacted topic ke offset 0 se naya consumer shuru karo aur saare messages order mein padho. Log mein har key ki sabse recent value guaranteed hoti hai, aur kuch purani values bhi ho sakti hain. Isliye source database ka doosra snapshot liye bina tumhe database ki poori copy mil jaati hai.

Apache Kafka yeh log compaction feature support karta hai. Kleppmann ka point hai ki isse message broker sirf transient messaging nahi, durable storage ke liye bhi use ho sakta hai.

Change streams ke liye API support

Databases ab badhte taur par change streams ko first-class interface ki tarah offer kar rahe hain, CDC ko baad mein retrofit aur reverse-engineer karne ke liye chhodne ke bajaye. Book mein kai examples hain. RethinkDB mein query subscribe kar sakti hai ki uske results badlein toh notification mile. Firebase aur CouchDB ek change feed par based data synchronization dete hain, jise applications bhi padh sakti hain. Meteor MongoDB oplog use karke data changes subscribe karta hai aur user interface update karta hai.

VoltDB transactions ko data ko continuously stream ke roop mein export karne deta hai. Database ek output stream ko special table ki tarah expose karta hai, jisme transactions rows insert kar sakte hain, lekin us table ko query nahi kiya ja sakta. Stream un rows ka log hai jo committed transactions ne is table mein likhe, commit order mein. External consumers ise asynchronously padhte hain aur derived systems update karne ke liye use karte hain. Kafka Connect ek koshish hai jo kai database systems ke CDC tools ko Kafka ke saath jodti hai. Change events Kafka mein aa jaayein, toh woh search indexes update kar sakte hain aur stream processors ko feed kar sakte hain.

Event Sourcing

Upar ke ideas aur event sourcing mein kaafi similarities hain. Event sourcing domain-driven design (DDD) community mein develop hua tha. Ise discuss karna isliye zaroori hai ki streaming systems ke liye isme kuch kaam ke ideas hain.

CDC ki tarah event sourcing bhi application state ke har change ko change events ke log ke roop mein store karta hai. Main farak yeh hai ki idea kis level of abstraction par apply hota hai.

  • CDC mein application database ko mutable tarike se use karti hai. Woh records ko jaise chahe update aur delete karti hai. Changes ka log database se low level par nikala jaata hai, jaise replication log parse karke. Isse nikale gaye writes ka order wahi rehta hai jis order mein woh actually hue the, aur Figure 11-4 wali race avoid ho jaati hai. Database mein likhne wali application ko pata hone ki zaroorat nahi ki CDC chal raha hai.
  • Event sourcing mein application logic seedha immutable events par bani hoti hai jo event log mein likhe jaate hain. Event store append-only hota hai, aur updates ya deletes ko discourage ya forbid kiya jaata hai. Events isliye design hote hain ki woh application mein hui cheezein describe karein, stored state ke low-level changes nahi.

Kleppmann event sourcing ko data modeling ki ek powerful technique kehte hain. Application ke point of view se yeh zyada meaningful hai ki user ne kya kiya woh immutable events ki tarah record ho, bajaye is ke ki un actions ka effect mutable database par record ho. Event sourcing se applications ko waqt ke saath badalna aasaan ho jaata hai. Debugging mein bhi madad milti hai, kyunki baad mein dekhna aasaan hota hai ki kuch kyun hua. Yeh application bugs se bhi bachata hai, jaisa chapter mein aage discuss hua hai.

Example

Ek aisa event socho jo record karta hai ki student ne apna course enrollment cancel kiya. Yeh event ek action ka intent neutral tarike se saaf-saaf bata deta hai.

Ab isse compare karo ki agar side effects record kiye jaate: enrollments table se ek entry delete hui, aur student feedback table mein cancellation reason add hua. Side effects mein bahut saari assumptions hoti hain ki data baad mein kaise use hoga. Agar koi naya feature aaye, jaise freed place waiting list ke agle bande ko offer karna, toh event-sourcing wale version mein yeh naya step seedha existing cancellation event se jod sakte hain. Side-effect wale version mein toh data ke saath kya hoga, yeh pehle hi tay ho chuka hai.

Event sourcing chronicle data model jaisa hai, aur event log star schema ke fact table jaisa lagta hai (Chapter 3). Event Store jaise specialized databases un applications ke liye bane hain jo event sourcing use karti hain. Lekin yeh approach kisi particular tool par depend nahi karti. Conventional database ya log-based message broker se bhi is style ki applications banayi ja sakti hain.

Trade-offs
ApproachKya log hota haiKya aasaan hota hai
Change data captureRows ke changes, jo mutable database se low level par nikaale jaate hain, aur application ko pata nahi hotaDoosre systems ko existing database ke saath sync mein rakhna. Log compaction har row ke purane versions hata sakta hai.
Event sourcingImmutable application events jo user intent describe karte hain, aur application khud likhti haiApp ko evolve karna, past behavior ke baare mein reason karna, aur bugs se recover karna. Poori history rakhni padti hai, isliye compaction alag tarah kaam karta hai.

Event log se current state nikalna

Sirf event log akela zyada kaam ka nahi hota, kyunki users ko aam taur par system ki current state chahiye, ab tak hue har change ki list nahi. Shopping site par customer ko dikhna chahiye ki cart mein abhi kya hai, cart ke har change ki append-only history nahi.

Isliye jo application event sourcing use karti hai, use event log lekar use aisi application state mein badalna padta hai jo users ko dikhane layak ho. Yeh transformation koi bhi logic use kar sakta hai, lekin use deterministic hona chahiye. Aise tum use dobara chala kar same event log se same application state pa sakte ho.

Event log replay karke tum current state dobara bana sakte ho, jaise CDC mein. Lekin dono cases mein log compaction alag tarah handle karna padta hai.

  • Update ke liye CDC event mein aam taur par record ka poora naya version hota hai. Isliye kisi primary key ki current value uske sabse recent event se poori tarah tay ho jaati hai, aur compaction usi key ke pehle wale events hata sakta hai.
  • Event sourcing mein events higher level par model hote hain. Event aam taur par user action ka intent express karta hai, us se hue state change ki mechanics nahi. Baad ke events pehle wale events ko override nahi karte. Isliye final state dobara banane ke liye events ki poori history chahiye, aur isi tarah ka compaction possible nahi hai.

Event-sourced applications aam taur par log se nikali current state ke snapshots bhi store karti hain, taaki har baar poora log reprocess na karna pade. Lekin snapshots sirf performance optimization hain, reads aur crash ke baad recovery tez karne ke liye. Idea yeh hai ki system saare raw events hamesha ke liye store kar sake aur zaroorat padne par poora log reprocess kar sake. Kleppmann is assumption par limitations wali discussion mein wapas aate hain.

Commands aur events

Event sourcing commands aur events ko alag rakhta hai. User ki request jab pehli baar aati hai, toh woh command hoti hai. Is stage par woh fail ho sakti hai, jaise kisi integrity rule ke toot jaane se. Application ko pehle check karna padta hai ki use command execute karne ki permission hai. Check pass ho jaaye aur command accept ho jaaye, toh woh event ban jaati hai, jo durable hai aur badli nahi ja sakti.

Maan lo koi user username register karna chahta hai, ya plane ya theater mein seat reserve karna chahta hai. Application ko pehle check karna hoga ki username ya seat pehle se taken toh nahi. Yeh wahi example hai jo book ne pehle fault-tolerant consensus (Chapter 9) discuss karte time use kiya tha. Check succeed hone ke baad application ek event bana sakti hai ki ek particular username ek particular user ID ne register kiya, ya ek particular seat ek particular customer ke liye reserve hui.

Event ban jaane ke baad woh ek fact hai. Maan lo customer baad mein reservation badalna ya cancel karna chahta hai. Yeh fact sach rehta hai ki us seat ke liye unka reservation tha. Change ya cancellation ek alag event hai, jo baad mein log mein add hota hai.

Event stream ka consumer kisi event ko reject nahi kar sakta. Consumer jab tak use dekhta hai, event log ka immutable hissa ban chuka hota hai, aur doosre consumers use pehle hi padh chuke ho sakte hain. Isliye command ki koi bhi checking command ke event banne se pehle honi chahiye. Ek tarika hai serializable transaction use karna, jo command check karta hai aur event ko ek atomic step mein publish karta hai. Doosra tarika hai request ko do events mein baantna. Pehla tentative reservation hai. Doosra alag confirmation event hai, jo reservation validate hone ke baad likha jaata hai. Is split se validation asynchronous process mein chal sakti hai, jaisa Chapter 9 mein total order broadcast par bane linearizable storage ke liye bataya tha.

Example

Theater seat ki request split approach se aise hoti hai.

  1. Customer seat C5 maangta hai. Application ek command likhti hai, abhi event nahi.
  2. Application check karti hai ki C5 free hai ya nahi, aur free ho toh us customer ke liye tentative reservation event append kar deti hai.
  3. Ek alag process tentative reservation ko seat map ki current state ke against validate karta hai.
  4. Valid ho toh process confirmation event append karta hai. Seat ab customer ke liye held hai.
  5. Customer baad mein cancel kare toh naya cancellation event append hota hai. Reservation event kabhi edit ya remove nahi hota.

State, Streams aur Immutability

Chapter 10 mein dekha tha ki batch processing ko apni input files ki immutability se fayda hota hai. Tum existing input par job ke saath experiment kar sakte ho, bina input kharab hone ke darr ke. Yahi principle event sourcing aur CDC ko itna powerful banata hai.

Hum aam taur par sochte hain ki databases application ki current state store karte hain. Yeh representation reads ke liye optimized hai, aur queries ka jawab dene ke liye aam taur par sabse convenient hai. State badalti hai, isliye databases insert ke saath data update aur delete karna bhi support karte hain. Toh yeh immutability ke saath kaise fit hota hai?

Jo bhi state badalti hai, woh un events ka result hai jinhone use waqt ke saath badla. Abhi available seats ki list ab tak process hui reservations ka result hai. Kisi account ka current balance us par hue credits aur debits ka result hai. Web server ka response-time graph saari requests ke individual response times ka aggregation hai. State chahe jaise badle, hamesha events ka ek sequence hota hai jisne woh changes kiye. Jab cheezein ho ke undo bhi ho jaayein, tab bhi events hue the.

Toh mutable state aur immutable events ka append-only log ek doosre ke contradict nahi karte. Yeh ek hi sikke ke do pehlu hain. Saare changes ka log, jise Kleppmann changelog kehte hain, record karta hai ki state waqt ke saath kaise evolve hui.

Kleppmann ek mathematical comparison dete hain. Application state woh hai jo event stream ko time ke upar integrate karne se milta hai. Change stream woh hai jo state ko time ke respect mein differentiate karne se milta hai. Is comparison ki limits hain: state ke second derivative ka koi clear matlab nahi lagta. Lekin data ke baare mein sochne ke liye yeh ek achha starting point hai.

Changelog ko durably store karein, toh state hamesha usse reproduce ho sakti hai. Event log ko system of record maanein aur kisi bhi mutable state ko usse derived maanein, toh system mein data ka flow samajhna aasaan ho jaata hai. Pat Helland yeh idea aise kehte hain: “The truth is the log.” Book yeh bhi batati hai ki log compaction log aur database state ke beech ka gap bharne ka ek tarika hai, kyunki woh har record ka sirf latest version rakhta hai aur overwrite hue versions hata deta hai.

Immutable events ke advantages

Databases mein immutability purana idea hai. Accountants ise sadiyon se financial bookkeeping mein use karte aa rahe hain. Jab transaction hota hai, toh use append-only ledger mein record kiya jaata hai, jo essentially events ka log hai aur batata hai ki paisa, saaman ya services kaise ek haath se doosre mein gaye. Profit and loss statement ya balance sheet jaise accounts ledger se transactions jodkar nikaale jaate hain.

Galti ho jaaye toh accountant galat entry ko mitata ya badalta nahi. Uski jagah ek aur transaction add hota hai jo galti ko compensate karta hai. Jaise, galat charge ko refund se theek kiya jaata hai. Galat transaction ledger mein hamesha rehta hai, kyunki audits ke liye woh zaroori ho sakta hai. Galat ledger par based figures pehle hi publish ho chuke hon, toh agle accounting period ke figures mein correction shamil hota hai. Kleppmann ke hisaab se accounting mein yeh process bilkul normal hai.

Auditability financial systems ke liye khaas taur par zaroori hai, lekin kai doosre systems ko bhi isse madad milti hai. Chapter 10 ki tarah, agar buggy code galti se database mein bad data likh de, toh recovery kaafi mushkil hoti hai jab code data ko destructively overwrite kar sakta ho. Immutable events ke append-only log ke saath yeh samajhna ki kya hua aur recover karna kaafi aasaan hota hai.

Immutable events current state se zyada information bhi capture karte hain. Shopping site socho. Customer cart mein item add karta hai, phir use hata deta hai. Order fulfillment ke liye doosra event pehle wale ko cancel kar deta hai. Lekin analytics ke liye yeh jaanna kaam ka ho sakta hai ki customer ne us item ke baare mein socha aur phir mana kar diya. Ho sakta hai woh baad mein khareede, ya use koi substitute mil gaya ho. Yeh information event log mein record hoti hai, lekin jo database item ko cart se hatate hi delete kar deta hai, woh ise kho dega.

Ek hi event log se kai views banana

Mutable state ko immutable event log se alag karne ka ek aur fayda hai. Tum same events se kai alag read-oriented views derive kar sakte ho. Yeh waisa hi hai jaise ek stream ke kai consumers hon, jaise Figure 11-5 mein. Book mein examples hain. Analytic database Druid isi tarah Kafka se seedha data ingest karta hai. Pistachio, ek distributed key-value store, Kafka ko apne commit log ki tarah use karta hai. Kafka Connect sinks Kafka se data ko kai databases aur indexes mein export kar sakte hain. Kleppmann ka argument hai ki search servers jaise kai doosre storage aur indexing systems bhi isi tarah distributed log se apna input le sakte hain.

Event log se database tak ek explicit translation step hone se application ko waqt ke saath badalna bhi aasaan ho jaata hai. Maan lo tumhe naya feature chahiye jo tumhara existing data naye tarike se dikhaye. Tum event log se us feature ke liye alag, read-optimized view bana sakte ho. Woh existing systems ko badle bina unke saath chalta hai. Purane aur naye systems ko side by side chalana aksar existing database mein complicated schema migration se aasaan hota hai. Purana system jab zaroori nahi rahe, toh use band karke uske resources wapas le lete hain.

Data store karna kaafi seedha hai agar tumhe is ki chinta na karni pade ki use query aur access kaise kiya jaayega. Schema design, indexing aur storage engines ki bahut saari complications kuch khaas query aur access patterns support karne se aati hain (Chapter 3). Isliye data likhne ke form ko padhne ke form se alag karne, aur kai alag read views allow karne se bahut flexibility milti hai. Is idea ko kabhi-kabhi command query responsibility segregation, yani CQRS, kehte hain.

Kleppmann ka kehna hai ki database design ka traditional approach ek galti par tika hai: ki data usi form mein likha jaana chahiye jis form mein use query kiya jaayega. Agar tum write-optimized event log se data ko read-optimized application state mein translate kar sakte ho, toh normalization aur denormalization (Chapter 2) wali debates kaafi had tak irrelevant ho jaati hain. Read-optimized views ko denormalize karna bilkul theek hai, kyunki translation process unhe event log ke saath consistent rakhta hai.

Chapter 1 ki Twitter ki home timelines ek aur example hain. Har timeline un logon ke recent tweets ka cache hai jinhe user follow karta hai, ek tarah ka mailbox. Yeh bahut denormalized hai, kyunki har tweet apne saare followers ki timelines mein copy hota hai. Fan-out service is duplicated state ko naye tweets aur naye follow relationships ke saath sync mein rakhti hai, aur isse duplication manageable rehta hai.

Concurrency control

Event sourcing aur change data capture ka sabse bada nuksan yeh hai ki event log ke consumers aam taur par asynchronous hote hain. User log mein write kar sakta hai, phir usse derived view se read kare, aur dekhe ki uska apna write view mein abhi aaya hi nahi. Chapter 5 mein is problem ko reading your own writes kaha tha.

Ek fix hai ki event append karte waqt hi read view bhi update kar do. Iske liye transaction chahiye, taaki dono writes ek unit ki tarah ho. Ya toh log aur view ek hi storage system mein hon, ya dono systems ke beech distributed transaction chahiye. Book ek doosra option batati hai, jo Chapter 9 mein cover hua: total order broadcast ke upar linearizable storage banana.

Doosri taraf, event log se current state nikalne se kuch concurrency control aasaan ho jaata hai. Multi-object transactions (Chapter 7) ki zyadatar zaroorat isliye padti hai ki ek user action ko kai jagah data badalna hota hai. Event sourcing mein tum event ko user action ka self-contained description bana sakte ho. Tab action ko sirf ek write chahiye, yani events ko log mein append karna, aur single write ko atomic banana aasaan hai.

Agar event log aur application state same tarah se partitioned hain, toh simple single-threaded log consumer ko writes ke liye concurrency control ki zaroorat nahi. By construction woh ek time par ek event handle karta hai, jo Chapter 7 ke actual serial execution wala hi idea hai. Log har partition ke andar events ka serial order define karke concurrency ki unpredictability hata deta hai. Agar ek event kai state partitions ko touch kare, toh zyada kaam chahiye, aur Chapter 12 mein uski baat hai.

Immutability ki limitations

Kai systems jo event sourcing use nahi karte, woh bhi immutability par depend karte hain. Alag-alag databases andar se immutable data structures ya data ke kai versions use karte hain, taaki point-in-time snapshots le sakein (Chapter 7). Git, Mercurial aur Fossil jaise version control systems bhi files ki history rakhne ke liye immutable data par depend karte hain.

Kya tum har change ki immutable history hamesha rakh sakte ho? Yeh is par depend karta hai ki data mein kitna churn hai. Kuch workloads mostly data add karte hain aur update ya delete bahut kam karte hain, aur unhe immutable rakhna aasaan hai. Doosre chhote dataset ke andar bahut saara data update aur delete karte hain. Wahan history bahut badi ho sakti hai, fragmentation problem ban sakti hai, aur system ke reliably chalne ke liye compaction aur garbage collection essential ho jaate hain.

Kabhi-kabhi administrative wajah se data delete karna padta hai, immutable system mein bhi. Privacy rules ke hisaab se user ke account close karne ke baad uski personal information delete karni pad sakti hai. Data protection law galat information hatane ko keh sakta hai. Sensitive data ka accidental leak contain karna pad sakta hai. In cases mein “deleted” event append karna kaafi nahi hai. Tum history rewrite karna chahte ho taaki data aisa lage jaise kabhi likha hi nahi gaya. Datomic is feature ko excision kehta hai, aur Fossil version control system mein milta-julta feature hai jise shunning kehte hain.

Data ko sach mein delete karna kaafi mushkil hai, kyunki copies kai jagah reh sakti hain. Storage engines, filesystems aur SSDs aksar in-place overwrite karne ke bajaye nayi location par likhte hain, aur backups aksar intentionally immutable banaye jaate hain taaki accidental deletion ya corruption na ho. Isliye deletion ka matlab data ko retrieve karna impossible banana kam, aur mushkil banana zyada hai. Kabhi-kabhi tumhe aur koshish karni padti hai, jis par Kleppmann Chapter 12 mein legislation aur self-regulation ki discussion mein wapas aate hain.

Streams ko process karna

Ab tak chapter mein humne dekha ki streams kahan se aate hain (user activity, sensors, aur database writes) aur woh kaise travel karte hain (direct messaging, message brokers, aur event logs). Ab sawal yeh hai ki stream haath mein aane ke baad tum uske saath kya kar sakte ho. Mota-mota teen options hain.

  1. Events ka data lekar kisi database, cache, search index ya similar store mein likh do, jahan baaki clients baad mein use query kar sakein. Figure 11-5 mein dikha tha ki is tarah database doosri jagah hue changes ke saath in sync rehta hai. Yeh tab sabse achha chalta hai jab us database mein likhne wala stream consumer akela client ho. Is tarah store mein likhna Chapter 10 ke batch outputs ka streaming version hai.
  2. Events ko logon tak push karo, jaise email alerts, push notifications ya live dashboard ke form mein. Yahan stream ka final consumer ek insaan hota hai.
  3. Ek ya zyada input streams ko process karke ek ya zyada output streams banao. Ek stream option 1 ya option 2 tak pahunchne se pehle aise kai stages ki pipeline se guzar sakti hai.

Chapter ka baaki hissa option 3 par focus karta hai, yani streams ko process karke doosre, derived streams banana. Jo code yeh kaam karta hai use operator ya job kehte hain. Yeh Chapter 10 ke Unix processes aur MapReduce jobs ke kaafi kareeb hai. Dataflow pattern bhi similar hai. Stream processor apne input streams ko bina badle padhta hai, aur output ko kisi doosri jagah append-only tarike se likhta hai.

Stream processors ko partition aur parallelize karne ke patterns MapReduce aur Chapter 10 ke dataflow engines se bahut milte-julte hain, isliye book unhein dobara nahi dohrati. Records ko transform aur filter karne jaise basic operations bhi bilkul waise hi kaam karte hain.

Asli idea

Batch jobs se ek bahut zaroori fark yeh hai ki stream kabhi khatam nahi hoti. Isse do cheezein badal jaati hain. Sorting ka matlab nahi rehta, isliye sort-merge joins use nahi ho sakte. Aur failure ke baad restart karna ab simple nahi rehta.

Jis dataset ka end hi nahi hai, usse sort karne ka koi matlab nahi, kyunki tumhe kabhi pata nahi chalega ki poora data dekh liya. Isliye Chapter 10 ke sort-merge joins yahan use nahi ho sakte. Fault tolerance bhi badal jaata hai. Agar batch job kuch minute chala hai aur koi task fail ho jaaye, toh use shuru se restart kar sakte hain. Lekin jo stream job saalon se chal raha hai, crash ke baad shayad shuru se restart na ho paaye. Book is baat ko chapter ke last section mein dekhti hai.

Stream processing ke use cases

Stream processing ka use bahut pehle se monitoring ke liye hota aa raha hai, jahan organization chahti hai ki kuch cheezein hone par use alert mile. Book chaar examples deti hai.

  • Fraud detection check karta hai ki credit card ka usage pattern achanak badla toh nahi, aur card chori hua lage toh use block kar deta hai.
  • Trading systems financial market ke price changes dekhte hain aur set rules ke hisaab se trades execute karte hain.
  • Manufacturing systems factory ki machines ka status watch karte hain, aur koi machine kharab ho toh jaldi wajah dhoondh lete hain.
  • Military aur intelligence systems kisi possible aggressor ki activity track karte hain aur attack ke signs dikhein toh alarm bajate hain.

In use cases ko kaafi sophisticated pattern matching aur correlation chahiye hota hai. Waqt ke saath stream processing ke doosre use cases bhi aaye. Agle kuch sections mein hum unmein se kuch ko compare karenge.

Complex event processing

Complex event processing, yani CEP, 1990s mein develop hua ek approach hai. Yeh event streams ko analyze karta hai aur un applications ke liye bana hai jo events ke particular patterns dhoondhti hain. Yeh regular expression jaisa kaam karta hai. Regular expression se tum kisi string mein characters ka pattern search karte ho. CEP mein tum aise rules likhte ho jo stream mein events ka pattern search karte hain.

CEP systems aksar ek high-level declarative query language (jaise SQL) ya graphical interface use karte hain, taaki detect karne wale event patterns describe kiye ja sakein. Queries ek processing engine ko submit hoti hain. Engine input streams consume karta hai aur matching ke liye ek internal state machine rakhta hai. Match milne par engine ek complex event emit karta hai, jisme detect hue pattern ki details hoti hain.

CEP mein queries aur data ke roles normal database se ulte hote hain. Database data ko lambe time tak store karta hai aur queries ko temporary maanta hai. Query aati hai, database matching data search karta hai, aur phir query ko bhool jaata hai. CEP engine iska ulta karta hai. Queries lambe time tak stored rehti hain, aur events un par se continuously guzarte rehte hain, aur dekhte hain ki kaun si query match karti hai.

Book ke hisaab se implementations mein Esper, IBM InfoSphere Streams, Apama, TIBCO StreamBase aur SQLstream shaamil hain. Samza jaise distributed stream processors mein bhi streams par declarative queries ke liye SQL support aa raha hai.

Stream analytics

Stream processing analytics ke liye bhi use hota hai. CEP aur stream analytics ke beech ki line thodi dhundhli hai. Mota rule yeh hai ki analytics ko events ke specific sequences dhoondhne ki parwah kam hoti hai, aur bahut saare events par aggregations aur statistics ki zyada. Typical examples yeh hain:

  • naapna ki kisi type ka event har time interval mein kitni baar hota hai;
  • kisi value ka ek period par rolling average nikalna;
  • current statistics ko pichhle time intervals se compare karna, jaise trend pakadne ke liye, ya aisi metric flag karne ke liye jo pichhle hafte ke same time ke mukable unusually high ya low ho.

Aisi statistics aam taur par fixed time intervals par compute hoti hain. Maan lo tumhe pichhle 5 minute mein kisi service ko average kitni queries per second aayi, aur usi period ka 99th percentile response time chahiye. Kuch minute par average lene se ek second se doosre second ke chhote fluctuations smooth ho jaate hain. Phir bhi traffic ke changes ki timely tasveer mil jaati hai. Jis time interval par tum aggregate karte ho use window kehte ho. Windows ki detail chapter mein aage aayegi.

Stream analytics systems kabhi-kabhi probabilistic algorithms use karte hain. Bloom filters, jo Chapter 3 mein aaye the, set membership test karte hain. HyperLogLog andaza lagata hai ki kitni distinct values hain. Kuch aur algorithms percentiles estimate karte hain (Chapter 1). Yeh approximate jawab dete hain, lekin processor mein exact methods se bahut kam memory lagti hai. Isse kuch log maan lete hain ki stream processing hamesha lossy aur inexact hoti hai. Book kehti hai ki yeh galat hai. Stream processing mein kuch bhi inherently approximate nahi hai. Probabilistic algorithms bas ek optimization hain.

Kai open source frameworks analytics ko dhyaan mein rakhkar bane hain, jaise Apache Storm, Spark Streaming, Flink, Concord, Samza aur Kafka Streams. Hosted services mein Google Cloud Dataflow aur Azure Stream Analytics hain.

Materialized views maintain karna

Change streams wale pichhle section mein dekha tha ki database changes ki stream se caches, search indexes aur data warehouses jaise derived systems up to date rakhe ja sakte hain. Yeh sab materialized views maintain karne ke special cases maane ja sakte hain. Materialized view dataset ka ek alternative view hota hai, jo is tarah store hota hai ki use jaldi query kiya ja sake. Underlying data badalne par yeh update hota rehta hai. Chapter 3 mein data cubes ke context mein materialized views aaye the.

Event sourcing bhi isi tarah kaam karta hai. Application state events ka log apply karke maintain hota hai, isliye application state bhi ek tarah ka materialized view hai.

Stream analytics se ek fark hai. Analytics ke liye aksar time window ke andar ke events dekhna kaafi hota hai. Materialized view banane ke liye aam taur par kisi bhi arbitrary period ke saare events chahiye, shayad bilkul shuru tak ke. Sirf obsolete events exception hain, jinhein log compaction hata deta hai. Matlab tumhe aisi window chahiye jo time ki shuruaat tak pichhe jaaye.

Principle mein koi bhi stream processor materialized views maintain kar sakta hai. Lekin kai analytics frameworks maan ke chalte hain ki woh limited length ki windows par kaam karte hain, isliye events ko hamesha ke liye rakhna unke design ke khilaf jaata hai. Samza aur Kafka Streams is tarah ke use ko support karte hain. Yeh Kafka ke log compaction support par bane hain.

Streams par search

CEP kai events se bane patterns dhoondhta hai. Kabhi-kabhi tumhe kuch simpler chahiye hota hai: individual events search karna jo complex criteria se match karein, jaise full-text query. Maan lo media monitoring services news articles aur broadcasts ke feeds subscribe karti hain. Woh har item mein companies, products ya interest ke topics ka zikr search karti hain. Search query pehle se likhi hoti hai, aur har news item aate hi us query se match kiya jaata hai. Real estate websites bhi aisa feature deti hain. User keh sakta hai ki jab bhi uske criteria se match karti nayi property market mein aaye, use notify kiya jaaye. Elasticsearch mein percolator naam ka feature hai jo is tarah ki stream search support karta hai.

Normal search engine pehle documents ko index karta hai aur phir index par queries chalata hai. Stream par search isse ulti hoti hai. Queries store rehti hain, aur documents un par se guzarte hain, bilkul CEP ki tarah. Sabse simple version mein har document ko har query ke against test kiya jaata hai. Jab queries bahut zyada hon toh yeh slow ho jaata hai. Ise tez karne ke liye documents ke saath queries ko bhi index kar sakte hain, aur is tarah narrow down kar sakte hain ki kaun si queries kisi document se match ho sakti hain.

Message passing aur RPC

Chapter 4 mein message-passing systems ko RPC ke alternative ke taur par describe kiya tha. In systems mein services messages bhejkar communicate karti hain, jaise actor model mein. Yeh messages aur events par based hain, phir bhi Kleppmann inhein aam taur par stream processors nahi maante. Iski teen wajah hain.

  • Actor frameworks mainly un modules ki concurrency aur distributed execution manage karne ka tarika hain jo aapas mein baat karte hain. Stream processing mainly data manage karne ka tarika hai.
  • Actors ke beech communication aksar temporary aur one-to-one hota hai. Event logs durable hote hain aur unke kai subscribers ho sakte hain.
  • Actors kisi bhi pattern mein communicate kar sakte hain, requests aur responses ke cycles bhi. Stream processors aam taur par acyclic pipelines ki tarah set up hote hain, jahan har stream kisi ek particular job ka output hoti hai aur well-defined input streams se derive hoti hai.

Phir bhi thoda overlap hai. Apache Storm mein distributed RPC naam ka feature hai. Yeh user queries ko un nodes ke set tak bhejta hai jo event streams bhi process karte hain. Queries input streams ke events ke saath mix ho jaati hain, aur results aggregate hokar user ko wapas bheje jaate hain. Actor frameworks se streams process karna bhi possible hai. Lekin kai actor frameworks guarantee nahi dete ki node crash hone par messages deliver honge. Isliye jab tak tum apna retry logic na jodo, processing fault-tolerant nahi hoti.

Time ke baare mein sochna

Stream processors ko aksar time se deal karna padta hai, khaaskar jab woh analytics ke liye use hote hain. Analytics mein aksar time windows hoti hain, jaise pichhle paanch minute ka average. Lagta hai ki iska matlab saaf hai. Par yeh hairaan karne wali had tak tricky hai.

Batch process mein tasks historical events ke bade collection par tezi se kaam karte hain. Agar data ko time ke hisaab se todna ho, toh batch job har event ke andar ka timestamp dekhta hai. Job khud kis time chal raha hai, isse farak nahi padta, kyunki us time ka events ke hone ke time se koi lena-dena nahi. Batch job ek saal ke historical events kuch minute mein padh sakta hai. Jo timeline matter karti hai woh ek saal ki history hai, kuch minute ki processing nahi. Events ke timestamps use karne se job deterministic bhi ho jaata hai. Same input par dobara chalane se same result milta hai (Chapter 10).

Kai stream processing frameworks alag raasta lete hain. Woh windows decide karne ke liye processing machine ki local system clock use karte hain. Ise processing time kehte hain. Yeh simple hai, aur tab theek hai jab event banne aur uske process hone ke beech ka delay na ke barabar ho. Lekin jab significant lag ho, yani processing event hone ke kaafi baad ho, tab yeh tarika toot jaata hai.

Event time versus processing time

Processing kai wajah se late ho sakti hai. Inmein queueing, network faults (Chapter 8), performance problems jinse message broker ya processor mein contention ho, stream consumer ka restart, aur fault se recover karte waqt ya bug fix karne ke baad past events ka reprocessing shaamil hain.

Message delays ki wajah se messages unpredictable order mein bhi aa sakte hain. Yeh book ka example hai.

Example
  1. Ek user ek web request karta hai, jise web server A handle karta hai.
  2. Phir user doosri request karta hai, jise web server B handle karta hai.
  3. Servers A aur B dono apni handle ki hui request ko describe karta ek event emit karte hain.
  4. Event B, event A se pehle message broker tak pahunch jaata hai.
  5. Isliye stream processor ko pehle event B dikhta hai aur phir event A, jabki requests ulte order mein hui thi.

Book ek analogy deti hai. Star Wars films ek order mein release hui thi: Episode IV 1977 mein, Episode V 1980 mein, aur Episode VI 1983 mein. Episodes I, II aur III baad mein aaye, 1999, 2002 aur 2005 mein. Episode VII 2015 mein aaya. Agar tum unhein release order mein dekho, toh jis order mein tum unhein process karte ho woh story ke order se match nahi karta. Episode number event timestamp jaisa hai. Jis date par tum film dekhte ho woh processing time jaisi hai. Insaan aisi jumps aasaani se sambhaal lete hain, lekin stream processing algorithms ko khaas taur par aise timing aur ordering problems handle karne ke liye likhna padta hai.

Event time ko processing time se confuse karne par bad data milta hai. Socho ek stream processor requests ka rate naap raha hai, yani har second kitni requests aayi. Agar tum processor ko redeploy karo, toh woh ek minute ke liye band rehkar wapas aane par events ka backlog process kar sakta hai. Agar tum rate processing time se naapoge, toh backlog requests mein achanak spike jaisa dikhega. Asal mein requests ka real rate steady tha. Book ka Figure 11-7 yeh artifact dikhata hai.

Kab ready hain, yeh kaise pata chalega

Event-time windows ki ek tricky problem yeh hai ki tum kabhi pakka nahi kar sakte ki ek window ke saare events aa gaye. Hamesha aur events aane baaki ho sakte hain.

Maan lo tum events ko one-minute windows mein group kar rahe ho taaki requests per minute count kar sakein. Tumne kuch events count kiye hain jinke timestamps ghante ke 37th minute mein aate hain. Time aage badh chuka hai, aur zyadatar naye events ab 38th aur 39th minute mein aa rahe hain. 37th minute ki window ko tum kab finished declare karo aur uska count output karo?

Tum timeout kar sakte ho, yani kuch der tak koi naya event na aaye toh window ko ready declare kar do. Lekin kuch events abhi bhi kisi doosri machine ke buffer mein atke ho sakte hain, network problem ki wajah se late. Isliye tumhe stragglers handle karne ka tarika chahiye, yani woh events jo window complete declare hone ke baad aate hain. Book do options deti hai.

  1. Stragglers ko ignore karo. Normal conditions mein woh shayad events ka chhota hissa hote hain. Kitne drop hue, ise metric ki tarah track karo, aur agar kaafi data drop hone lage toh alert raise karo.
  2. Correction publish karo. Window ki updated value output karo jisme stragglers shaamil hon. Ho sakta hai pichhla output retract bhi karna pade.

Kuch systems mein ek special message announce kar sakta hai ki time t se pehle ke timestamp wale koi aur messages nahi aayenge. Consumers us message se apni windows trigger kar sakte hain. Lekin agar alag machines par kai producers apne-apne minimum timestamps ke saath events banate hain, toh consumer ko har producer ko alag se track karna padta hai. Phir producers add aur remove karna zyada complicated ho jaata hai.

Aakhir tum kiski clock use kar rahe ho?

Events ko timestamps dena tab mushkil ho jaata hai jab events system mein kai jagah buffers mein ruk sakte hain. Ek mobile app lo jo server ko usage events report karta hai. App offline device par bhi use ho sakta hai. Woh events locally store kar leta hai aur connection wapas aane par bhejta hai, jo ghanton ya din baad bhi ho sakta hai. Kisi bhi consumer ko woh events bahut late stragglers jaise dikhte hain.

Ideal toh yeh hai ki timestamp woh time ho jab user ne action kiya, device ki clock ke hisaab se. Lekin jis device ko user control karta hai woh bharose ki clock nahi hai. Use galti se ya intentionally galat time par set kiya ja sakta hai (clock accuracy Chapter 8 mein cover hui hai). Server ne event kis time receive kiya, server ki clock ke hisaab se, woh zyada accurate hone ki possibility rakhta hai, kyunki server tumhare control mein hai. Lekin woh user ke asli action ke baare mein kam batata hai.

Galat device clock ko correct karne ke liye book teen timestamps log karne ka suggestion deti hai.

  1. Event kab hua, device clock ke hisaab se.
  2. Event server ko kab bheja gaya, device clock ke hisaab se.
  3. Event server ko kab mila, server clock ke hisaab se.

Teesre timestamp mein se doosra minus karo, isse device clock aur server clock ke beech ka offset estimate hota hai. Yeh maanta hai ki network delay tumhari zaroori accuracy ke mukable negligible hai. Phir us offset ko event timestamp par apply karo, jisse andaza milta hai ki event asal mein kab hua tha. Yeh bhi maanta hai ki event hone aur bheje jaane ke beech device clock ka offset nahi badla.

Author ka kehna hai ki yeh problem sirf stream processing ki nahi hai. Batch processing mein bhi time ke baare mein sochte waqt bilkul yahi issues aate hain. Bas streaming mein yeh zyada dikhte hain, kyunki wahan tumhe time guzarne ka zyada ehsaas hota hai.

Windows ke types

Ek baar pata ho ki event ka timestamp kaise decide hoga, toh agla step yeh decide karna hai ki time par windows kaise define hongi. Window aggregations ke liye use ho sakti hai, jaise uske andar ke events count karna ya values ka average lena. Book chaar common types batati hai.

  • Tumbling window. Tumbling window ki length fixed hoti hai, aur har event bilkul ek window ka hissa hota hai. 1-minute tumbling window mein 10:03:00 se 10:03:59 tak ke timestamp wale events ek window banate hain, 10:04:00 se 10:04:59 tak ke agli, aur aise hi aage. Ise banane ke liye har event ke timestamp ko nearest minute tak neeche round kar do.
  • Hopping window. Hopping window ki length bhi fixed hoti hai, lekin windows overlap kar sakti hain, jisse thodi smoothing milti hai. 1 minute ke hop size wali 5-minute window mein 10:03:00 se 10:07:59 tak ke events hote hain. Agli window 10:04:00 se 10:08:59 cover karti hai, aur aise hi aage. Ise banane ke liye pehle 1-minute tumbling windows compute karo, phir kai adjacent windows ko combine kar do.
  • Sliding window. Sliding window mein woh saare events hote hain jo ek-doosre se kisi interval ke andar hue hon. 5-minute sliding window 10:03:39 aur 10:08:12 ke events ko cover karegi, kyunki woh 5 minute se kam door hain. Tumbling aur hopping 5-minute windows in do events ko saath nahi rakhengi, kyunki unki boundaries fixed hoti hain. Sliding window banane ke liye time ke hisaab se sorted events ka buffer rakho aur purane events expire hote hi hata do.
  • Session window. Session window ki koi fixed length nahi hoti. Yeh ek hi user ke woh saare events group karti hai jo time mein paas-paas hue hon. Window tab khatam hoti hai jab user kuch der inactive rahe, jaise 30 minute tak koi event na aaye. Website analytics mein sessionization ki zaroorat aam hai (GROUP BY ki baat Chapter 10 mein hui thi).
Trade-offs
WindowLengthOverlapKis ke liye achhi
TumblingFixedNahi. Har event ek hi window mein.Simple per-minute ya per-hour counts.
HoppingFixedHaan, windows hop size ke hisaab se overlap karti hain.Smooth, regularly update hone wale averages.
SlidingEvents ke beech ke gap se set hoti haiHaan, har event ke liye ek windowAise events ke pairs jo paas-paas hain, chahe unka clock time kuch bhi ho.
SessionQuiet gap ke baad khatam hoti haiLagu nahiEk user ki activity ko visits mein group karna.
Try karo

10:03:39 aur 10:08:12 wale do example events lo. Kaun se window types inhein ek hi window mein rakhenge? Ab doosre event ko 10:08:45 kar do. Kya sliding window ke liye tumhara jawab badlega, aur kyun?

Stream joins

Chapter 10 mein dekha tha ki batch jobs datasets ko key par kaise join karte hain, aur yeh joins data pipelines ka kitna zaroori hissa hain. Stream processing data pipelines ko unbounded datasets ki continuous, incremental processing bana deti hai. Isliye streams par joins ki bilkul wahi zaroorat hai.

Lekin stream par naye events kisi bhi time aa sakte hain, isliye stream joins batch joins se zyada mushkil hain. Kleppmann teen types ke join alag karte hain: stream-stream joins, stream-table joins aur table-table joins. Neeche har ek ko example se samjhaya hai.

Stream-stream join (window join)

Maan lo tumhari website par search feature hai, aur tum dekhna chahte ho ki log kin URLs ko search kar rahe hain, unke recent trends kya hain. Jab bhi koi query type karta hai, tum ek event log karte ho jisme query aur dikhaye gaye results hote hain. Jab bhi koi result par click karta hai, tum doosra event log karte ho jo click record karta hai. Results ke har URL ka click-through rate nikalne ke liye tumhe search events aur click events ko saath laana padega. Dono ek shared session ID se linked hain. Advertising systems mein bhi aise hi analyses hote hain.

Click shayad kabhi aaye hi na, agar user search chhod de. Aaye bhi toh search aur click ke beech ka gap bahut alag-alag ho sakta hai. Aksar yeh kuch seconds hota hai, lekin din ya hafte bhi ho sakte hain, agar koi search chalaye, tab bhool jaaye, aur baad mein kisi result par click kare. Network delays ki wajah se click event search event se pehle bhi pahunch sakta hai. Isliye tum join ke liye ek window choose karte ho. Jaise, click ko search ke saath join karo agar dono mein zyada se zyada ek ghante ka fark ho.

Join chhodkar search ki details seedhe click event mein daal dena tempting lagta hai. Lekin yeh equivalent nahi hai. Isse tumhe sirf un searches ka pata chalega jinmein user ne result click kiya. Woh searches miss ho jaayengi jinmein usne kuch click nahi kiya. Search quality naapne ke liye accurate click-through rates chahiye, aur uske liye dono tarah ke events chahiye.

Yeh join chalane ke liye stream processor ko kuch state rakhni padti hai. Woh pichhle ek ghante ke saare events rakhta hai, session ID se indexed. Jab koi search ya click event aata hai, processor use matching index mein add karta hai. Saath hi doosre index mein check karta hai ki same session ka koi event pehle aa chuka hai ya nahi. Match mil jaaye toh woh ek event emit karta hai jo batata hai ki kaun sa search result click hua. Agar koi search event bina matching click ke window se expire ho jaaye, toh woh ek event emit karta hai jo batata hai ki kisi result par click nahi hua.

Stream-table join (stream enrichment)

Chapter 10 mein ek batch job tha jo user activity events ko user profiles ke database se join karta tha. Activity events ko stream maanna aur wahi join stream processor mein continuously chalana natural hai. Input activity events ki stream hai, har event mein ek user ID. Output ek stream hai jisme har user ID ko profile information ke saath expand kar diya gaya hai. Ise database ki information se activity events ko enrich karna kehte hain.

Har event ke liye processor database mein user ID look up karta hai aur profile ko event mein add kar deta hai. Lookup ke liye remote database ko query kiya ja sakta hai. Lekin Chapter 10 mein bataya tha ki remote queries slow hoti hain aur database overload hone ka risk rehta hai. Doosra approach yeh hai ki database ki ek copy stream processor mein load kar lo, taaki use locally query kiya ja sake, bina network round trip ke. Yeh Chapter 10 ke hash joins se bahut milta hai. Local copy agar chhoti ho toh in-memory hash table ho sakti hai, ya local disk par ek index.

Batch job database ka point-in-time snapshot padhta hai. Stream processor lambe time tak chalta hai, aur chalte waqt database badalne ki poori possibility hai. Isliye local copy ko up to date rakhna padta hai. Change data capture isse solve karta hai. Stream processor user profile database ke changelog ko subscribe karta hai, activity events ki stream ke saath. Jab koi profile create ya change hoti hai, processor apni local copy update kar deta hai. Result do streams ke beech ka join hai: activity events aur profile updates.

Stream-table join, stream-stream join se kaafi milta-julta hai. Main fark window ka hai. Table ke changelog ke liye join aisi window use karta hai jo time ki shuruaat tak pichhe jaati hai, aur record ke naye versions purane versions ko overwrite kar dete hain. Stream input ke liye join mein shayad koi window rakhi hi nahi jaati.

Table-table join (materialized view maintenance)

Chapter 1 mein Twitter ki home timelines ki baat hui thi. Jab user apni home timeline kholta hai, toh jin logon ko woh follow karta hai un sabko look up karna, unke recent tweets dhoondhna aur merge karna bahut mehnga padta hai. Isliye system ek timeline cache rakhta hai, yani har user ka ek inbox jisme tweets bheje jaate hi likh diye jaate hain. Phir timeline padhne ke liye bas ek lookup lagta hai. Is cache ko up to date rakhne ke liye chaar tarah ki event processing chahiye.

  1. Jab user u naya tweet bhejta hai, toh woh tweet u ko follow karne wale har user ki timeline mein add ho jaata hai.
  2. Jab koi user tweet delete karta hai, toh woh har user ki timeline se hat jaata hai.
  3. Jab user u1, user u2 ko follow karna shuru karta hai, toh u2 ke recent tweets u1 ki timeline mein add ho jaate hain.
  4. Jab user u1, user u2 ko unfollow karta hai, toh u2 ke tweets u1 ki timeline se hat jaate hain.

Yeh stream processor mein karne ke liye tumhe tweets (bhejna aur delete karna) aur follow relationships (follow aur unfollow karna) ke events ki streams chahiye. Processor ko har user ke followers ka database bhi rakhna padta hai, taaki naya tweet aane par use pata ho ki kaun si timelines update karni hain.

Ise dekhne ka ek aur tarika yeh hai ki stream processor ek aisi query ka materialized view maintain karta hai jo do tables, tweets aur follows, ko join karti hai. Book ise kuch aise likhti hai.

SELECT follows.follower_id AS timeline_id,
  array_agg(tweets.* ORDER BY tweets.timestamp DESC)
FROM tweets
JOIN follows ON follows.followee_id = tweets.sender_id
GROUP BY follows.follower_id

Do streams ka join seedha us query mein do tables ke join se match karta hai. Timelines asal mein query ke result ka cache hain, aur underlying tables badalne par har baar update hoti hain. Ek footnote mein Kleppmann batate hain ki yeh calculus ke product rule se match karta hai. Joined result mein change kisi bhi ek input ke change se aata hai, jo doosre input ki current state se join hota hai. Isliye koi bhi naya tweet current followers se join hota hai, aur followers mein koi bhi change current tweets se join hota hai.

Joins ki time-dependence

Teeno types ke join mein bahut kuch common hai. Har ek mein stream processor ko ek join input ke basis par kuch state rakhni padti hai, jaise search aur click events, user profiles ya follower lists. Phir doosre input se messages aane par woh us state ko query karta hai.

Jo events yeh state banate hain unka order matter karta hai. Isse farak padta hai ki tum pehle kisi ko follow karte ho aur phir unfollow, ya ulta. Partitioned log mein ek partition ke andar events ka order bana rehta hai. Lekin alag-alag streams ya partitions ke beech aam taur par koi ordering guarantee nahi hoti.

Isse ek sawal uthta hai. Agar alag streams ke events lagbhag ek hi time par hue hon, toh unhein kis order mein process kiya jaayega? Stream-table join mein maan lo koi user apni profile update karta hai. Kaun se activity events purani profile ke saath join honge, kyunki woh update se pehle process hue the, aur kaun se nayi profile ke saath? Doosre words mein: agar state time ke saath badalti hai aur tum us state ke saath join karte ho, toh join ke liye tum kaun sa point in time use karte ho?

Yeh time dependence kai jagah dikhti hai. Maan lo tum products bechte ho. Tumhe har invoice par sahi tax rate lagana hoga. Woh rate country ya state, product ke type aur sale ki date par depend karta hai, kyunki tax rates samay-samay par badalte rehte hain. Jab tum sales ko tax rates ki table se join karte ho, toh aam taur par tum sale ke time par lagu rate chahte ho. Agar tum historical data reprocess kar rahe ho, toh woh current rate se alag ho sakta hai.

Agar streams ke beech events ka order fixed nahi hai, toh join nondeterministic ho jaata hai. Matlab tum same input par wahi job dobara chalakar zaroori nahi ki same result paao, kyunki doosri baar events alag tarah se interleave ho sakte ho.

Data warehouses mein ise slowly changing dimension kehte hain. Ise aksar aise handle kiya jaata hai ki joined record ke har version ko ek unique identifier de diya jaata hai. Tax rate jab bhi badalta hai, use naya identifier milta hai, aur har invoice sale ke time lagu rate ka identifier record karta hai. Isse join deterministic ho jaata hai. Lekin iski ek cost hai: records ka har version rakhna padta hai, isliye log compaction possible nahi hota.

Trade-offs
Join typeInputsKya state rakhi jaati haiTypical example
Stream-stream (window join)Do activity streamsTime window ke andar ke events, key se indexedEk ghante ke andar same session ki searches ko clicks se match karna
Stream-table (enrichment)Ek activity stream aur ek table ka changelogTable ki local copy, jo uske changelog se current rakhi jaati haiHar activity event mein user profile fields jodna
Table-table (view maintenance)Do changelogsDono tables, taaki har change ko doosri side ki latest state se join kiya ja sakeHome timeline caches ko up to date rakhna
Try karo

Tum sales events ko tax rates ke saath join kar rahe ho. Ek tax rate badal jaata hai jab pichhle mahine ki kuch sales abhi stream mein hain. Join mein sale date par lagu rate use karna chahiye ya current rate? Tumhe kya store karna padega taaki reprocessing har baar same jawab de?

Fault Tolerance

Chapter ke aakhri hisse mein sawaal yeh hai ki stream processors faults ko kaise tolerate karte hain. Chapter 10 mein dekha tha ki batch frameworks faults aasaani se handle kar lete hain. MapReduce job ka koi task fail ho jaaye, toh use bas doosri machine par dobara start kar do, aur failed task ka output discard ho jaata hai. Yeh transparent retry isliye chalta hai kyunki input files immutable hoti hain, har task apna output alag file mein likhta hai, aur output tabhi visible hota hai jab task successfully complete ho jaaye.

Isliye batch job ka output waisa hi rehta hai jaise kuch galat hua hi nahi, chahe kuch tasks fail hue ho. Aisa lagta hai ki har input record ek hi baar process hua. Koi record skip nahi hota, aur visible result mein koi record do baar process nahi hota. Restart hue tasks shayad kuch records ek se zyada baar process karein, lekin visible effect aisa hota hai jaise har record ek hi baar process hua. Book ise exactly-once semantics kehti hai, aur saath mein yeh bhi bataati hai ki effectively-once zyada sahi naam hota.

Stream processing mein bhi yahi problem aati hai, lekin use handle karna itna seedha nahi hai. Task ke khatam hone tak wait karke output visible nahi kar sakte, kyunki stream kabhi khatam hi nahi hoti. Wait karna koi option nahi hai.

Microbatching aur checkpointing

Ek solution yeh hai ki stream ko chhote blocks mein kaat do, aur har block ko ek miniature batch job ki tarah treat karo. Ise microbatching kehte hain, aur Spark Streaming yahi use karta hai. Batch size aam taur par lagbhag ek second hota hai. Yeh ek performance compromise hai. Batches chhote hon toh scheduling aur coordination ka overhead badhta hai. Batches bade hon toh stream processor ke results visible hone mein zyada delay lagta hai.

Microbatching se tumhe batch size ke barabar ek tumbling window bhi mil jaati hai, jo event timestamps ki jagah processing time se window hoti hai. Jin jobs ko bade windows chahiye, unhe state ko ek microbatch se agle microbatch tak explicitly carry karna padta hai.

Apache Flink mein ek variant use hota hai, jisme regular intervals par state ke rolling checkpoints liye jaate hain aur durable storage mein likh diye jaate hain. Agar koi stream operator crash ho jaaye, toh woh apne sabse recent checkpoint se restart hota hai. Us checkpoint aur crash ke beech jo output bana tha, woh discard kar diya jaata hai. Checkpoints barriers se trigger hote hain. Barriers aise markers hain jo message stream mein se guzarte hain, bilkul microbatches ki boundaries jaise. Lekin checkpoints par koi particular window size force nahi hota.

Stream processing framework ke andar microbatching aur checkpointing batch processing jaisi hi exactly-once semantics dete hain. Lekin jaise hi output stream processor se bahar jaata hai, framework use discard nahi kar sakta. Jaise database mein write karna, external broker ko messages bhejna, ya emails bhejna. Failed task restart ho, toh woh external side effect do baar ho jaata hai. Sirf microbatching ya checkpointing se yeh nahi rukta.

Atomic commit dobara

Fault hone par bhi exactly-once processing ka appearance dene ke liye, ek event ko process karne ke saare outputs aur side effects tabhi effect mein aane chahiye jab processing succeed ho. Isme yeh sab aate hain: downstream operators ya external messaging systems ko bheje gaye messages (email aur push notifications bhi), database writes, operator state ke changes, aur input messages ka acknowledgment. Log-based broker mein aakhri cheez ka matlab hai consumer offset ko aage badhana.

Yeh sab ya toh saath mein hone chahiye, ya koi bhi nahi. Inka aapas mein out of step hona theek nahi. Yeh tumhe jaana-pehchaana lagega, kyunki Chapter 9 mein exactly-once message processing ke naam par yahi idea distributed transactions aur two-phase commit ke context mein discuss hua tha.

Chapter 9 mein XA jaise traditional distributed transaction implementations ki problems bhi batayi thi. Lekin zyada restricted environments mein atomic commit facility efficiently implement ho sakti hai. Google Cloud Dataflow aur VoltDB aisa karte hain, aur Apache Kafka mein bhi aise features add karne ke plans hain. XA ke ulat, yeh implementations alag-alag technologies ke beech transactions dene ki koshish nahi karte. Woh transactions ko stream processing framework ke andar hi rakhte hain, aur state changes aur messaging dono wahin manage karte hain. Transaction protocol ka cost kam karne ke liye ek hi transaction mein kai input messages process kiye ja sakte hain.

Idempotence

Goal yeh hai ki kisi bhi failed task ka partial output discard ho jaaye, taaki use safely retry kiya ja sake aur effect do baar na ho. Distributed transactions us goal tak pahunchne ka ek tarika hain. Doosra tarika hai idempotence par rely karna.

Idempotent operation woh hai jise tum kai baar kar sakte ho, aur effect waisa hi rehta hai jaise ek hi baar kiya ho. Key-value store mein kisi key ko ek fixed value par set karna idempotent hai. Value dobara likhne se bas wahi value overwrite ho jaati hai. Counter increment karna idempotent nahi hai, kyunki dobara karne par ek aur add ho jaata hai.

Jo operation naturally idempotent nahi hota, use bhi thoda extra metadata laga kar aksar idempotent banaya ja sakta hai. Kafka se messages consume karte waqt har message ka ek persistent, hamesha badhne wala offset hota hai. External database mein value likhte waqt, tum value ke saath us message ka offset bhi store kar sakte ho jisne last write kiya tha. Phir tum pata laga sakte ho ki update pehle hi apply ho chuka hai ya nahi, aur ho chuka ho toh use skip kar sakte ho.

Example

Book is idea ko general terms mein batati hai. Yeh check kaise kaam kar sakta hai, uska ek tarika yahan hai.

  1. Offset 42 ka ek message aata hai aur external database mein ek value update karta hai. Database value ke saath number 42 bhi store kar leta hai.
  2. Consumer crash ho jaata hai, aur restart ke baad broker offset 42 ka message dobara deliver karta hai.
  3. Consumer stored number padhta hai. Woh pehle se 42 hai, matlab update pehle apply ho chuka hai, isliye consumer use skip kar deta hai.

Storm ke Trident ka state handling bhi isi tarah ke idea par based hai. Idempotence par rely karne ke saath kuch assumptions aate hain. Failed task restart ho toh wahi messages wahi order mein replay hone chahiye, jo log-based broker karta hai. Processing deterministic honi chahiye. Aur koi doosra node usi value ko usi waqt update na kare. Ek processing node se doosre par failover karte waqt fencing ki zaroorat pad sakti hai, taaki jo node dead maana ja raha hai lekin actually zinda hai, woh beech mein interfere na kare (Chapter 8 mein leader aur lock ke saath yeh cover hua hai). In conditions ke baad bhi, idempotent operations sirf thode se overhead ke saath exactly-once semantics paane ka effective tarika ho sakte hain.

Failure ke baad state rebuild karna

Jo bhi stream process state rakhta hai, use failure ke baad woh state recover karna aana chahiye. Isme windowed aggregations aate hain, jaise counters, averages aur histograms, aur joins ke liye use hone wale tables aur indexes bhi.

Ek option yeh hai ki state ko remote datastore mein rakho aur wahin replicate karo. Lekin har message ke liye remote database query karna slow ho sakta hai, jaisa stream-table join section mein discuss hua tha. Doosra option yeh hai ki state ko stream processor ke local rakho, aur use periodically replicate karo. Processor failure se recover kare, toh naya task replicated state padhta hai aur bina data khoye aage badh jaata hai.

Alag-alag systems yeh alag tarike se karte hain. Flink periodically operator state ke snapshots leta hai aur unhe HDFS jaise durable storage mein likhta hai. Samza aur Kafka Streams state changes ko log compaction wale ek dedicated Kafka topic mein bhej kar replicate karte hain, kaafi had tak change data capture jaise. VoltDB state ko aise replicate karta hai ki har input message ko kai nodes par redundantly process karta hai, jaisa Chapter 7 ke actual serial execution wale section mein bataya gaya hai.

Kabhi-kabhi state ko replicate karne ki zaroorat hi nahi hoti, kyunki use input streams se rebuild kiya ja sakta hai. Agar state ek chhote window par aggregations ki hai, toh us window ke input events ko replay karna kaafi fast ho sakta hai. Agar state kisi database ki local copy hai jo change data capture se up to date rakhi gayi hai, toh us copy ko log-compacted change stream se rebuild kiya ja sakta hai.

Yeh saare trade-offs is par depend karte hain ki underlying infrastructure kitna fast hai. Kuch systems mein network delay disk access time se kam hota hai, aur network bandwidth disk bandwidth ke comparable hoti hai. Koi ek universally ideal trade-off nahi hai. Storage aur networking technology badalne par local versus remote state ke fayde bhi badal sakte hain.

Trade-offs
ApproachKaise kaam karta haiCosts
MicrobatchingChhote blocks, lagbhag ek second ke, mini batch jobs ki tarah process hote hainBatches chhote hon toh scheduling overhead. Batches bade hon toh latency. Bade windows ke liye batches ke beech state carry karni padti hai.
CheckpointingState ke periodic snapshots, barriers se trigger hote hain, crash ke baad restore hote hainCheckpoints ko durable storage mein likhna. Aakhri checkpoint ke baad ka output discard hota hai aur dobara banta hai, aur external side effects ke liye phir bhi care chahiye.
Atomic commitOutputs, state changes aur offsets sab saath mein effect mein aate hain, ya bilkul nahiTransaction overhead, jo ek transaction mein kai input messages batch karke kam kiya ja sakta hai. Ek hi framework ke andar sabse behtar chalta hai.
Idempotent writesAise writes jo safely repeat ho sakte hain, aksar input offset ko value ke saath store karkeDeterministic processing, replay ho sakne wala input order, aur ek hi value par koi concurrent writer na hona zaroori hai.
Rule of thumb

Koi bhi mechanism free nahi hai. Wahi chuno jo tumhare system mein repeated effects ke cost se match kare. Jahan effects stream processor se bahar jaate hain, wahan aam taur par idempotent writes ya careful external commits chahiye, kyunki framework unhe undo nahi kar sakta.

Summary

Short mein
  • Streams unbounded hoti hain. Batch jobs endless data ko fixed chunks mein kaat deti hain, jisse results late aate hain. Stream processing har event ko tabhi handle karti hai jab woh hota hai. Stream woh data hai jo waqt ke saath thoda-thoda karke available hota hai.
  • Events aur transport. Event kisi hui cheez ka chhota, immutable record hota hai, aam taur par timestamp ke saath. Producers events bhejte hain, aur consumers unhe padhte hain. Messaging systems messages drop, buffer ya backpressure kar sakte hain, aur disk par likhe ya replicate kiye bina crash par messages kho sakte hain.
  • Do broker styles. AMQP aur JMS-style brokers single messages consumers ko assign karte hain, jo har message acknowledge karte hain. Acknowledged messages delete ho jaate hain, jo asynchronous task queues ke liye sahi hai. Log-based broker ek partition ke saare messages ek consumer ko assign karta hai, unhe order mein rakhta hai, aur consumers ko offsets se apni position track karne deta hai. Woh messages disk par rakhta hai, isliye consumers peeche jaakar purane messages dobara padh sakte hain. Parallelism partitions se aati hai.
  • Databases as streams. Database mein hue changes ko stream ki tarah capture kiya ja sakta hai, ya toh implicitly change data capture se, ya explicitly event sourcing se. Log compaction se stream database contents ki poori copy rakh sakti hai. Search indexes, caches aur analytics systems jaise derived systems ko change log consume karke current rakha ja sakta hai. Log ki shuruaat se start karke naye views build kiye ja sakte hain.
  • State aur replay. State ko stream ki tarah rakhna aur messages replay karna stream joins aur fault tolerance ki buniyaad hai. Stream processing mein complex event processing (event patterns dhundhna), stream analytics (windowed aggregations), aur materialized views (derived data ko up to date rakhna) aate hain.
  • Time mushkil hai. Stream processors ko processing time aur event timestamps alag rakhne padte hain. Window band hone ke baad aane wale stragglers ko ignore karke count kiya ja sakta hai, ya corrections se handle kiya ja sakta hai. Device clocks galat ho sakti hain, isliye book suggest karti hai ki send aur receive times log karke offset estimate karein.
  • Teen joins. Stream-stream joins ek time window ke andar related events match karte hain. Stream-table joins event stream ko table ki locally rakhi copy se enrich karte hain. Table-table joins do changing tables ke join ka materialized view maintain karte hain. Har join events ke order par depend karta hai, aur jab woh order fixed nahi hota, toh rerun par join alag results de sakta hai.
  • Fault tolerance. Stream processors ko wahi exactly-once effect chahiye jo batch jobs ko failed output discard karne se milta hai. Microbatching, checkpointing, atomic commits aur idempotent writes sab alag-alag tarike se yeh achieve karte hain. External side effects sabse mushkil hissa hain, kyunki framework woh cheez discard nahi kar sakta jo already usse bahar ja chuki hai.

Chapter ke end mein lagbhag 100 references hain, papers, blog posts aur talks ke, jo uske claims ko support karte hain. Yeh retelling woh list reproduce nahi karti. Kleppmann ke hisaab se, jo event kai state partitions ko touch karta hai, usme zyada kaam lagta hai, aur woh yeh topic Chapter 12 par chhod dete hain.

Check yourself
